Water mineralization is primarily controlled by water–sediment interactions, including silicate weathering, carbonate dissolution, and cation exchange. In contrast, DOM exhibits systematic variations related to source, degree of processing, and residence time. Groundwater contains moderately processed and variably humified DOM, reflecting transport within the aquifer under heterogeneous residence times, whereas river water is characterized by fresher, biologically influenced DOM associated with rapid renewal. Lagoon waters show highly humified and refractory DOM consistent with longer residence times and discharge conditions. Multivariate statistical analysis (PCA and HCA) reveals coherent patterns linking hydrochemical evolution and DOM composition, allowing differentiation of recharge, groundwater flow, and discharge sectors within the system. These results demonstrate that DOM provides complementary information to hydrochemistry and acts as a sensitive indicator of biogeochemical processing along flow paths in lowland environments.

title: Resolving barium matrix interferences in rare earth element analysis of seep barites: Implications for europium anomalies and fluid sources
description: Publication date: September 2026 Source: Applied Geochemistry, Volume 207 Author(s): Tongtong Bai, Xudong Wang, Lanlan Zhang, Zhaoyang Wang, Zice Jia, Dong Feng
abstract: Barite is an important archive for tracing fluid-rock interactions in marine systems. However, accurate determination of rare earth elements (REEs) in barite by ICP-MS is strongly hindered by polyatomic ion interferences derived from high barium (Ba) matrix, particularly affecting europium (Eu) measurements. This analytical limitation has restricted the application of REE geochemistry in studies of barites from seeps (hereafter seep barites). Here we investigate barite-carbonate pairs from seeps in the Gulf of Mexico and develop a robust analytical protocol for reliable REE determination. The procedure integrates (1) selective removal of carbonate phases by mild acetic acid leaching, (2) complete digestion of the purified barite fraction using a mixed HNO3–HF–HClO4 acid system, and (3) efficient separation of Ba from REEs using DGA resin chromatography prior to ICP-MS analysis. Comparison of REE data before and after Ba removal demonstrates that extremely positive Eu anomalies observed in untreated samples (Eu/Eu∗ up to 122) may result from BaO+/BaOH+ interferences, highlighting the importance of careful matrix separation for reliable Eu determination. After matrix separation, the barite samples display moderate positive Eu anomalies (Eu/Eu∗ = 1.25–3.85), consistent negative Ce anomalies, and heavy REE-enriched patterns. These corrected REE signatures indicate precipitation from pore fluids interacting with surrounding sediments under suboxic to oxic conditions, rather than from high temperature hydrothermal fluids. Our results suggest that some previously reported extreme Eu anomalies in barite, particularly where Ba removal or interference correction was not documented, may warrant careful re-evaluation as potential analytical artifacts, and emphasize the necessity of matrix separation for reliable REE analysis in Ba-rich minerals.

title: Hydrochar-Amended bioreactors for passive treatment of acid mine drainage
description: Publication date: September 2026 Source: Applied Geochemistry, Volume 207 Author(s): Aliching Marma, Natalie Kruse Daniels, Nigel Daniels
abstract: This study was based on a batch bioreactor experiment to investigate the effectiveness of using hydrochar as an amendment to promote the growth of sulfate-reducing bacteria (SRB) in acid mine drainage (AMD) treatment, with a primary focus on Copper (Cu), Zinc (Zn) and Cadmium (Cd) removal. This study evaluated the effect of hydrochar amendment in reducing bioreactors utilizing a mixture of organic substrates such as cow manure, maple woodchips, and cornflour acquired from a local granary, blended with hydrochar in triplicate, varying the amount of hydrochar: 0%, 5%, 10%, and 20% of the total volume in the bioreactors. Bioreactors were operated for 98 days, and water quality parameters (pH, ORP, sulfate, total sulfur, metal concentration, COD) were analyzed periodically to determine the effect of variation in bioreactor substrate. Additionally, 16S rRNA sequencing was used to determine the presence of SRB in the bioreactors at the end of the tests. The results suggested that bioreactors without hydrochar content performed better in raising pH and removing metals, likely as metal sulfides, with removal percentages of Cu (89–100%), Zn (97–100%), Cd (100%), and sulfate (50–100%), following the removal trend of Cd > Zn > Cu. Statistical analysis results demonstrated no significant influence of hydrochar on metal removal (p > 0.05), but time had a significant effect (p < 0.05), indicating that removal effectiveness improved with time regardless of hydrochar quantity. The presence of SRB was confirmed in all bioreactors, although their relative abundance varied across treatments.

title: Can river chemistry in a karst region under human influences be used for catchment rock weathering estimation?
description: Publication date: September 2026 Source: Applied Geochemistry, Volume 207 Author(s): Yan Liu, Y. Jun Xu, Xingxing Cao, Guangxi Long, Pan Wu, Zhangxing Liu
abstract: River chemistry is commonly used to estimate the weathering-induced carbon sink from rocks. However, the reliability of this approach in urbanized and agricultural watersheds remains unclear, particularly within fragile karst systems. This study examines the spatiotemporal variations in water chemistry of karst rivers across three catchments with different land use/land cover types in southwestern China. Our results reveal that rivers draining urban and agricultural catchments exhibit higher ionic loads of K+, Na+, and Cl− coupled with perturbed dissolved inorganic carbon dynamics, underscoring the influence of human activities on fluvial carbon fluxes. Especially, wastewater inputs substantially increase the concentrations of major ions (e.g., Na+, Cl−, NO3 −) and reduce ionic ratios such as Ca2+/Na+, Mg2+/Na+, and HCO3 −/Na+, shifting the river chemical signatures toward silicate weathering end-members, despite negligible actual silicate contribution, and the effect is modulated by rainfall. Such anthropogenic interference can bias assessments of natural weathering end-members and carbon source apportionment. Furthermore, nitrification in wastewater from urban and agricultural activities generates exogenous acids that participate in carbonate rock dissolution. Coupled with deviations in carbon source allocation, these processes affect the assessment of the rock weathering carbon sink. These findings highlight the need to account for anthropogenic inputs when evaluating karst carbon sink in urban and agricultural watersheds.

title: Microscopic and spectroscopic insights into uranium speciation and mobilization pathways associated with carnotite weathering in sediments
description: Publication date: September 2026 Source: Applied Geochemistry, Volume 207 Author(s): Martina Wiejski-López, Gonzalo L. Bia, Eduardo D. Wannaz, Laura Borgnino
abstract: The speciation and mobility of uranium (U) in sediments are influenced by biogeochemical factors such as redox conditions, microbial activity, and the presence of organic matter (OM) and mineral phases. This study investigates the mechanisms controlling U behavior in sediments from the Punilla Valley (Córdoba, Argentina), using an integrated suite of analytical techniques including pXRF, XRD, SEM-EDS, XPS, and XAS. Field observations, together with geochemical and mineralogical analyses, indicate that U–V mineralization (i.e., carnotite) is heterogeneously distributed within reddish pelitic sediments and occurs as coatings on carbonates, micas, and plant roots. Grain-size and compositional data show U enrichment in fine sediment fractions, reflecting remobilization and secondary concentration under supergene conditions. Uranium redistribution appears to occur through the dissolution of carnotite, followed by interactions with plant roots and authigenic carbonates, as well as partial reduction to U(IV) mediated by Fe-bearing micas and dissolved organic matter. Synchrotron-based XAS analyses indicate that U(VI) is associated with calcite, whereas both U(IV) and U(VI) are associated with Fe-bearing micas, organic matter, and plant roots. These results demonstrate active U mobilization from carnotite, likely due to meteoric water infiltration, and highlight the important role of inorganic and organic sediment components as secondary sinks controlling U dynamics in sedimentary basins.

title: Crushed fines from basic rocks of the Serra Geral Group as the sole substrate for assessing bioweathering and nutrient release in elephant grass cultivation ( Cenchrus purpureus )
description: Publication date: September 2026 Source: Applied Geochemistry, Volume 207 Author(s): Simone Zwirtes, Cassiana R.L. Michelin, Carlos Augusto Sommer, Andrea Sander, Carlos Augusto Posser Silveira
abstract: Tropical agriculture, generally developed on acid and leached soils, is highly dependent on soluble synthetic fertilizers (SSF), highlighting the need for local, economically viable, and more sustainable alternatives. Although intensive agriculture has increased global productivity through the use of these inputs, inadequate replacement of secondary nutrients and micronutrients has contributed to the progressive depletion of soil nutrients. In this context, agrogeology, particularly through the use of silicate agrominerals (SiA), emerges as a promising approach to assist developing countries in reducing their dependence on imported SSF by promoting the use of regional geological resources, such as crusher fines (CF) generated in the aggregate production chain for civil construction. This study evaluated nutrient release and plant uptake from CF derived from basic rocks of the Serra Geral Group (basalt and diabase), using an agronomic trial in which CF were used as the sole substrate, without soil addition. Elephant grass (cultivar BRS Kurumi) was grown with and without organic matter (OM) over 182 days in a greenhouse experiment arranged in a 2 × 2 factorial design, in addition to a control treatment.Reductions in Ca, Mg, K, and Si contents were observed in CF from plant treatments, more pronounced in the presence of OM, and were accompanied by substantial increases in nutrient uptake by elephant grass (up to 6.5-fold for basalt and 6-fold for diabase with OM) and in shoot dry matter (5.1 to 5.8-fold). The higher proportion of fine fractions in basalt CF favored nutrient release compared to diabase.The results indicate that bioweathering, driven by plant–OM interactions, intensified mineral dissolution and short-term release of K, Ca, Mg, Fe, and Si over months, supporting the use of CF from the studied lithologies as silicate agrominerals. The integration of SiA, plants, and OM increases biological activity, intensifies mineral dissolution in CF, and enhances agronomic efficiency, representing a viable strategy to reduce dependence on SSF in tropical agricultural systems.

title: Glucose promotes iron bi-directional redox transformation mediated by a single strain Comamonas sp. HJ-2
description: Publication date: September 2026 Source: Applied Geochemistry, Volume 207 Author(s): Rong Peng, Rui Yang, Yuhang Liang, Haichuan Sun, Hui Liu
abstract: In anaerobic underground environments, the iron redox cycle is fundamentally driven by microbial activities, wherein the metabolic capacity of individual strains plays a pivotal role. This study investigated the regulatory mechanisms of three carbon sources — acetate, glucose, and lactate — on the iron redox cycle mediated by Comamonas sp. HJ-2 under neutral pH anaerobic conditions in Fe(III)–Fe(II) coexisting and Fe(III)-free systems. The results demonstrated that glucose enhanced Fe(II) bio-oxidation and Fe(III) bio-reduction by promoting energy metabolism. Glucose promoted sustained FMN accumulation, which is consistent with a potential contribution of the glycolysis-pentose phosphate pathway-riboflavin synthesis axis, which accumulated to a final concentration of approximately 0.40 μM. The accumulated FMN may function as an electron shuttle and thereby contribute to Fe(III) reduction. Mineralogical analyses further showed system-dependent effects of glucose. In ferrihydrite-containing systems, glucose inhibited the transformation of ferrihydrite toward more crystalline iron phases, whereas in ferrihydrite-free systems it shifted the product distribution toward a higher proportion of ferrihydrite and a lower proportion of lepidocrocite. Glucose also increased the content of surface-bound Fe(II) on minerals. In conclusion, glucose emerged as the most effective carbon source for optimizing the HJ-2-driven iron redox coupling process, likely due to its association with enhanced energy metabolism, FMN accumulation, and altered mineral phase transformation. This study elucidates the carbon source-dependent mechanisms governing microbial iron cycling in anaerobic environments and highlights the critical role of carbon source selection in enhancing iron biotransformation efficiency.

title: Fluid inclusion effects on boron isotope fractionation during halite crystallization
description: Publication date: September 2026 Source: Applied Geochemistry, Volume 207 Author(s): Xuehai Ma, Huaide Cheng, Qingyu Hai, Wenhua Han, Haizhou Ma
abstract: Salt lakes are highly sensitive to climate fluctuations, making them valuable archives of past environmental changes. Among the various geochemical proxies used to reconstruct paleoclimate, the boron isotopic composition of evaporite minerals has emerged as a powerful tool for tracking brine salinity variations. Currently, carbonates in evaporites are the primary carriers for boron isotopic composition analysis due to their relatively high boron content. However, carbonates only exist during the initial stages of salt lake evaporation, occur in limited quantities, and are difficult to separate as single minerals, introducing significant uncertainties in reconstructing paleoclimate evolution. Given the presence of halite throughout nearly all stages of salt lake evolution, its boron isotopic record holds great potential for investigating global climate change. However, the exceptionally low partition coefficient of boron in halite has sparked ongoing debate regarding the incorporation mechanisms of boron in halite and the processes governing boron isotope fractionation between brine and halite. To address these uncertainties, this study examines the boron isotopic composition of halite precipitated from evaporation experiments using underground brine from the Wuyunbulake Salt Lake (Kumish Basin, Xinjiang) alongside experiments with pure sodium chloride solutions and simulated natural samples. Our results reveal that residual fluid trapped within halite plays a crucial role in boron isotope fractionation. When halite contains residual brine, the boron fractionation factor αhalite-brine approaches 1, indicating negligible fractionation. In contrast, when halite is free of residual brine, the fractionation factor falls below 1. These findings offer new insights into boron isotope behavior in evaporative systems and strengthen the application of halite as a paleoclimate proxy.

title: A Sobol-based ensemble framework for integrating multi-method geochemical anomaly detection
description: Publication date: September 2026 Source: Applied Geochemistry, Volume 207 Author(s): Zohre Hoseinzade, Mobin Saremi, Moslem Fatehi, Amin Beiranvand Pour
abstract: In geochemical exploration, the geochemical anomalies identified by applying different methods within a study area often show considerable divergence and differences in terms of spatial distribution. Combining results from various methods across a region is challenging but crucial for producing reliable geochemical maps that help locate mineralized areas. To address this, the Sobol method was adopted to integrate the outputs of seven individual methods, including Isolation Forest (IF), Autoencoder (AE), Variational autoencoder (VAE), AE-one class support vector machine (AE1SVM), Deep One-Class Classification (Deep SVD), Cook's distance (CD), and Copula-based outlier detection (COPOD). To investigate the efficiency of the proposed approach, the Moalleman region located in NE Iran was selected as the real-case study. After that, the individual models were combined using a novel Sobol-based approach in which pseudo-random numbers were generated through quasi-Monte Carlo sampling. Then, a suitable statistical criterion was defined to identify and select the most stable weighted combination, and the final ensemble map was binarized using a percentile threshold. The identified anomalies through the Sobol approach show strong spatial correlation with known mineral occurrences (KMOs), major fault systems, and favorable lithological units. The proposed Sobol-based ensemble modeling framework effectively reduces model-related uncertainty and enhances the reliability of multi-element geochemical anomaly detection. Its demonstrated capacity to integrate diverse anomaly detection methods provides a robust decision-support tool for mineral exploration programs. The results underscore the approach's potential for delineating polymetallic mineralization targets and guiding future exploration in data-scarce or geologically complex regions.

title: Corrosion of borosilicate glass under unsaturated conditions: temperature-dependent evolution of secondary phases and surface alteration layer
description: Publication date: September 2026 Source: Applied Geochemistry, Volume 207 Author(s): Yuhan Jiao, Xuan Wang, Wenxu Yin, Junjiang Zhu, Zhentao Zhang, Laurent Charlet, Qi Sun, Kaifeng Wang
abstract: Predicting the long-term performance of borosilicate glass for nuclear waste immobilization under unsaturated repository conditions requires a fundamental understanding of the evolution of the surface alteration layer (SAL) and secondary phases during corrosion. In this study, long-term static leaching experiments (up to 760 d, 50-90 °C) were conducted in pre-equilibrated solutions to investigate the corrosion behavior of borosilicate glass under unsaturated conditions. The evolution of aqueous chemistry, secondary phases, and the SAL was characterized using solution analysis combined with XRD, SEM, and STEM techniques. The results show that B release increases continuously with temperature and reaction time, whereas dissolved Si initially increases and subsequently exhibits slight variations associated with SAL evolution and secondary phase precipitation. XRD and SEM analyses reveal the progressive formation of secondary phases on the glass surface, including zeolites, analcime, calcium silicate, smectite, and barite. STEM-EDS observations further demonstrate that the SAL develops a multilayer structure consisting of a relatively dense inner alteration layer, a porous outer alteration region, and a compositional gradient region near the glass-SAL interface. These findings provide new insights into the coupled processes controlling borosilicate glass durability and improve the basis for performance assessment of vitrified nuclear waste in geological disposal environments.

title: Lead exposure in an urban population: isotopic evidence reveals contributions from dietary and inhalation pathways
description: Publication date: September 2026 Source: Applied Geochemistry, Volume 207 Author(s): Shuhui Mu, Jin Wu, Jiaxin Ye, Jiemin Liu, Guangle Qiu, Xiaoyuan Lin, Xiangyang Bi
abstract: Environmental lead (Pb) exposure remains a persistent global public health concern. Dietary intake is widely recognized as the predominant exposure pathway, while the contribution of inhalation of Pb-containing particles to elevated blood lead levels (BLLs) has not been adequately explored. This study analyzed BLLs and lead isotopic fingerprints of residents in Guiyang, a typical city in Southwest China, and compared them with dietary samples, environmental media, and major lead emission sources to identify the primary sources and exposure pathways of lead in local residents. The results reveal strikingly elevated BLLs in both adults (57.8 μg/L) and children (44.0 μg/L), which are markedly higher than the U.S. national reference values (35 μg/L). A clear age-dependent trend was also observed, with BLLs generally increasing with age. The IsoSource model based on lead isotopic signatures revealed that lead in residents' blood primarily originated from lead-zinc smelting emissions (29.7%), historical vehicle emissions (29.5%), current traffic emissions (24.9%), and coal combustion emissions (15.9%). Furthermore, lead isotopic signatures showed that dietary intake and inhalation were the two major exposure pathways, with a binary mixing model estimating their relative contributions as 45.3% and 54.7%, respectively. This study demonstrates that lead isotope fingerprinting is a powerful tool for tracing environmental lead sources and human exposure routes, providing essential complementary insights to conventional exposure assessment models. These findings underscore the importance of integrated public health strategies that address both inhalation and dietary pathways to effectively mitigate lead exposure risks.

title: Disentangling the controls on fossil bone geochemistry using partial redundancy analysis
description: Publication date: September 2026 Source: Applied Geochemistry, Volume 207 Author(s): Michał P. Surowski, Krzysztof Owocki, Bogusław Bagiński, David Chew, Foteini Drakou
abstract: Bones undergo severe diagenesis after burial, which leads to significant changes in their geochemistry during fossilization. There are many factors that influence the final composition of a fossilized bone, including the local burial conditions (further called the locality), cortical thickness, and skeletal part. In this study, we used partial redundancy analysis (pRDA) to investigate how these factors influence the geochemical composition of dinosaur bones from the Nemegt and Djadokhta Formations from the Gobi Desert (southern Mongolia). Four pRDA models were created to estimate the impact of these factors (locality, cortical thickness and skeletal part) on bone geochemistry. The results demonstrate that all of these factors exhibit statistically significant impact on bone geochemistry. The most significant factor is the locality. The elements most applicable for differentiating between localities are the medium to heavy rare earth elements (REE). Cortical thickness is a more significant factor than the skeletal part. Despite this, when cortical thickness and skeletal parts were analysed together, the thinnest bones and tibiae proved to have the largest impact on the model. Thinner bones are usually more enriched in REE and especially in heavy REE. This relationship becomes less clear with increasing thickness due to potential mechanical damage during diagenesis. The thicker bones tend to prefer Zn, Sr, Ba, and U over REE during diagenesis. The results also show that tibiae contain relatively more Ca than other bones, which may be related to their resistance to diagenetic processes.

title: A GIXAFS study of the Fe oxide precipitates on quartz surfaces
description: Publication date: September 2026 Source: Applied Geochemistry, Volume 207 Author(s): Francesco Di Benedetto, Giordano Montegrossi, Francesco d’Acapito, Massimo Innocenti, Maurizio Romanelli
abstract: This study investigates the interaction between quartz surfaces and iron-bearing solutions through the precipitation of Fe oxide phases under controlled physicochemical conditions. Three differently oriented quartz crystal surfaces were exposed to buffered and unbuffered Fe(II) and Fe(III) solutions, and the resulting surface precipitates were analysed by GIXAFS spectroscopy. Due to the extremely low amount of deposited material, GIXAFS represented the only suitable technique capable of simultaneously probing iron oxidation state and local structural arrangement. The results demonstrate that Fe precipitates as nanoscale clusters rather than continuous surface coatings, independently of the crystallographic orientation of the quartz substrate. XANES, pre-edge, and EXAFS analyses reveal that the final Fe speciation frequently differs from the nominal redox state imposed by the starting solutions, with widespread occurrence of mixed Fe(II)–Fe(III) species and hematite-like local structures. Thermodynamic modelling performed with PHREEQC and Pourbaix diagrams successfully explains part of the observed behaviour, particularly the tendency toward Fe(III) oxide formation during evaporation and maturation of the precipitates. However, some experimental observations, including unexpected redox transformations, cannot be fully accounted for by bulk thermodynamics alone, suggesting an additional contribution from quartz surface effects or surface defects. These findings provide new insights into Fe oxide nucleation and redox evolution on silica surfaces, with potential implications for geochemical processes, environmental remediation, and the reactivity of crystalline silica in biological environments. In particular, the observed mixed-valence Fe precipitates may represent an additional contribution to the complex mechanistic framework linking crystalline silica exposure, persistent oxidative stress, and silica-related lung diseases.

title: Behaviour of 15 non-REE trace elements in Late Triassic vertebrate fossils: new insights into incorporation mechanisms and palaeoenvironmental proxy potentials
description: Publication date: September 2026 Source: Applied Geochemistry, Volume 207 Author(s): Aishee Sanyal, Sanghamitra Ray
abstract: Trace elements, usually present in negligible amounts in natural systems and living organisms, often show elevated concentrations in fossil remains due to diagenetic uptake. Concentrations of 15 non-rare earth elements (REE) (Be, Sc, Co, Ga, Rb, Sr, Y, Zr, Nb, Cs, Ba, Hf, Pb, Th, and U) were analysed in fossil bones and associated host rocks from the Upper Triassic Tiki Formation, India to document for the first time measurable concentrations of elements such as Be and Ga. Overall trace element distribution patterns in the fossils and host rocks indicate comparable diagenetic conditions, though relatively higher concentrations in the former are interpreted to reflect enrichment primarily from diagenetic fluids rather than surrounding sediments. Enrichment factor (EF) calculations highlight significant enrichment of Sr, Y, Ba, and U in fossils (EF > 1), reflecting incorporation through Ca2+ substitution in apatite and adsorption into pore spaces during fluid-mediated diagenesis. In contrast, Be, Sc, Co, Ga, Rb, Zr, Nb, Cs, Hf, Pb, and Th yield EF values < 1, suggesting retention within detrital mineral phases. Several elements such as Co and Pb acted as redox indicators, with low Th/U ratios and modest U concentrations suggesting localised reducing microenvironments formed by organic matter decay. Principal Component Analysis further supports the dominating influence of fluid-mediated and lithogenic inputs on trace-element distribution in the Tiki bonebeds. Elevated Sr and Ba concentrations together with host rock Sr/Cu and Rb/Sr ratios suggest deposition under a seasonally variable semi-arid climatic regime. This study represents one of the first comprehensive investigations of non-REE trace elements in fossil bones, demonstrating their independent significance relative to REEs in reconstructing diagenetic palaeoenvironments, provenance, and palaeoclimatic conditions.

title: Rare earth element quantification in sedimentary systems: recommendations for pXRF methods
description: Publication date: Available online 15 July 2026 Source: Applied Geochemistry Author(s): Haley H. Coe, Lauren P. Birgenheier, Diego P. Fernandez, Peyton D. Fausett, Emma A. Morris, Ryan D. Gall, Michael D. Vanden Berg, Andrew Giebel
abstract: Quantifying rare earth elements (REEs) in coal-bearing sedimentary strata requires reliable geochemical methods, yet the comparability of portable X-ray fluorescence (pXRF) and inductively coupled plasma mass spectrometry (ICP-MS) datasets remains poorly constrained. This study evaluates method comparability across 230 samples from the Uinta Region of Utah and western Colorado, spanning coal, mudstone, siltstone, claystone, carbonaceous shale, sandstone, and igneous lithologies. Three hierarchical factors govern method agreement: sample preparation, lithology, and elemental atomic weight. Powdered samples show stronger ICP-MS agreement than whole rock samples across all lithologies (R2 = 0.614 vs. 0.126), as homogenization minimizes grain-size and mineralogical heterogeneity. In powdered samples, pXRF-derived Y serves as a reliable heavy REE proxy (R2 = 0.743, m = 1.00, b = 7 ppm). Coal outperforms other lithologies in both preparation approaches; mudstone whole rock samples show near-zero correlation. Agreement degrades with increasing atomic weight; pXRF-derived Pr and Nd should not be used quantitatively without independent validation. Recommended methodologies optimize pXRF as a non-destructive REE screening tool: spatial grid analysis (n ≥ 8 per sample) yields bulk-representative REE values statistically comparable to ICP-MS; coefficient of variation values of 37.7–67.9% confirm that single-point measurements inadequately represent bulk REE content. Complementary analyses along a stratigraphic transect show no statistically significant method difference (p = 0.093). A uniform correction factor of 1.214 ± 0.066 provides moderate REE estimation accuracy (R2 = 0.661, RMSE = 54.66 ppm) suitable for first-order enrichment screening. These findings establish a validated, cost-effective framework for pXRF deployment in sedimentary critical mineral assessments.

title: Speciation transformation and (im)mobilization of ferrihydrite-adsorbed arsenic in river sediment environments: impact of leaf litter
description: Publication date: Available online 14 July 2026 Source: Applied Geochemistry Author(s): Li Zhang, Bolin Li, Hulong Yi, Qianhua Chen, Tianci Liu, Jianqiao Wang, Enzong Xiao, Yi Wang, Jinli Cui
abstract: Plant leaf litter substantially increases the content and diversity of dissolved organic matter (DOM) in river sediment environments and may influence the mobility and transformation of arsenic (As), but the underlying mechanism remains unclear. In this study, microcosm incubations of ferrihydrite-adsorbed arsenate in simulated river sediment environments, supplemented with tree leaf litter, were employed. During the incubations, the amount of arsenic initially released from the spent ferrihydrite materials into solution continuously decreased. Speciation analysis revealed the dominance of arsenate (98.5–100%) and lesser amounts of arsenite (0.9–1.5%) in the solution of all incubations. In the sequential extraction of solid fractions, water-extractable fraction contributed <1.0% and arsenite reached 39.4–100% in the presence of sediment and 86.8-100% in the presence of leaves or coexisting leaves and sediment. Arsenic in the solid phase was predominantly associated with amorphous (24.2–45.1%) and crystalline iron (oxyhydr)oxide fractions (54.1–75.7%). The iron (oxyhydr)oxide-associated arsenic was dominated by arsenate (92.2–100%), whereas arsenite was observed only in the presence of coexisting leaves and sediment at the end of incubation, reaching 3.6–7.8%. Coupled with the observation of ferrous iron in the amorphous and crystalline iron fractions, these findings confirm the reduction of iron and arsenic in the ferrihydrite-adsorbed arsenate material in sediment environments following leaf litter deposition. Fluorescence analysis confirmed that leaf-derived DOM contained terrestrial humic-like components, microbial humic-like components, and protein-like components, which strongly controlled As sorption behavior, likely via competitive interactions and DOM-mediated reactions, including the adsorption properties and reductive transformation of iron (oxyhydr)oxides. Compared with the control, leaf-derived DOM facilitated arsenate reduction largely via microbial processes (99.9%) mediated by sedimentary microbes. Metagenomic analysis further supported that iron/arsenate reduction was potentially driven by specific dissimilatory respiration genes for Fe (e.g., pilA) and As (e.g., arrAB) and the detoxifying arsenate reductase gene (arsC) identified in Geobacter and Pseudomonas. This study demonstrated that reactive leaf-derived DOM can be substantially involved in the microbial redox transformation of arsenic and iron in riverine sediment scenarios.

title: Inhalation Exposure to Uranium and Thorium-Rich Dust in Hazm Al-Jalamid Phosphate Mines: Occupational and Environmental Risk Assessment
description: Publication date: Available online 13 July 2026 Source: Applied Geochemistry Author(s): Khalid G. Alsafi, Othman A. Fallatah
abstract: Phosphate mining poses a significant risk of workers being exposed to naturally occurring radioactive materials like 238U and 232Th, which are found in sedimentary phosphate deposits. A key site for phosphate mining is Hazm al-Jalamid in northern Saudi Arabia, known for its rich phosphate reserves that also contain notable amounts of uranium and thorium. This situation raises important concerns about the risk of inhalation exposure to miners from contaminated dust. This study offers a detailed evaluation of the radiation risks associated with inhaling dust that contains uranium and thorium during various mining operations, like crushing and processing. Alpha and gamma spectrometry were used for measured 238U–232Th isotopes and 40K activity concentrations. We also measured external gamma radiation dose rates in different work areas using a vehicle-mounted radiation monitoring system. The radioactivity levels we found were then used to estimate airborne radionuclides and calculate effective inhalation doses based on respiratory models and dose conversion factors for different work scenarios. Our results showed that while 238U was present in both the ore and enrichment products, 232Th concentrations were lower but still significant from a radiological perspective. The inhalation dose assessment revealed that exposure to inhalable dust indoors is a crucial contributor to the overall occupational dose, especially in high-dust settings like open-pit mines and material handling zones. The estimated annual effective inhalation doses for workers near or even above locally recommended occupational safety levels may be pointed to an increased risk of cancer over a worker's lifetime. These results highlight the urgent need for effective dust management, better ventilation, proper use of personal protective equipment, and regular radiation monitoring that specifically addresses inhalation exposure. Overall, this research sheds light on the occupational and environmental exposure risks linked to natural radioactive phosphate mining and will help develop strategies for better environmental and occupational radiation protection.

title: Aging Biomarkers and a Quantitative Diagnostic Model for Baltic Amber Degradation: A Multi-Analytical Study of Unearthed Archaeological Artefacts
description: Publication date: Available online 13 July 2026 Source: Applied Geochemistry Author(s): Yan Li, Qing Su, Jiarong Li, Qi Liu, Yamei Wang
abstract: Due to the lack of quantitative tools to diagnose the aging state and predict long-term stability, the irreversible degradation of organic polymers poses a fundamental challenge to preserve organic archaeological heritage. This research systematically analyzed 50 Song-to-Qing dynasty Baltic amber artifacts using a comprehensive suite of analytical techniques, including multiple spectra and chromatography/mass spectrometry. The findings identify key aging biomarkers in unearthed amber, and it resolves a long-term argument by demonstrating that hydrolytic cleavage of ester bonds, rather than solely oxidation, is the main aging mechanism in long-term buried amber. By integrating multidimensional data within grey relational analysis, a non-destructive quantitative model was developed to rank aging degrees, achieving high concordance with macroscopic observations. This quantitative model for archaeological preservation elucidates amber’s oxidative-hydrolytic degradation mechanism and enables a shift from reactive repair to proactive conservation. This diagnostic approach elucidates amber's oxidative-hydrolytic degradation mechanism and enables a shift from reactive repair to proactive conservation planning for Baltic amber collections. The analytical framework may be adaptable to other fossil resins, though further validation is required.

title: Investigating reservoir-scale heterogeneity in Li-enriched oil field brines of the Devonian Leduc and Nisku formations, Alberta Basin, Canada.
description: Publication date: Available online 10 July 2026 Source: Applied Geochemistry Author(s): M.R. Blake, K.L. Butler, L.A. Munk, D.F. Boutt, N. Morris, J. Kennedy, P. Saha, J. Serotta, H. Tompkins, G. Williams, A. Vengosh, J. Evaristo, D.E. Ibarra
abstract: Securing a North American lithium (Li) pipeline is pivotal to the clean energy transition and national security. The low-temperature sedimentary basin brines of the Devonian Alberta Basin, Canada are emerging as a promising unconventional domestic Li resource. This study integrates new and published geochemical and isotopic data from the Devonian Leduc and Nisku formation oil field brines to investigate brine origin, evolution, and Li enrichment mechanisms at the reservoir scale. Despite receiving considerably less attention than the Leduc Formation, the Nisku Formation brines display broadly similar geochemical and isotopic characteristics, suggesting common Li enrichment processes. Here we subdivide the Leduc and Nisku brines into geochemically distinct groups associated with four Devonian carbonate reef reservoirs (Redwater, Leduc, Chedderville, Bashaw) and evaluate the combined behavior of Li-B-radiogenic Sr-O-H isotope systems and major-element chemistry. Shallow reef complexes in hydraulic communication with surrounding formations contain low δ2H and δ18O values (avg. -78‰ and -3‰, respectively) and Li concentrations (avg. ∼32 mg/L), suggesting meteoric infiltration diluted the Li resource. Brines from structurally deeper reef complexes approaching the Rocky Mountain deformation front display high Li concentrations (avg. ∼67 mg/L), high δ18O (avg. 3.4‰) and radiogenic strontium values (avg. 0.70899), and low δ11B and δ7Li values (avg. 24‰ and 15‰, respectively), consistent with increased diagenetic interaction between brines and marine shales. Results suggest that Li enrichment and preservation are controlled by distinct but related processes, where shale-fluid interactions likely contributes Li to the basin brines while hydrologic isolation controls the preservation of elevated Li concentrations.

title: Applications of sulfur isotopes to discriminate natural and anthropogenic sulfate sources with stoichiometric approaches in the Fukui Ono Basin alluvial aquifer, Japan
description: Publication date: Available online 9 July 2026 Source: Applied Geochemistry Author(s): Mingzhe Zhao, Toshiro Yamanaka, Masaru Yamanaka
abstract: In agricultural fields, since chemical fertilizers are one of the most important potential sources of anthropogenic sulfur in groundwater, a quantitative comprehension of this element is crucial for assessing human impacts on groundwater systems. By using hydrochemical and sulfur isotopic tracers (δ34S), this study identifies and quantifies the sources of groundwater sulfate in the Lowland of Fukui Ono Basin (LFOB), where agricultural fields are widely distributed. Along the northward flow paths, both sulfate and nitrate concentrations increase in the LFOB groundwater, likely attributed to the oxidation processes of ammonium sulfate fertilizer. In more detail, δ34S analysis reveals the existence of the other sulfate source: soil organic matter with high δ34S values (6.33∼12.73‰) in addition to chemical fertilizers with low δ34S values (−0.60 to 0.60‰). The quantitative discriminations based on δ34S signatures demonstrate that anthropogenic sulfate from chemical fertilizers accounts for 58∼82% of the total sulfate associated with nitrate concentrations in the groundwater. On the other hand, natural sulfate from soil organic matter (18∼42%) is consistent with partial CO2 pressure, an indicator of organic matter decomposition in aquifers. In addition, a spatial analysis reveals distinct hydrological pathways; anthropogenic sulfate progressively accumulates along northward groundwater flow paths due to agricultural inputs, whereas natural sulfate distributions are controlled by localized hydrogeological features. Especially for the latter, low natural sulfate concentrations in the central basin reflect dilution from river water infiltration, while elevated natural sulfate concentrations in the western basin are likely derived through the decomposition of organic-rich lacustrine deposits. Thus, this study demonstrates that combining isotopic tracers with stoichiometric indicators provides a robust framework for understanding contaminant transport and geological influences in complex alluvial aquifer systems.

title: Source of Uranium (U) and Rare Earth Elements (REE) for Unconformity-Related U and REE Mineralization in the Athabasca Basin, Canada: Insights from Accessory Minerals in Sandstones
description: Publication date: Available online 25 June 2026 Source: Applied Geochemistry Author(s): Goktug Harmanci, Guoxiang Chi, Jeremy Powell, Janina Czas, Victoria Tschirhart, Huimin Su, Yumeng Wang, Nahanni Danylczuk
abstract: The Athabasca Basin in Canada hosts the world’s largest and highest-grade unconformity-related uranium (URU) deposits, many of which are also enriched in rare earth elements (REE). There has been a long-lasting debate whether the U and REE were sourced from the basin or basement. This study investigates the potential contribution of detrital accessory minerals in the basin, particularly zircon and Ti-oxide (rutile), to U and REE mineralization. The textural and compositional characteristics of these detrital accessory minerals, as well as diagenetic minerals, including Ti-oxide (anatase), iron oxide/hydroxide (IOH) and aluminium phosphate sulfate (APS) minerals, were examined using multiple in-situ analytical methods. The results show that detrital zircon and rutile exhibit extensive dissolution and alteration features and large and irregular variations of U and REE concentrations within individual grains suggesting strong fluid-rock interactions. Large amounts of U and REE, especially heavy REE (HREE), were leached into the basinal brines, while some of them, especially light REE (LREE), were retained by diagenetic minerals. The resulting diagenetic basinal fluids are characterized by strong HREE enrichment, which broadly match the REE patterns of uraninite in the URU ores. Mass balance calculations suggest that 40 to 70 million tonnes of U and 80 to 330 million tonnes of REE, depending on the methods of calculation, could be leached from zircon and rutile. Despite the large variations and uncertainties, these estimations far exceed the amounts found in the URU deposits, implying significant potentials for further U and REE exploration. The results also highlight the vulnerability of zircon and rutile to hydrothermal alteration under certain conditions in sedimentary basins and its significance for large-scale U and REE mineralization.

title: Titanium isotope fractionation in hydrous and oxidized large igneous provinces
description: Publication date: 30 September 2026 Source: Chemical Geology, Volume 720 Author(s): Sheng-Zhu Zhu, Xiao-Long Huang, Peng-Li He, Fan Yang, Jin-Long Ma, Yang Yu, Xin-Yue He, Le Zhang, Gang-Jian Wei
abstract: Titanium (Ti) isotopes have been utilized as tracers to determine the affinity of felsic rocks with either plumes or arcs, given that greater Ti isotope fractionation occurs in plume-related magmatism. However, it is essential to investigate whether this conclusion is universally applicable in hydrous and oxidized large igneous provinces (LIPs), as previous studies have primarily focused on water-poor and reduced plume-related rocks. This study presents the Ti isotope compositions of whole-rock samples and mineral separates from early Permian ultramafic–mafic–felsic rocks in the Wajilitag area of the hydrous and oxidized Tarim LIP (TLIP). The Wajilitag igneous rocks display Ti isotope fractionation (δ49Ti = −0.332‰ to +0.803‰), which is more pronounced than that in arc-related rocks, yet less significant compared to other plume-related rocks. Clinopyroxene, hornblende, biotite, and feldspar are slightly enriched in heavier Ti isotopes compared with their host rocks, whereas ilmenite and titanite are enriched in lighter Ti isotopes. Magnetite exhibits a wide range of Ti isotope compositions (δ49Ti = −0.120‰ to +2.247‰), with δ49Ti values increasing as TiO2 content decreases, heavier than equilibrium ilmenite. The mineral Ti isotopes indicate that primary magma TiO2, water contents (H2O), and oxygen fugacities (fO2) were the main factors controlling Ti isotope fractionation during magmatism. The primary magma of the TLIP has high TiO2 contents, as well as high H2O and fO2, which account for its medium Ti isotope fractionation between arc and plume magmatism. The interaction between plumes and subducted slab materials in the upper mantle is a key mechanism for the formation of hydrous and oxidized LIPs, resulting in deviations in Ti isotopes from typical plume magmas.

title: Heavy sulfur isotope of arc ultramafic cumulates revealed by S-rich apatite from the Dongwanzi intrusion, North China
description: Publication date: 30 September 2026 Source: Chemical Geology, Volume 720 Author(s): Huan Jennifer Chang, Mei-Fu Zhou, Wen-Jun Hu, Shengbiao Yang, Jian-Feng Gao
abstract: Arc magmas generally have higher sulfur (S) contents and higher δ34S values than mid-ocean ridge basalts. However, it remains debated whether the enrichment of S is due to crustal processes or mantle metasomatism. We present elemental and S-Sr isotopic compositions of apatite from the Early Permian Dongwanzi ultramafic intrusion, northern margin of the North China Craton. This arc intrusion is composed of clinopyroxenite and hornblendite based on textural relationships. Clinopyroxenites contains interstitial apatite and euhedral cumulus apatite. Interstitial apatite grains have high Cl (0.36–1.10 wt%), and Th (16.1–130 ppm), and La/Yb ratios (52.1–112), high 87Sr/86Sr ratios (0.70370–0.70391), and low δ34SV-CDT values (−10.5 to +4.44 ‰), consistent with crystallization from late-stage trapped melts. In contrast, euhedral cumulus apatite grains have low Cl (0.23–0.71 wt%), high δ34SV-CDT values (∼ + 7.9 ‰), and La/Yb ratios (33.4–64.6), and low initial 87Sr/86Sr ratios (∼0.70337), indicative of growth from a relatively primitive magma. Compared to cumulus apatite in clinopyroxenites, cumulus apatite grains in hornblendites contain high F (1.45–2.69 wt%) and total REE + Y (1510–9830 ppm), and high 87Sr/86Sr ratios (0.70333–0.70351), but slightly low Cl (0.01–0.50 wt%) and δ34SV-CDT (7.06 ‰ to 8.25 ‰), which were attributed to progressive fractional crystallization coupled with limited wall-rock contamination from clinopyroxenite to hornblendite. As a result, the consistently high δ34S values of cumulus apatite indicate that crustal contamination only caused a limited S isotope variation (∼1 ‰) during the formation of the Dongwanzi intrusion. Using S isotopic compositions of cumulus apatite in clinopyroxenite, the parental magma has δ34S values of ∼ + 7.9 ‰. Such high δ34S values are best explained by sub-arc mantle metasomatism rather than by crustal contamination. Collectively, our study highlights that S isotopic composition of apatite can be used to track the S isotope evolution and to constrain S sources in arc mafic-ultramafic cumulates.

title: Coupled δ 18 O–δ 13 C covariation and depositional architecture diagnose hydrologic state in barrage-cascade tufa systems
description: Publication date: 30 September 2026 Source: Chemical Geology, Volume 720 Author(s): Khalil Azennoud, Yassine Ait Brahim, Franziska Lechleitner, Hai Cheng, Radouan El Bamiki, Abdennasser Baali, Mohammed Hssaisoune, Hicham El Asmi, Xiaodong Jiang, Heather Stoll
abstract: Tufa carbonates are widely distributed terrestrial archives, yet lamina-scale geochemistry and system-scale depositional architecture have traditionally been studied in isolation: the former as a climate proxy, the latter as a geomorphic question. Here we show that these two scales are coupled, and that their coupling provides a direct diagnostic of hydrologic state in barrage-cascade systems. Combining U-Th chronology, petrography, stable isotope geochemistry, and geomorphic observations from a groundwater-fed barrage-cascade system in northern Morocco, we resolve six independent depositional intervals from the Middle Pleistocene to the Late Holocene, each preserving laminated microbialites and most retaining well-developed buttress architectures. Across these intervals, the magnitude of microbialite δ18Oc–δ13Cc covariation tracks upstream pool confinement and water residence time, defining a continuum from hydrologically open to evaporatively restricted configurations. These geochemical states correspond systematically to differences in buttress size, relief, and stacking geometry, providing an independent architectural validation of the proxy. This dual-scale approach helps reduce the ambiguity of single-proxy interpretations in continental carbonate archives. Comparison with modeled precipitation and regional context suggests that hydrologic state is better explained by temperature-modulated carbonate productivity and barrage-growth feedbacks than precipitation-driven discharge alone. These results establish a process-based framework that resolves barrage-cascade tufa systems as integrated geochemical–architectural archives of Earth-surface hydrology.

title: New evidence for normal seawater dolomitization in the middle Permian
description: Publication date: 30 September 2026 Source: Chemical Geology, Volume 720 Author(s): Heting Gao, Jiakai Hou, Manfei Chen, Xi Li, Sheng Li, Jianing Wang, Guangyou Zhu
abstract: Whether normal seawater drives platform-scale dolomitization remains debated. The viability of conventional evaporative brine or hydrothermal models is questioned by new studies favoring normal or slightly modified seawater. This study presents an example from the Middle Permian Maokou Formation (Sichuan, China) while, some evidence suggest dolomite formed in association with evaporative or hydrothermal fluid, re-evaluation from new data sets suggest dolomitization by normal seawater. The Maokou Formation comprises three main petrographic types of dolomites (micro-, fine-, and medium-coarse crystalline), that lack evaporites, exhibit dull-red cathodoluminescence, near-ideal cation ordering (0.56–1.0), and are cross-cut by fitted fabric microstylolites, which was interpreted to have formed penecontemporaneously into the early burial diagenetic realm. Their relatively constant δ13C values (2.79–6.03‰), 87Sr/86Sr ratios (0.70737–0.70768), negative Ce and no positive Eu anomalies match coeval seawater. Negative δ18O values and few samples with Mn/Sr ratios <2 reflect closed-system recrystallization. Restored primary temperatures (27.9°C to 56.3°C), corrected for solid-state reordering via forward Δ47 modeling, and δ18Ofluid values (−0.8 to +1.2‰ VSMOW) are within the normal seawater range. U-Pb dating gives ages of 254.2±3.9 Ma (D1), 250.7±5.1 Ma (D2), and 249.2±2.5 Ma (D3), indistinguishable from each other but significantly older than saddle dolomite (244.8±1.5 Ma). This analysis strongly suggests that the dolomite was replaced by Permian normal seawater and subsequently experienced closed-system recrystallization during burial stage. The vertical variation of C-O isotopes and elemental data correlate with high-frequency sea-level fluctuations, confirming sea-level-driven sustained seawater circulation and cyclic reflux recharge as the driving mechanism for dolomitization. This study has revealed that the normal-seawater dolomitization could also proceed in a shallow-water platform, providing insights for coeval reservoirs in the Yangtze Block and similar settings worldwide.

title: Biomass-burning smoke water-soluble organic matter reverses ferrihydrite colloid-inhibited mobility of Cd 2+ through saturated porous media via interface fractionation and selective binding
description: Publication date: 30 September 2026 Source: Chemical Geology, Volume 720 Author(s): Bin Wang, Nan Yang, Kunyu Wen, ZhiWei Chen, Boyun Zheng, Yanbin Ma, Li Zhang, Zhichong Qi
abstract: Biomass burning events release large amounts of pyrogenic dissolved organic matter (BBS-WSOM) into terrestrial ecosystems, where it interacts with iron oxides and trace metals. However, how the molecular heterogeneity of BBS-WSOM governs colloid-facilitated metal transport remains poorly constrained. Here, we combined column transport experiments with multispectral analysis to elucidate how BBS-WSOM modulates the co-mobility of ferrihydrite (Fh) colloids and Cd2+ in saturated porous media. We found that humic-like components with higher aromaticity and hydrophobicity were preferentially retained on sand surfaces, whereas protein-like components remained largely in the aqueous phase. Protein-like components were the primary agents responsible for Cd2+ complexation, thus facilitating Cd2+ mobility. Although Fh colloids alone suppressed Cd2+ transport, the presence of BBS-WSOM not only neutralized this suppression but further enhanced Cd2+ mobility in the ternary system (Cd2+ + Fh + WSOMs) compared to the binary system (Cd2+ + WSOMs). This counterintuitive enhancement arose from molecular fractionation at the Fh-water interface: Fh preferentially adsorbed humic-like components, enriching the aqueous phase with protein-like components that bound Cd2+ more effectively. These findings reveal that the trade-off between humic-like and protein-like components within pyrogenic DOM critically controls the direction and magnitude of colloid-mediated metal transport. Our study provides mechanistic insights into how wildfire-derived or burning-derived DOM alters subsurface Cd geochemistry, with implications for the coupled cycling of carbon, iron, and trace metals in fire-impacted terrestrial environments.

title: Mechanisms of iodate reduction by sediment siderite and its contribution to iodide enrichment in groundwater
description: Publication date: 30 September 2026 Source: Chemical Geology, Volume 720 Author(s): Shilin Zhao, Junxia Li, Yinchun Su, Daolian Deng, Wenyi Zhang, Qian Liao, Xianjun Xie, Yanxin Wang
abstract: The enrichment of iodine in groundwater poses serious health risks worldwide, yet the abiotic mechanisms driving iodine mobilization in anoxic aquifers remain incompletely understood. Siderite, a ubiquitous Fe(II)-bearing mineral in reducing environments, may play an important role in iodine speciation; however, its reactivity toward iodine species transformation remains largely unexplored. Herein, we investigated the reduction of iodate (IO3 −) by siderite and the subsequent mechanisms of iodine release using both synthetic minerals and natural sediments from the Hetao Basin with varying Fe(II)‑carbonate contents. Batch kinetic experiments demonstrated that structural Fe(II) in siderite rapidly reduced IO3 − to highly mobile iodide (I−) within 20 min. The reduction kinetics and mineral transformation pathways were strongly controlled by the initial Fe(II)siderite:IO3 − molar ratio: excess IO3 − promoted the oxidation of siderite to goethite (FeOOH), whereas excess Fe(II)siderite favored the formation of magnetite (Fe3O4). Incubation experiments with natural sediments further revealed the critical role of intrinsic Fe(II)‑carbonate content in determining the IO3 − reduction capacity of sediments. Deep sediments enriched in siderite rapidly reduced IO3 − to I−, whereas shallow, siderite-depleted sediments exhibited negligible reduction. In addition, amendment of these shallow sediments with exogenous siderite induced the release of intrinsic sediment-bound iodine into the aqueous phase as I−. Overall, this study highlights the importance of siderite in iodine species transformation and provides new mechanistic insights into iodine enrichment in reducing groundwater systems.

title: Carboxyl-Fe and phosphonate-Fe interactions control the redistribution of organic phosphate during ferrihydrite transformation
description: Publication date: 30 September 2026 Source: Chemical Geology, Volume 720 Author(s): Xiaofan Pan, Zhenzhen Zhao, Xin Huang, Ning Deng
abstract: Transformation of poorly crystalline ferrihydrite (Fh) into crystalline phases is a critical process controlling mineral stability and element cycling. However, the molecular mechanisms by which organic phosphorus (OP) compounds influence Fh transformation remain unclear. Here, we investigated the effects of three representative OPs with distinct functional groups—triethyl phosphate (TEP), 2-phosphonobutane-1,2,4-tricarboxylic acid (PBTC), and 1-hydroxyethylidene-1,1-diphosphonic acid (HEDP)—on Fh transformation. Results showed that TEP, containing only a phosphate group, showed negligible adsorption and minimal effect, whereas PBTC and HEDP strongly bound to Fh via carboxyl and phosphonate groups, respectively, significantly slowing transformation. Synchrotron-based FTIR indicated that PBTC predominantly bound to Fh through strong Fe-carboxyl interactions, while HEDP mainly formed Fe-phosphonate complexes on Fh surfaces. The stronger carboxyl-mediated surface complexation of PBTC resulted in persistent association with the solid phase throughout the transformation process. In contrast, HEDP exhibited dynamic redistribution during Fh transformation, characterized by initial release followed by re-immobilization. Geochemical modeling showed that the complexation of HEDP with aqueous Fe3+ favored the incorporation of Fe3+-HEDP complexes into growing secondary mineral phases, leading to HEDP refixation. These results reveal that OP functional groups govern both Fe mineral stability and OPs fate, providing mechanistic insights into organic ligand-mediated Fe mineral evolution.

title: Subseafloor processes in ultramafic-influenced volcanic-hosted hydrothermal systems: An insight from the Gnitahei massive sulfide mineralization, Arctic Mid-Ocean Ridges
description: Publication date: 30 September 2026 Source: Chemical Geology, Volume 720 Author(s): Sabina Strmić Palinkaš, Marie Wold, Rolf Birger Pedersen, Håvard Hallås Stubseid, Fredrik Sahlström, Lahaye Yann, Leif-Erik Rydland Pedersen, Jorge E. Spangenberg
abstract: The extinct Gnitahei seafloor massive sulfide (SMS) deposit was discovered in 2019 on the ultraslow spreading Mohns Ridge (Arctic Mid-Ocean Ridge System, 72.8°N, 3.81°E, 3022–2760 mbsl). It provides a unique opportunity to study subseafloor hydrothermal processes without drilling, as tectonic uplift and ongoing mass wasting expose the deeper parts of the hydrothermal system. The deposit is hosted by hydrothermally altered basalts within the footwall of a NE–SW striking normal fault, in proximity to the active Fåvne Vent Field. Driven by extensional tectonics and facilitated by the thin oceanic crust along the ultraslow-spreading Mohns Ridge, hydrothermal circulation likely extends deep into the serpentinized upper mantle. Hydrothermal alteration exhibits vertical zonation. Chloritization accompanied by remobilization of silica, LILEs, and REEs dominate the deeper parts of the system. In contrast, silicification associated with an enrichment in LILEs and REEs characterizes the upper part of the Gnitahei SMS deposit. The paleosurface is clearly marked by a layer of red jasper. The sulfide mineralization is dominated by pyrite and marcasite, with euhedral pyrite prevailing in deeper zones and colloform pyrite being more abundant near the paleosurface. Native gold occurs mostly as inclusions in pyrite. Trace-element data obtained from pyrite, including elevated Ni and Co concentrations and a high Au/Ag ratios, are consistent with fluid interaction with underlying ultramafic rocks. Sulfur isotope composition of pyrite reveals a strong 34S enrichment (bulk δ34SVCDT = 11.1–15.9‰; in-situ δ34SVCDT = 10.8–17.3‰), indicating a significant contribution of reduced seawater sulfate, which constitutes ∼50% of the total sulfur according to a two-component mixing model. The high influx of reduced sulfate is attributed to reducing conditions driven by serpentinization of ultramafic lithologies. Under these conditions, seawater sulfate can be reduced prior to anhydrite deposition, allowing isotopically heavy sulfur to infiltrate the hydrothermal system. Depth-dependent decreases in δ34S values likely reflect greater contributions of reduced seawater sulfate in shallower zones and/or enhanced fractionation at lower temperatures.

title: A first principles critique of the back calculation method: Understanding and assessing the alteration of atmospheric gases trapped in ancient fluid inclusions
description: Publication date: 30 September 2026 Source: Chemical Geology, Volume 720 Author(s): Justin G. Park, Morgan F. Schaller
abstract: The extraction of atmospheric gases from fluid inclusions has emerged as an extremely promising approach for directly constraining the composition of Earth's ancient atmosphere. However, the veracity of data obtained from these inclusions critically depends on how well one can account for the effects of physical chemistry and post-depositional alteration. The Back Calculation Method (BCM) attempts to discern unaltered atmospheric compositions from variably modified inclusion gases, primarily O2 and CO2, but fails to account for the effects of gas solubility. Moreover, the method lacks an explicit mathematical formulation, and limited articulation of its implicit assumptions and limitations has introduced ambiguity in the interpretation of reconstructed atmospheric compositions. From first principles, we derive the formulation underlying the BCM and use it to formally evaluate the limitations of the method. We expand this framework to include the variable effects of gas solubility and incorporate recent techniques to partition inclusion volatiles trapped in the gaseous and aqueous phases. Re-examination of modern inclusion gases reveals evidence of heterogeneous entrapment of gas and brine, as well as post-entrapment alteration of O2 and CO2, with distinct stoichiometric relationships observed between samples. These observations violate the core assumptions of the BCM, suggesting the technique has been applied inappropriately to ancient samples and that their interpreted atmospheric compositions require thorough reevaluation. We conclude by demonstrating carbon isotope measurements of inclusion CO2 can be incorporated to assess the extent of gas alteration and provide an outline for future work intending to reconstruct atmospheric compositions from these inclusions.

title: The influence of coral nutritional status on its skeletal carbon isotope fractionation and δ 13 C values
description: Publication date: 30 September 2026 Source: Chemical Geology, Volume 720 Author(s): Shendong Xu, Jie Gao, Zhinan Zhang, Kefu Yu, Yiqi Zhao, Biao Chen
abstract: Almost all scleractinian corals are mixotrophic organisms and their skeleton stable carbon isotopes (δ13Cs) were widely used for environmental and climatic records. However, the interpretation of coral δ13Cs is still complicated and controversial. In particular, the impact of nutritional status (i.e. relative intensity of autotrophic photosynthetic and heterotrophic predation) and related photosynthesis/respiration ratio (P/R) on the coral δ13Cs was not well understood. In this study, coral samples (Favia palauensis) were collected from three coral reefs of different latitudes in the South China Sea (SCS), Weizhou (∼21°N), Xisha (∼16°N) and Nansha (∼9°N) Islands. Different types of physiological and geochemical parameters, including symbiodiniaceae (i.e. symbiotic zooxanthellae) density, tissue biomass, δ13C of zooxanthellae (δ13Cz), host tissue (δ13Ch), skeleton (δ13Cs) were measured. We also collected environmental and ambient seawater parameters, including ‌Sea Surface Temperature, ‌Sea Surface Salinity, Photosynthetically Active Radiation, Rainfall and Seawater δ18O and δ13CDIC. The P/R ratio was calculated based on these parameters. We conducted this study to analysis the spatial distribution characteristics of coral nutritional status, and then explore the potential impacts of coral's nutritional status on their P/R ratios and skeletal δ13C in the SCS. Our results show that corals have relatively high autotrophic photosynthesis intensity and P/R ratios in Weizhou reef. On the contrary, corals in relatively low latitude Xisha and Nansha reefs are more dependent on heterotrophic predation and have lower P/R ratios. Correspondingly, coral δ13Cs is more positive in Weizhou than that in Xisha and Nansha. In particular, there are high correlations between δ13Cs and δ13Cz of corals in Weizhou, but not in Xisha and Nansha. Overall, the corals in all three reef areas showed a positive correlation between P/R and δ13Cs values (p<0.05). These results indicate that different coral nutritional status and related P/R have different effects on δ13Cs. This maybe one of the important factors leading to the spatial variation of skeletal δ13C in the SCS. We suggest that special attention should be paid to this case when using coral skeletal δ13C for paleoclimate reconstruction, especially when conducting comparative analysis of climate in different regions of the world based on coral skeletal δ13C.

title: Selenium isotope fractionation during pyrite oxidation and acid mine drainage formation: Combined field and experimental constraints
description: Publication date: 30 September 2026 Source: Chemical Geology, Volume 720 Author(s): José Luis Guerrero, Stephan König, Rafael Pérez-López, Carolina Rosca, Carlos J. Garrido, José Miguel Nieto
abstract: Selenium (Se) is a redox-sensitive chalcophile element whose isotopes provide valuable constraints on oxidative processes at the Earth's surface. This study presents a combined field and experimental investigation of Se isotope fractionation (δ82/76Se) during pyrite (FeS2) oxidation under acid mine drainage (AMD) conditions, integrating field observations, column experiments, geochemical modeling, and mineralogical characterization. Field leachates from the Tharsis mining district (Iberian Pyrite Belt) exhibit extreme acidity (pH ≈ 1–2), elevated Eh values (> 600 mV) consistent with ongoing pyrite oxidation, elevated Se concentrations (up to 1.3 × 103 μg/L), and significant isotopic variability, with δ82/76Se values ranging from −4.1 ± 0.53‰ at the waste dump outflow to +1.19 ± 0.07‰ in a receiving pond. Column experiments reproduce and extend this trend, with early leachates showing slightly negative values (≈ −1‰) attributed to rapid flushing of isotopically light, labile Se pools, followed by a progressive increase to a stable plateau of +12 ± 1‰. Speciation modeling indicates that dissolved Se occurs predominantly as Se(IV), excluding redox partitioning between aqueous oxidation states as the main control on Se isotope fractionation. Rayleigh-type calculations show that adsorption alone cannot account for the observed >10‰ isotopic shift. Instead, the isotopic evolution reflects open-system processes involving continuous Se release from sulfide oxidation, surface interactions with Fe(III) phases, and localized redox transformations. The agreement between field and experimental trends defines a coherent framework for Se isotope behavior during sulfide weathering. These results demonstrate the high mobility of Se under AMD conditions and highlight the potential of δ82/76Se as a tracer of oxidative release and attenuation processes in natural and mining-impacted environments.

title: Experimental insights into chlorine and bromine isotope fractionation during evaporation and mineral precipitation in multicomponent brines
description: Publication date: 30 September 2026 Source: Chemical Geology, Volume 720 Author(s): Yon-Gyung Ryuh, Randy L. Stotler, Shaun K. Frape
abstract: Chloride and bromide are commonly used as tracers in various aqueous geochemistry fields as a result of their well-known conservative behaviors. However, the behavior of their stable isotopes during evaporation and mineral precipitation remains poorly constrained. This study investigates how chlorine and bromine isotopes fractionate during evaporation of seawater. Synthetic seawater was evaporated under controlled conditions, and the isotopic compositions of chlorine and bromine were measured in brine, solids, and gas phase throughout sequential mineral precipitation. The results show that chlorine and bromine isotopes respond to distinct processes that vary with mineralogy and evaporation stage. Bromine isotopes fractionate during early calcium-phase precipitation through lattice substitution into aragonite, but mineralogical shifts with increasing salinity result in Br incorporation into precipitates through physical brine entrapment limiting further fractionation. In contrast, during halite precipitation, chlorine isotopes exhibit systematic lattice-controlled fractionation behavior broadly consistent with near-equilibrium fractionation, while bromine isotopes exhibit more complex behavior. Bromine isotope evolution during this stage is interpreted to reflect a combination of inefficient lattice incorporation and selective loss of isotopically light bromine to the gas phase. These findings suggest that chlorine and bromine isotopes may respond differently due to mineral-specific and process-dependent mechanisms, highlighting processes that may influence halogen isotope signatures in natural evaporite and saline systems.

title: Organic carbon enrichment in carbonate concretions of the Rincon Shale, California, USA: Implications for organic matter preservation in concretions
description: Publication date: 30 September 2026 Source: Chemical Geology, Volume 720 Author(s): Sean J. Loyd, Melonie D. Reyes, Natasha Kuhn, Adam D. Woods, Allyson M. Fry-Petit, Ashley E. Godoy
abstract: Carbonate concretions often form as a byproduct of the degradation of organic matter and/or methane in sediments. Despite these origins, concretions may subsequently protect sedimentary organic matter from degradation after precipitation. The degree to which concretions preferentially preserve organic material is poorly characterized, as are the degradation processes/environments against which they are most effective. Here, concretions and host sediment of the Miocene Rincon Shale are compared geochemically to assess the preservation capacity of concretions. Magnesian calcite and dolomite concretions of the Rincon Shale express carbonate carbon isotope compositions (δ13Ccarb) consistent with formation via microbial oxidative reactions and methanogenesis, respectively. Host shale laminae deflection around the concretions and high cement contents suggest that concretions formed at relatively shallow sediment depths during early diagenesis. Concretions contain higher concentrations of total carbonate-free organic carbon (TOCCF), iron, and manganese than neighboring host shales. When considered collectively, host shale and concretion Oxygen Index (OI) data correlate with TOCCF contents, consistent with oxidative weathering. However, most concretions express lower OI compositions than neighboring shales. Combined lower OI and higher TOCCF, iron, and manganese in concretions suggest that concretions protect organic matter and metal sulfides from oxidative weathering in outcrop. This preferential preservation indicates that concretions 1) represent a better target for outcrop-based study using organic archives and 2) may delay the weathering of sedimentary organic matter and impact carbon cycling.

title: 40 Ar/ 39 Ar geochronology, Sr Nd isotopes and melting conditions of the Dahongshan alkaline basalts: Constraints on mantle modification beneath the northern Yangtze Craton
description: Publication date: 30 September 2026 Source: Chemical Geology, Volume 720 Author(s): Yue Song, Xuan-Ce Wang, Simon A. Wilde, Xiang-Zhong Li, Chong-Jin Pang, Si-Yu Hu, Yang Luo, Jia-Xu Tang, Si-Zhe Fu
abstract: We present new groundmass 40Ar/39Ar ages, whole-rock major and trace element data, SrNd isotopic compositions, and P–T estimates for the Dahongshan alkaline basalts in the northern Yangtze Craton, China. Integrating these data with regional records demonstrates that Late Cretaceous mafic magmatism in the northern Yangtze Craton records a transition from subduction-modified lithospheric mantle to increasingly asthenosphere-influenced melting. Four representative samples yield concordant plateau-like weighted mean 40Ar/39Ar ages of 83.4–84.1 Ma (2σ), constraining the eruption of Dahongshan magmas to ca. 84 Ma. The basalts have intraplate, OIB-like trace element patterns, elevated LREE/HREE ratios, and a narrow range of SrNd isotopic compositions ((87Sr/86Sr)ᵢ = 0.704358–0.704800; εNd(t) = −0.80 to +1.35), indicating derivation from a moderately enriched, pyroxenite-influenced mantle source with a mafic component and only limited syn-ascent crustal assimilation. Low Ce/Pb and Nb/U ratios, together with pronounced positive Pb anomalies, are interpreted as source-inherited features rather than evidence for significant crustal assimilation. Primary melt reconstruction and complementary whole-rock major element modelling yield low- to moderate-pressure P–T estimates of 1.4–2.1 GPa and 1252–1356 °C, interpreted to record final melt–mantle equilibration or segregation during ascent rather than the depth of melt initiation. In contrast, REE systematics indicate a garnet-influenced melting signal, suggesting that melt generation was initiated deeper, probably near the garnet–spinel transition, before undergoing re-equilibration at shallower lithospheric levels. Regional comparisons support a temporal shift from Early Cretaceous lithosphere-derived arc-like magmatism to Late Cretaceous increasingly asthenosphere-influenced volcanism, followed by Cenozoic deeper-sourced alkaline basalts consistent with garnet-facies melting during post-extension thermal adjustment.

title: Mineralogical and geochemical fingerprints for quantifying modern glacial and paleo-weathering sediments in the Amundsen Sea, West Antarctica
description: Publication date: 30 September 2026 Source: Chemical Geology, Volume 720 Author(s): Hebin Shao, Yong Yu, Shouye Yang, Jianfeng He, Yulong Guo, Di Cai, Guangfu Luo, Yingchun Cui, Li Wu, Hao Zhang
abstract: Silicate weathering regulates Earth's carbon cycle and climate, yet paleo-weathering products in Antarctic marine sediments obscure primary weathering signatures, a major challenge in polar carbon cycle studies. The Amundsen Sea, a key marginal sea of West Antarctica, contains abundant paleo-weathering products (i.e. materials sourced from Pre-Oligocene sedimentary rocks and reworked into modern sediments), but quantitative constraints on their contributions to sediment provenance remain lacking. We analyzed 12 clay-sized surface sediment samples from the western Amundsen Sea via mineralogical, elemental geochemical, and Sr-Nd-Li-Mg isotopic analyses. Results show clear spatial heterogeneity: samples from the east side of this area show higher kaolinite, chemical index of alteration (CIA) and δ26Mg, along with lower δ7Li. The proxies reveal intense chemical weathering of the source bedrock in the pre-glacial warm interval. By contrast, samples from the west side are dominated by chlorite and illite, with lower CIA and δ26Mg but higher δ7Li, reflecting limited chemical weathering of the source bedrock. Mineralogical and geochemical indices effectively distinguish three sediment provenance endmembers (Post-Oligocene igneous rocks, Pre-Oligocene igneous rocks, and Pre-Oligocene sedimentary rocks), and a mass balance model based on εNd and δ26Mg isotopes was established to quantify their relative contributions to shelf sediment provenance. This model shows that paleo-weathering sediments account for up to 60% of clay-sized sediments from the eastern side of the western Amundsen Sea, with contributions of 30%–50% in coastal areas via ocean current transport, while clay-sized sediments from the west side are dominated by modern glacial weathering products of Post-Oligocene volcanic rocks (up to 64%). Our findings establish a multi-proxy mineralogical and geochemical fingerprint framework for distinguishing and quantifying modern glacial and paleo-weathering sediments in West Antarctica, and provide critical insights for paleoclimatic reconstruction and understanding the impact of glacial erosion on marine carbon cycle dynamics in Antarctica.

title: Alteration kinetics of basaltic glass in acidic conditions: The effect of temperature and pH on glass dissolution and alteration layer formation
description: Publication date: 30 September 2026 Source: Chemical Geology, Volume 720 Author(s): Arpad Pusztai, Bastien Wild, Samuel Tardif, Zijie Liu, François Guyot, Imene Esteve, Alejandro Fernandez-Martinez, Damien Daval
abstract: Quantifying basaltic glass alteration kinetics is essential for modelling carbon sequestration and global biogeochemical cycles. However, current literature rates diverge by up to two orders of magnitude due to surface area normalization uncertainties (BET vs. geometric) and conflicting reports on the pH-dependence of activation energies (E a ). In this study, we resolve these inconsistencies by combining Vertical Scanning Interferometry (VSI) and in situ synchrotron X-ray Reflectivity (XRR) to decouple glass network dissolution from Amorphous Silica-rich Surface Layer (ASSL) growth between 5 and 60 °C and pH 2–5. Our results demonstrate that both dissolution and ASSL growth proceed linearly over time, following a surface-reaction-controlled regime. We show that the surface retreat method (VSI) provides a robust, normalization-independent proxy for network breakdown, yielding rates consistent with Si release. Furthermore, XRR data reveal that steady-state ASSL densities decrease with increasing growth rates, suggesting the formation of more porous structures at low pH. Contrary to common assumptions in long-term field rates, we find no evidence of surface passivation: ASSLs remain permeable and do not act as diffusion barriers over weeks-long experiments, accounting for up to 80% of the total altered volume.
