Following calibration and validation, the integrated model was applied to quantitatively evaluate the response of reservoir water quality under different hydrological year types (wet/normal/dry) to multi-source pollution control measures. The results revealed clear variations in the total nitrogen (TN) reduction efficacy of different pollution control measures. Among these, livestock manure recycling (utilization rate ≥ 90%) was the most effective, followed by township sewage treatment. In contrast, fertilizer reduction yielded limited benefits (TN reduction < 1%), while wastewater treatment upgrading had no significant effect under the tested scenarios. Hydrological conditions also influenced the effectiveness of these measures, with TN reductions of 2–6% in normal years but less than 1% in dry years. Spatially, inflow responses exhibited pronounced heterogeneity among tributaries. Analyses of tracer-based transport and mean residence time indicated that reservoir-scale buffering and transport delays constrain the rapid transmission of upstream load reductions to downstream outflows. These findings indicate that reservoir water-quality responses to watershed pollution-control measures are jointly influenced by pollution-source type, hydrological conditions, and variability among inflowing tributaries, highlighting the need to prioritize management strategies in drinking-water reservoir systems.

title: Climate change and irrigation water demand: a review of modelling approaches and biophysical considerations
description: Publication date: September 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology, Volume 677, Part C Author(s): Shahin Solgi, Paul R. Petrie, Matthew J. Knowling, Ana Horta, Andrew Hall
abstract: Rising temperatures, shifting precipitation patterns, and elevated atmospheric CO2 concentrations are expected to influence future irrigation water demand (IWD) through complex interactions with crop growth and evapotranspiration processes. These biophysical dynamics are required for generating reliable seasonal and long-term projections under climate change. This systematic literature review analysed 80 peer-reviewed studies published between 2017 and 2024 to evaluate the methods used for projecting IWD under future climate scenarios. Due to differences in study design, model assumptions, and reporting formats, formal statistical comparison was not feasible. Instead, this review used evidence mapping to summarise the distribution and characteristics of the selected studies. Trends were identified for methodology, crop focus, and regional variation. maize, wheat, and rice dominated the research, collectively representing 70% of the studied crops. Although 40% of studies employed process-based simulation (PS) approaches, potential evapotranspiration (ET-P) methods were the most widely applied, used for 52% of the crops examined. Approximately 53% of studies projected an increase in IWD, 13% a decrease, and 28% reported mixed trends, depending on crop type, region, and scenario. Despite the relevance of CO2 fertilisation and climate-induced phenological changes, only 14% of studies accounted for both, with most incorporating either one or neither. The findings indicate that, despite the increasing complexity of PS models, simpler approaches such as ET-P and irrigation scheduling (Sch) continue to be widely used due to their lower data and resource demands. These methods potentially overlook crucial climate-sensitive processes, which may introduce bias into IWD projections. This review highlights how methodological choices can influence long-term projections of climate change impacts. The recommended research roadmap in this review would guide future studies to compare different IWD projection methodologies under identical climate, crop, soil, and crop/irrigation management conditions to achieve more robust and reliable projections and decision-making tools.

title: Design of stream gauge network using fuzzy entropy approach considering impact of climate change
description: Publication date: September 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology, Volume 677, Part C Author(s): Lisha Basheer
abstract: Stream gauge stations are important for measuring the discharge of streams and understanding flow. Designing stream gauge networks under climate change scenarios could provide valuable insights for hydrological monitoring and water resource management. This paper presents a fuzzy entropy-based methodology for the design of stream gauge network considering impact of climate change. Study area comprising of three river basins in Kerala (Periyar, Chalakkudi and Bharathappuzha) has seven stream gauge stations maintained by Central Water Commission (CWC). For incorporating impact of climate change, the input variables (rainfall, temperature and wind speed) for predicting future runoff are downscaled from Regional Climate Model (RCM). Analysis of existing stream gauge network is done considering observed and predicted flow values. Fuzzy Mutual Information Index (FMII) value is computed for each station and stream gauge deficit zones are identified. As per minimum density requirements of WMO (2008), required number of stations are calculated as ten which is more than the existing number of stations. For the design of new stream gauge network, possible locations of additional stations are chosen from outlet points obtained by delineating study area which yielded twelve stations. Flows at the possible locations of new stations together with the flows at the existing stations are used to compute entropy measures to determine the optimal locations of stations required for the new stream gauge network. For determining optimal station locations, one objective is to minimize fuzzy mutual information and the other is to maximize fuzzy joint entropy. The design stream gauge network thus obtained consists of ten stations in which five stations are existing stations and five stations are new locations. The design network can be regarded as best network in economical point of view and in satisfying minimum density requirements of WMO.

title: Deep learning-enhanced sequential updating of hydraulic parameters and state variables in groundwater models
description: Publication date: September 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology, Volume 677, Part C Author(s): Huiyang Qiu, Zejun Wang, Wanzhou Wang, Qi Li, Yuanzheng Zhang, Jiangjiang Zhang
abstract: As a fundamental component of the hydrological cycle, groundwater systems play a critical role in sustaining ecosystems, securing water resources, and supporting socio-economic development. However, substantial uncertainties remain in both parameter estimation and state prediction, limiting the reliability of groundwater models. Improving predictive accuracy therefore requires the sequential, real-time updating of model states and parameters using newly acquired observations. Although the ensemble Kalman filter (EnKF) has been widely applied for this purpose, its performance can degrade in non-Gaussian and strongly nonlinear systems, for which approaches based on transformations or multiple-point geostatistics have been proposed as effective remedies. In this study, we present an alternative strategy by introducing a deep learning (DL)-based update strategy into the EnKF framework, resulting in a hybrid ensemble filtering approach that integrates DL-based nonlinear updates with Kalman-type linear updates, termed EF(DL-K). The proposed method is designed to more effectively fuse information from numerical models and observations in complex groundwater systems. Compared with the conventional EnKF and a purely DL-based ensemble filter [EF(DL)], EF(DL-K) exhibits enhanced flexibility and robustness in the sequential updating of both hydraulic parameters and state variables in subsurface aquifer systems. The impact of the placement of the DL step within the EF(DL-K) framework is systematically investigated. The results show that EF(DL-K) yields assimilation performance comparable to that of the EnKF under Gaussian conditions, while achieving substantially improved joint state-parameter estimation under non-Gaussian conditions. Overall, EF(DL-K) provides a promising filtering-based data assimilation framework for real-time model-data integration and the dynamic updating of both parameters and state variables in groundwater systems.

title: Multi-resolution downscaling of inundation extents using deep learning
description: Publication date: September 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology, Volume 677, Part C Author(s): Chanyu Yang, Fiachra O’Loughlin
abstract: The application of deep learning models for downscaling flood inundation extents has been brought into focus in recent years. Considered as an alternative to physics-based models, deep learning models have the advantage of faster computational efficiency with acceptable accuracy. However, recent approaches in downscaling flood inundation extents have either: (1) taken a considerable amount of computational effort for model training; (2) focused on large flood events or large flood extents; or (3) only considered downscaling using a small number of scenarios and often only one. Inspired by the hybrid modelling approach, this study uses a hydrodynamic model to generate a time-series of low-resolution flood inundation extents and depths. This series is then downscaled into high-resolution flood inundation extents using a generative deep learning model. The proposed method is applied to an urbanised area in Dublin, Ireland, which covers 16.3 km 2 . Ten combinations of low- and high-resolution flood maps are used to evaluate the models’ performance. The results show that: (1) there is no obvious relationship between model performance and the magnitude of downscaling; (2) a deeper model architecture can provide better predictions and is more robust in classifying deeper flood depths without increasing prediction computational cost; (3) 18 times downscaling (90 m to 5 m) was found to be the most efficient and accurate model tested. The proposed deep learning model offers potential for real-time flood inundation forecasting, where coarser, faster inundation models can be downscaled to useful inundation maps without a significant loss in accuracy and without real-time computational overhead.

title: Catchment controls on nutrients at coastal outlets: a national typology for England and Wales
description: Publication date: September 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology, Volume 677, Part C Author(s): Hassan Mohamed, Naomi Greenwood, Richard J. Cooper, Carolyn Graves, Yi He
abstract: Riverine nutrient concentrations at coastal outlets reflect upstream catchment controls and underpin nutrient flux estimates. Existing catchment classifications are not tailored to this scale, limiting their application for interpreting land-to-sea patterns and informing management of marine pressures. This study develops a data-driven typology for 178 coast-draining catchments across England and Wales, grouping them into eight types through geospatial characterisation and clustering. Nutrient concentrations (2000–2024) were retrieved from water quality archives at 271 near-tidal sites. The resulting typology is structured along a topographic gradient, further differentiated by dominant bedrock permeability. A two-way analysis of variance (ANOVA) confirmed significant differences between types for NH4 +, NO3 − and PO4 3− (p < 0.001), with a significant seasonal effect for NO3 − and PO4 3− only. NO3 − exhibited strong seasonality in arable lowland low- and high-permeability catchments where winter medians (8.8 and 8.4 mg N/L) exceeded summer values (5.1 and 6.4 mg N/L), reflecting enhanced leaching. NH4 + showed limited seasonality, with variability governed by point-source inputs. PO4 3− displayed an inverse seasonal pattern, with higher summer concentrations from reduced dilution of point-source inputs. Despite representing only 1% of the total catchment area, the urban type dominated NH4 + and PO4 3− concentrations, peaking in winter for NH4 + (0.176 mg N/L) and summer for PO4 3− (0.51 mg P/L), while NO3 − was controlled by arable types, with increasing urban influence in recent years. These results provide a framework for targeting nutrient management to the dominant controls of each type, supporting more effective nutrient reduction measures under the UK Marine Strategy and OSPAR commitments.

title: Setting the standard? Comparison of the implementation of decision-support modeling standards in Australia and the Netherlands
description: Publication date: September 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology, Volume 677, Part C Author(s): J.O.E. Remmers, J.H.A. Guillaume, L.A. Melsen
abstract: Choices during model development can substantially affect its outcomes, raising concerns about accountability when these outcomes inform decision-making. One way to address accountability is through modeling standards. Yet, standards may seem at odds with expert judgment and the specificity of modeling question, raising questions about who initiates the standards, and how they are established and enforced in practice. We examine the initiation, development and establishment of hydrological modeling standards in two contrasting cases: the development of standard software for the Murray-Darling Basin in Australia, and the formulation of modeling guidelines in the Netherlands. In both cases, standards were introduced with the aim to address elements of accountability. We found that consensus played a central role, which required flexibility in the standardization, diluting its effect. Moreover, standards tend to prioritize certain ways of working, risking that certain methods lose value without any apparent reason. Like models themselves, standardization is not neutral, demanding careful development, application, evolution, maintenance and reflection.

title: Characterization of groundwater recharge in complex aquifer: an improved nonlinear Transfer Function-Noise model integrating groundwater reservoir mechanics
description: Publication date: September 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology, Volume 677, Part C Author(s): Xiangbo Meng, Xi Chen, Man Gao, Guangxuan Li, Yongda Liu
abstract: Accurate assessment of groundwater recharge is critical for sustainable water resource management. However, simulating recharge processes remains challenging in regions with deep groundwater depth, owing to the interplay among vadose zone heterogeneity, nonlinear recharge thresholds and switching behaviors, and delayed aquifer response. Conventional Transfer Function-Noise (TFN) models link stresses to groundwater fluctuations for recharge estimation, but their implicit curve fitting constrains physical interpretability in complex hydrogeological settings. To address these limitations, this study extends the TFN framework into the TFN-Tank formulation by coupling a root-zone-based nonlinear recharge model with a mechanistic groundwater reservoir module. Validated against six distinct dynamic patterns in the Daqing River Basin of North China Plain, the improved framework achieved high-fidelity groundwater simulations (NSE > 0.75) and consistently outperformed traditional TFN models (NSE gains of 0.014–0.089). Uncertainty analysis confirms that the improved model reduces simulation uncertainty and corrects lag-time overestimation in traditional TFN models. Applied to 186 monitoring wells in the Daqing River Basin, the improved model reveals that the infiltration recharge coefficient decreases spatially from 0.47 in piedmont areas to below 0.1 in the coastal plains. Notably, the infiltration recharge coefficient exhibits a non-monotonic pattern, first increasing and then decreasing with groundwater depth, while the lag time increases monotonically. As a physically informed, data-driven framework, TFN-Tank delineates the complete temporal evolution of recharge processes, thereby facilitating integration with regional groundwater models and sustainable groundwater resources management.

title: Spatial and temporal indicators of soil hydrodynamic response: the capillarity-gravity length and gravimetric time
description: Publication date: September 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology, Volume 677, Part C Author(s): D. Moret-Fernández, J. Tormo, J.J. Jiménez, B. Latorre
abstract: Understanding the dynamics of soil water movement is fundamental for hydrological research. This work uses two complementary indicators based on different relationships between the sorptivity, S(θi, θs) , and the saturated hydraulic conductivity (Ks ) to predict the hydrodynamic response of porous media. These indices are the gravimetric time (tgrav ) and the index defined as capillarity-gravity length, λ θ i , θ s = S θ i , θ s 2 K s . The parameter λ θ i , θ s , which is theoretically derived from the soil water retention curve, acts as a characteristic length that quantifies the equivalent water depth absorbed via capillarity during the infiltration process before the flow rate converges toward a constant, gravity-driven steady state. By evaluating the balance between capillary and gravity flows, both tgrav and λ θ i , θ s provides an assessment of the dominant hydrodynamic behavior of a porous medium based on simple tension disc infiltrometer measurements. Specifically, when gravity-driven flow dominates (low S θ i , θ s 2 and high Ks ), λ θ i , θ s and tgrav tends below 1 cm and 250 s, respectively, whereas capillary-dominant flow (high S θ i , θ s 2 and low Ks ) is reflected by λ θ i , θ s and tgrav values exceeding 3 cm and 2500 s, respectively. Both parameters were evaluated across a diverse range of porous media and subsequently contrasted with their corresponding cumulative infiltration curves. Then both indices were assessment through two field experiments. The first experiment compared λ θ i , θ s and tgrav measured at the soil surface across two regions with different aridity gradients. The second experiment assessed the soil matrix hydrodynamics across different soil managements. Analytical derivations showed that λ θ i , θ s defines the y-intercept of the long-term 1D infiltration function and both λ θ i , θ s and tgrav are sensitive to detect hydrodynamic differences between porous media, soil types, and management practices.

title: Biocrust functions in mitigating soil water and wind erosion after freezing-thawing
description: Publication date: September 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology, Volume 677, Part C Author(s): Yousong Cao, Yunxia Shen, Joshua Heitman, Bo Xiao
abstract: Freezing-thawing regulates soil structural stability in cold winters, and further governs soil responses to water and wind erosion during subsequent warm seasons. As multifunctional communities widespread in cold-winter drylands, biocrusts have been found to influence soil erosion. However, the specific mechanisms remain unclear. Particularly, previous studies have largely overlooked freezing-thawing, which is a critical prerequisite for water and wind erosion over the annual cycle. Here, we subjected biocrust and bare soil samples to 10–30 freezing-thawing cycles at varying antecedent moisture (0.15–0.35 cm3 cm−3), and then assessed their resistance to single raindrop splash, rainfall splash, runoff scouring, and wind erosion. After freezing-thawing, biocrusts exhibited 19.4%–61.9% higher raindrop penetration kinetic energy than bare soil, accompanied by a 16.2%–87.5% reduction in splash erosion amounts from both single raindrop and rainfall tests. Biocrusts also diminished the splash distance of soil particles by 5.4%–13.9%. Furthermore, after freezing-thawing, biocrusts increased the anti-scour coefficient of surface soil by 342%–1329% and decreased its detachment capacity by 77.0%–93.0%, thereby ultimately reducing the sediment yield. Moreover, after freezing-thawing, the wind erosion amount of biocrusts was much lower (3.14–12.58 g m−2) than that of bare soil (187–6144 g m−2). In essence, the erosion resistance of biocrusts after freezing-thawing mainly originated from their high structural stability, particularly higher macroaggregate content. Our study highlights the importance of biocrusts in soil protection after freezing-thawing, which could have broader potential implications for erosion-driven greenhouse gas emissions and ecosystem productivity in cold-winter drylands.

title: Determining and predicting single-storm erosion index in Sicily
description: Publication date: September 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology, Volume 677, Part C Author(s): V. Bagarello, V. Ferro, F. Gakunde, V. Pampalone
abstract: The single-storm erosion index, Re, expressing the rainfall erosive power, can be either calculated or estimated and it can be used for a variety of analyses, including the probabilistic assessment of soil water erosion phenomena. Calculation of Re according to the original procedure requires rainfall depth, he, and intensity data at short time intervals but their temporal resolution can change with the considered recording rain-gauge station. Estimating Re is sometimes necessary since rainfall intensity data could be unavailable in certain circumstances. An appropriate probability distribution law of the annual maximum values of Re has to be chosen for predicting single-storm erosivity values with a given return period. With reference to 8464 erosive rainfall events collected at 26 Sicilian stations in the 2002–2024 years, this investigation showed that: i) Re calculated by rainfall data measured at Δt = 30 min time intervals constituted the 88% of the corresponding calculations obtained by rainfall data collected at Δt = 10 min and time effects were particularly appreciable for relatively small rainfall depths (he ≤ 40 mm); ii) the power law relationship between Re and he parameterized by minimizing the sum of the squared residuals between the actual and the estimated Re values (optimization approach, OPT) yielded less biased Re predictions than the relationship parameterized by a linear regression analysis of the natural logarithm (ln-) transformed data; iii) power law relationships obtained in two different historical periods (1951–1970 and 2002–2024) yielded different Re predictions, likely as a consequence of climate change; iv) an envelope line of the Re vs. he data was usable to simply distinguish, for a given rainfall depth, expected from unexpected, Re values; and v) the annual maximum values of Re were distributed according to the Extreme Value Type-1 (EV1) distribution. In conclusion, rainfall temporal resolution effects on Re calculation can be expected to decrease as he increases. The OPT approach should be applied for parameterizing the Re predicting relationship. Using Re vs. he relationships developed in the past for estimating current erosivity is not recommended. The highest expected Re value for a given rainfall depth and the quantile, Re T, corresponding to a given return period, T, can easily be estimated and they should be taken into account for planning appropriate soil conservation measures given that total soil erosion in a long period is mostly due to a few particularly high erosive events.

title: Separating typhoon and non-typhoon rainfall reveals structural hydrological regime shifts in coastal-to-inland basins
description: Publication date: September 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology, Volume 677, Part C Author(s): Xiaojuan Qian, Sangyoung Son
abstract: Long-term hydrological change in typhoon-prone coastal-to-inland river basins presents growing challenges for flood risk assessment under a changing climate. Here, we develop a generalizable basin-scale diagnostic framework that separates typhoon and non-typhoon rainfall, embeds them in a Budyko-based runoff analysis, and quantifies spatially heterogeneous hydrological sensitivities applicable to coastal-to-inland systems worldwide. As a proof-of-concept demonstration, we apply this framework to the Qiantang River Basin (QRB), eastern China, a representative typhoon-prone coastal-to-inland basin influenced by the East Asian summer monsoon and Western North Pacific tropical cyclones. Using data from 11 stations during 1980–2020, the framework detects a precipitation-regime shift around 2009, after which annual rainfall increased by roughly 13–15% across subbasins and Budyko-estimated runoff potential also increased. The disproportionate runoff-potential increase in the coastal-adjacent Fuchun subbasin suggests possible amplification by land-surface modification and urbanization. Typhoon‑related precipitation, though only about 6% of annual totals, increased by nearly 50% after 2009 and showed a disproportionate contribution to extreme rainfall, reaching 28% of extreme volumes in the coastal‑adjacent subbasin, while inland extremes remained dominated by non‑typhoon processes. These results demonstrate that long-term hydrological changes in typhoon-prone coastal-to-inland basins can manifest as structural regime shifts in both precipitation composition and runoff generation. More broadly, the explicit separation of typhoon and non-typhoon rainfall within a Budyko framework provides a physically grounded and transferable diagnostic tool readily applicable to other typhoon-prone basins globally, supporting flood-risk and water-resources management under ongoing climate change.

title: Dynamic changes of vegetation in China under the stress of compound droughts
description: Publication date: September 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology, Volume 677, Part C Author(s): Anzhou Zhao, Wei Zhang, Xianfeng Liu, Lidong Zou, Shuaiqin Chen
abstract: Compound droughts characterized by the concurrent high vapor pressure deficit (VPD) and low soil moisture (SM) can intensify plant water stress and threaten ecosystem stability. However, their influence on vegetation has not been systematically quantified due to the absence of a unified metric. In this study, we developed a novel Standardized Compound Drought Index (SCDI) by integrating VPD and SM to capture the spatiotemporal evolution of compound droughts. We then investigated the dynamics of vegetation and its response to these compound droughts. The main findings are as follows: (1) From 1982 to 2020, the Normalized Difference Vegetation Index (NDVI) in China showed a significant upward trend (9.10 × 10−4 yr−1, p < 0.01), with the most pronounced increase observed in the Yellow River Basin (2.19 × 10−3 yr−1, p < 0.01). During the same period, the SCDI also exhibited a significant increasing trend (7.73 × 10−3 yr−1, p < 0.01), with the strongest increase found in the Continental River Basin (CRB) (2.77 × 10−2 yr−1, p < 0.01). Spatially, both NDVI and SCDI exhibited significant decreasing trends (p < 0.05) in northeastern and southwestern China; (2) Random forest modeling revealed that atmospheric CO2 concentration and the SCDI contributed 31.02% and 30.30% to the variability in vegetation dynamics, respectively. Although the CO2 fertilization effect partially mitigated the adverse impacts of compound droughts on vegetation growth. It was insufficient to fully offset the vegetation losses caused by these droughts in certain regions. Central and southwestern China demonstrated higher sensitivity to compound droughts, while southeastern China appeared more resilient. The SCDI thresholds corresponding to NDVI values below the 40th, 30th, 20th, and 10th percentiles were −1.30, −1.80, −2.11, and −2.30, respectively; (3) Under future climate scenarios (SSP1-2.6 to SSP5-8.5), the continued rise in atmospheric CO2 concentrations is expected to counterbalance the potential NDVI decline caused by compound droughts, maintaining an overall upward trend in vegetation greenness. This trend is expected to be more pronounced in inland western and northern China. Despite the anticipated intensification of soil-atmosphere compound droughts, the growing CO2 fertilization effect may play an increasingly important role in sustaining vegetation growth. Overall, this study advances the understanding of vegetation responses to compound droughts and provides a scientific basis for ecological restoration and regional climate adaptation strategies.

title: Multi-station rainfall–runoff–operation model for assessing flood characteristics in a cascading dam system under the impacts of climate change and sediment dynamics
description: Publication date: September 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology, Volume 677, Part C Author(s): Phuoc Sinh Nguyen, Sameh Ahmed Kantoush, Sohei Kobayashi, Seyed Amirreza Tabataba Vakili, Vahid Nourani
abstract: This study aimed at (i) developing a multi-station deep learning rainfall–runoff–operation (DL-RRO) model for cascading dam systems and (ii) applying the model through the large ensemble dataset for Policy Decision-Making for Future Climate Change (d4PDF) to assess flood characteristic changes. The DL-RRO model was developed using a Long Short-Term Memory network that coupled rainfall–runoff processes and mimicked existing dam operation rules by learning operational logic from observed data. Dynamic water level–storage curves were generated to account for time-varying increases in sediment storage. The proposed method was applied to the upper Chikugo River Basin (CRB), where the Shimouke and Matsubara Dams play a critical role in flood control in Kyushu, Japan. The model showed high performance when trained, validated, and tested with 40 years (1986–2025) of hourly hydrological observations (NSE = 0.89, RMSE = 18.90 m3/s). Subsequently, d4PDF rainfall data for the future scenarios (2031–2090 and 2051–2110; 1,440 ensemble-year) were imposed to the DL-RRO model. Analysis of 8,725 simulated flood events revealed increased flood frequency and notable changes in hydrograph characteristics. Projected 100-year return flood may increase by +53 % at Shimouke and +165 % at Matsubara under future scenarios, exceeding existing spillway design capacities. Under the synergistic impacts of climate change and sediment dynamics, amplified flood characteristics may intensify flood-driven sediment deposition, leading to further reductions in flood control capacity of up to +2.9 % at the Shimouke and +4.1 % at the Matsubara. These findings highlight the urgent need to upgrade dams, revise operations and sedimentation management strategies in the upper CRB.

title: Tide-induced groundwater table fluctuations in a coastal unconfined aquifer with the seaward boundary featuring a slope break
description: Publication date: September 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology, Volume 677, Part C Author(s): Huawen Zhao, Ye Ma, Xuan Wu, Xiaogang Chen, Ling Li
abstract: Analyzing tidal water table fluctuations can provide insights into the connectivity between coastal aquifers and the ocean. This study examined tidal propagation in an aquifer with a seaward boundary that has a slope break caused by a coastal levee. Such boundary conditions are common along reclaimed or protected shorelines but have been poorly studied. Field observations revealed a discontinuous and truncated groundwater response to tidal forcing, varying with the tidal range over the spring-neap cycle. Strong second harmonic tidal signals were also observed. We developed an analytical solution, based on a Fourier series approximation of the slope-break boundary condition, to examine the mechanism of the observed tidal groundwater dynamics, validated by numerical simulations. The results showed that the slope break truncates tidal forcing during ebb, due to the formation of an extensive seepage face. This truncation generated second harmonics, which propagated into the aquifer. The study presents an analytical method for dealing with complex tidal forcing associated with slope-break coastal morphology. The findings advance understanding of coastal groundwater table fluctuations in response to oceanic tides.

title: An efficient solver for the Richards equation for variably saturated flows in porous media
description: Publication date: September 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology, Volume 677, Part C Author(s): Xuelong Gu, Qi Wang
abstract: We present a nonlinear multigrid solver for the Richards equation in variably saturated porous media with strongly nonlinear and spatially heterogeneous hydraulic conductivity and water-retention relationships. In the solver, the governing equation is discretized using a second-order conservative finite-difference scheme in space and an implicit backward difference formula in time. The central innovation of the solver is a Nonlinear Gauss–Seidel (NGS) smoother that combines a triangular splitting of the diffusion operator with diagonal stabilization. This splitting yields an update scheme that consists of a sequence of locally decoupled scalar nonlinear problems, each of which can be solved efficiently and robustly with a few Newton iterations. Under monotonicity assumptions, we establish L ∞ -convergence of the NGS iteration and derive explicit conditions for the stabilization parameters. Numerical results for benchmark infiltration, drainage, and root-uptake problems demonstrate that the NGS-based multigrid framework is both computationally efficient and robust.

title: Tracking long-term dynamics of soil salinization using a model combining convolutional neural network and Transformer
description: Publication date: September 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology, Volume 677, Part C Author(s): Haohao Liu, Bin Guo, Xingchao Yang, Yilong Liu, Yujie Huo, Yuehua Zhong, Jianlin Wang
abstract: Accurately tracking long-term soil salinization dynamics remains challenging, particularly in highly heterogeneous regions. Here, we propose a novel approach based on the Convolutional Neural Network (CNN)-Transformer model for the spatiotemporal prediction of soil salinization using multi-source remote sensing data. The model adopts a cascaded structure that integrates the capabilities of CNN and Transformer to extract spatial contextual information and capture global spatiotemporal dependencies, enabling robust modeling of salinization dynamics. We compared the CNN-Transformer model with common machine learning and deep learning models in terms of soil salt content (SSC) prediction performance. To enhance model interpretability, we used SHapley Additive exPlanations (SHAP) to quantify the contributions of salinization-related features to SSC prediction. Using the proposed method, we achieved dynamic monitoring of soil salinization in the Yellow River Delta (YRD). The results indicate the following: (1) The CNN-Transformer model achieved the highest prediction accuracy (R2 = 0.71, RMSE = 3.36 g kg−1, RPIQ = 2.24) and demonstrated good spatial generalization under spatially independent validation, with spatial prediction results exhibiting fine-grained local details and accurately capturing the complex spatial distribution of soil salinity. (2) Vegetation type factors (VTFs) and the topographic factor contributed most to SSC prediction, followed by salinity indices, vegetation indices, and soil moisture-related indices. (3) Overall, from 2002 to 2022, soil salinization in the YRD was alleviated. Salinization intensity was markedly lower after autumn harvest than after spring plowing, primarily due to seasonal climatic-hydrological variations and the leaching effects of summer precipitation and irrigation. This study provides a paradigm combining deep learning with multi-source remote sensing data for the dynamic monitoring of soil salinization.

title: Hydroclimatic variability challenges apparent decadal improvements in riverine water quality across coastal watersheds
description: Publication date: September 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology, Volume 677, Part C Author(s): Shengyue Chen, Jinliang Huang, Ruping Zheng, Shijie Jiang
abstract: Coastal riverine environments face escalating degradation under dual climatic and anthropogenic pressures, yet high-resolution, systematic assessments remain constrained by spatiotemporally fragmented observations. Here we present a coupled deep-learning framework to robustly reconstruct daily runoff alongside multi-species pollutant concentrations and fluxes during 2010–2024 across 132 riverine sites in a representative coastal province of China. The reconstructed high-fidelity datasets reveal acute vulnerability in coastal regions and headwater systems, where intense anthropogenic stressors coincide with restricted dilution capacities. Over the past 15 years, riverine concentrations of total phosphorus, ammonia nitrogen, and permanganate index generally declined, whereas total nitrogen exhibited an upward trajectory; runoff reductions, concurrently, moderated downstream pollutant exports. Interpretable machine learning identifies urbanization, agriculture, runoff, and temperature as primary impacting factors of spatial variability in water quality baselines and trends. Critically, hydroclimatic shifts exert a stronger signature on long-term pollutant trends than human interventions alone, implying that the efficacy of current management interventions is likely overestimated due to natural climate variability over-amplification. This hydroclimatic non-stationarity is further manifested across interannual and event scales, where storm-induced pollutant pulses temporarily reverse decadal restoration gains. Our findings highlight the necessity of integrating hydroclimatic non-stationarity into watershed management, advocating for dynamic, targeted interventions in pollution hotspots and during high-flow periods to guarantee sustainable water security.

title: A general two-dimensional analytical solution for solute transport in anisotropic porous media with time-varying velocity field, different contaminant sources, and initial contamination
description: Publication date: September 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology, Volume 677, Part C Author(s): Luigi Cimorelli, Andrea D’Aniello
abstract: This study presents a novel two-dimensional analytical solution for solute transport in homogeneous porous media accounting for the effects of anisotropy in presence of adsorption and decay. The solution is derived using Green’s function for an infinite domain and extends existing analytical formulations by relaxing several simplifying assumptions commonly adopted in literature. In particular, the proposed analytical solution accounts for the effects of mechanical dispersion along the non-principal direction of groundwater flow as well as for the dependency of the dispersion tensor on the actual groundwater velocity field, without simplifications or convenient orientations of the model domain. The solution is also general as allows to account for: i) bi-directional groundwater velocity field and its variation over time; ii) source terms of different geometries (e.g., point, line, and surface sources) and temporal variability; iii) general initial concentration distributions of the contaminant concentration. The proposed analytical solution is also tested over benchmark problems conceived with a well-known numerical model for flow and transport in porous media (COMSOL Multiphysics®), and the agreement between the two is excellent.

title: Seasonal controls, recharge thresholds, and hydrological memory in karst groundwater dynamics revealed by interpretable deep learning
description: Publication date: September 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology, Volume 677, Part C Author(s): Linxian Huang, Henghua Zhu, Qichen Hao, Yong Xiao, Hao Liang, Zhenghe Xu, Chuanshun Zhi, Xiaonong Hu
abstract: Quantifying groundwater responses to climate forcing in karst systems remains difficult because recharge is nonlinear, threshold-dependent, and modulated by antecedent storage. We developed an interpretable deep learning framework to diagnose seasonal controls, threshold-like recharge behavior, and hydrological memory in the Baotu Spring karst watershed of northern China. A 66-year groundwater-level (GWL) record was segmented to isolate the period primarily controlled by meteorological forcing. Daily precipitation (P) and temperature (T) data from 2012 to 2024 were then used to train a long short-term memory model, and Expected Gradients together with Additive Decomposition quantified driver contributions and temporal memory. The model accurately reproduced groundwater dynamics in independent testing (Nash-Sutcliffe efficiency (NSE) = 0.93, coefficient of determination (R2) = 0.95, and root mean square error (RMSE) = 0.155 m). Attribution analysis revealed a clear seasonal hierarchy: summer exerted the strongest model-attributed control on groundwater variability, whereas autumn contributed secondarily through delayed recharge transmission. At the annual scale, P attributions became more positive when annual P exceeded 620 mm and GWLs were above 28.5 m, suggesting a threshold-like shift toward stronger positive model-attributed GWL sensitivity. At the event scale, the strongest positive P-related attribution occurred for daily P of 11.4–41.3 mm; smaller events were consistent with vadose-zone replenishment, whereas larger events suggested reduced marginal recharge efficiency due to greater runoff partitioning. High-GWL events were dominated by rainfall forcing, with short memory in summer, whereas winter rainfall memory extended to approximately five months; low-GWL events were linked to persistent P deficits, elevated T, and unfavorable rainfall-intensity distributions. These model-derived indicators support recharge assessment and groundwater-drought early warning in heterogeneous karst systems.

title: How does temperature causally influence short-term streamflow response? Evidence from 1604 catchments across the UK, Central Europe, and Australia
description: Publication date: September 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology, Volume 677, Part C Author(s): Hossein Abbasizadeh, Petr Maca, Urmi Ninad, Martin Hanel
abstract: Temperature is a key climatic driver of streamflow through its interactions with precipitation and hydrological processes. While its influence on streamflow has mainly been studied in terms of long-term mean changes, effects on precipitation, or extreme events, its short-term causal effects across long historical records remain poorly understood. Here, we investigate the immediate (within a few days) causal effect of temperature on streamflow across 1604 catchments spanning diverse hydroclimatic regions. We analyze 30 years (1985–2015) of daily temperature, precipitation, and streamflow data using the PCMCIplus causal discovery algorithm, applied to large catchment samples from Central Europe, the United Kingdom, and Australia. To quantify the nonlinear causal effect of temperature on streamflow, we use the optimal adjustment set method. This approach identifies 25 types of streamflow responses to temperature (Q ∼ T), which are grouped into 8 main categories. Results show similar Q ∼ T response patterns can occur across different Köppen–Geiger climate regions, even when driven by different processes. Also, substantial spatial heterogeneity is observed within individual climate regions, highlighting the complex causal interactions among temperature, precipitation, and streamflow at the catchment scale. Soil conductivity, snow fraction, and topographic characteristics are dominant controls on Q ∼ T variability. Catchments with high elevations and large snow fractions, primarily in Central Europe, frequently exhibit positive streamflow responses to warming, reflecting strong controls from snowmelt and storage. The influence of temperature on streamflow also varies across short timescales. Streamflow reductions associated with higher temperatures ( T max − ) become more pronounced above freezing at lag 0, suggesting stronger controls from evapotranspiration and atmospheric water demand, whereas at longer lags freezing-related processes dominate. In contrast, positive streamflow responses to warming ( T max + ) tend to occur at longer lags, potentially reflecting delayed snowmelt and catchment storage release processes. However, these lag-dependent behaviors vary substantially across hydroclimatic regions and catchment conditions. Tropical catchments show the most stable effective temperatures across lags, while arid, cold, and temperate catchments exhibit greater variability.

title: Tailoring soil moisture data to diverse accuracy needs: a multi-objective optimization and point-surface fusion framework
description: Publication date: September 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology, Volume 677, Part C Author(s): Xiaoxiao Min, Si-Bo Duan, Songchao Chen, Yulin Shangguan, Zhou Shi
abstract: Soil moisture (SM) data from various microwave remote sensing satellites and land surface models exhibit distinct accuracy characteristics across diverse landscapes and climates. Data fusion based on Linear Weighted Averaging (LWA) offers opportunities to achieve globally improved SM estimates. Different practical applications require specific accuracy metrics to define SM measurement requirements, and no single metric can encompass all attributes of SM. However, currently popular fusion techniques under LWA scheme, such as Triple Collocation Analysis (TCA) and Three-Cornered Hat (TCH), typically focus on enhancing only a single accuracy objective (e.g., maximizing temporal correlation or minimizing random errors) and impose strict requirements on the error covariances and the number of input datasets. Point-surface (P-S) fusion has gained increasing attention for its potential to overcome the inherent limitations of satellite retrievals or model simulations. This study proposes a novel Multi-objective (MO) P-S fusion framework that leverages Bayesian Model Averaging (BMA) to relax these stringent constraints while simultaneously incorporating ground measurements to calibrate coarse-scale SM estimates. Crucially, it considers multiple different but complementary accuracy metrics as optimization objectives, enabling application-oriented customization of SM products. Specifically, we combined four satellite products from the Soil Moisture Active Passive (SMAP), the Soil Moisture Ocean Salinity (SMOS), the Advanced Microwave Scanning Radiometer 2 (AMSR2), and the Advanced Scatterometer (ASCAT) sensors/missions, and three model products from the Global Land Data Assimilation System (GLDAS) Noah model, the Modern-Era Retrospective Analysis for Research and Applications Land version 2 reanalysis (MERRA2), and the European Centre for Medium-Range Weather Forecasts Reanalysis 5 (ERA5)-Land, calibrated using in-situ observations from the International Soil Moisture Network. Compared to traditional single-objective maximum likelihood (ML) estimator, this work concurrently optimized four objectives widely relevant to practical applications: unbiased Root Mean Squared Error (ubRMSE), Pearson correlation (R), Negative Log-Likelihood (NLL), and Continuous Ranked Probability Score (CRPS), through the Multi-ALgorithm Genetically Adaptive Multi-objective (AGLGAM) algorithm. In-situ validations demonstrated that the fusion products generated by MO optimization achieved statistically significant improvements in both deterministic and probabilistic accuracy, providing optimal SM information both overall and across distinct land covers and climates. Compared with the best-performing parent product, the fusion product achieved maximum overall improvements of 0.035 in R, 0.0046 cm3/cm3 in ubRMSE, 0.187 in NLL, and 0.004 cm3/cm3 in CRPS. Furthermore, they significantly outperformed the ML-optimized fusion product, as well as those based on other model averaging techniques (Bates–Granger Averaging (BGA) and Granger Ramanathan Averaging (GRA)) and collocation-based fusion techniques (TCA and TCH). This study is the first to introduce an application-oriented SM fusion framework. By generating Pareto-optimal weight solutions spanning the entire trade-off surface among diverse accuracy metrics, this framework produces high-quality SM fusion products optimized for specific metrics as well as those balanced across multiple metrics, fully addressing the diverse accuracy requirements of various practical applications.

title: Urbanization is associated with changes in the sensitivity of water quality to drought
description: Publication date: September 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology, Volume 677, Part C Author(s): Dongxin Tang, Pengcheng Sun, Shengzhi Huang, Xiaoting Wei, Yifei Li, Hao Cui, Dong Liu, Fuqiang Wang, Jingqing Gao
abstract: Rapid global urbanization has made water-quality degradation a core issue in assessing river health and aquatic ecosystem conditions. However, under a warming climate, the coupled relationships among urbanization, drought, and water quality remain unclear. In this study, we used regression analysis together with multiple statistical approaches to evaluate the sensitivity of two key water-quality indicators, specific conductance (SC) and water temperature (WT), to the relative discharge ratio (Q/MQ), which was used as a drought-related low-flow indicator. We also systematically analyzed how SC and WT varied with Q/MQ under different levels of urbanization. The results showed that SC followed a power-law response to Q/MQ and was significantly negatively correlated with the relative discharge ratio. WT showed clear seasonal contrasts in its response to Q/MQ: in the warm season, higher Q/MQ corresponded to lower WT, whereas in the cold season, higher Q/MQ corresponded to higher WT. We distinguished urbanization-related baseline shifts in water quality from drought-related low-flow sensitivity, defined as the response magnitude of SC or WT to changes in Q/MQ. The sensitivity of SC to relative discharge changes tended to be weaker at higher IMP levels. Based on the excess SC response, defined as P0.5 − 1, the SC response in low-urbanization basins was 23.48% and 129.03% higher than that in moderately and highly urbanized basins, respectively. In contrast, the response magnitude of WT to Q/MQ tended to be stronger at higher IMP levels. The WT response magnitude in highly urbanized basins was 47.89% and 70.34% higher than that in moderately and low-urbanization basins, respectively. Overall, urbanization was associated with changes in the sensitivity of water quality to relative discharge changes under drought-related low-flow conditions. This work characterized the response relationships between Q/MQ and SC and WT and documented how their sensitivities varied across urbanization levels. It provides scientific evidence to support watershed water-quality and river-health management for cities with different degrees of urban development.

title: Assessing streamflow depletion from agricultural groundwater use in headwater catchments using storage-discharge functions
description: Publication date: September 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology, Volume 677, Part C Author(s): Philip Georgakakos, David Dralle, Chris Dillis, Jesse Hahm, Dana Lapides, Theodore Grantham
abstract: Groundwater extraction can deplete streamflow in headwater catchments, but the complexity of subsurface hydrological processes make impacts difficult to detect. Using hydrograph-inferred hillslope groundwater storage and streamflow relationships, we propose a novel approach to estimate streamflow depletion from groundwater pumping that is well-suited to areas with limited groundwater monitoring infrastructure. We apply this method in two well-studied watersheds in California’s North Coast to quantify potential hydrologic impacts of cannabis agriculture, which is concentrated in the region and has been identified as a potential threat to salmon-bearing streams. We use a scenario-based approach to explore the relative effects of cannabis cultivation area, irrigation water source (groundwater pumping vs. surface diversion), irrigation efficiency, stream discharge at the onset of the growing season, and lithology on streamflow depletion risk. Our models show that Elder Creek, a perennial stream, could be de-watered by the late dry season with high levels (1% land cover) of cannabis irrigation from groundwater when dry season discharge is low at the start of the season (1 mm/day). In Dry Creek, a non-perennial stream, dry season flow cessation could be advanced by five weeks from similar levels of cannabis water demands. Streamflow impacts are more pronounced in drier years, and the impacts from well-water extraction exhibit a muted effect relative to surface water diversion of the same volume. Storage-discharge functions like those in our case study can estimate how groundwater extraction affects headwater streams wherever streamflow data exist.

title: Sources and transport of potassium in a typical carbonate-type lake (Bangor Co) on the Qinghai-Tibet Plateau: Constraints from potassium isotopes
description: Publication date: September 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology, Volume 677, Part C Author(s): Jiangdi Zhou, Binkai Li, Jiangang Jiao, Maoyong He, Zhongli Tang, Yuanyuan Cheng, Zhengyan Li, Jiaxin Luo, Huihui Rao, Jing Wen, Li Deng, Zhikang Liu
abstract: With the development of measurement techniques, K isotope composition (δ41K) has become a sensitive tracer of surface processes. The evolution of K-Li-B in salt lakes remains insufficiently constrained and a single isotope system cannot resolve the behavior of multiple elements. Bangor Co is a typical carbonate-type salt lake on the Qinghai-Tibet Plateau with relatively simple recharge condition and the absence of extensive K-salt mineral precipitation, making it an ideal site to study early-stage salt lake evolution. This study focuses on K isotope compositions in river (−0.12‰), cold springs (−0.72‰ to 0.02‰), and brines (−0.76‰ to − 0.36‰), together with hydrochemistry, Li and B isotopes. These data indicate that K in Bangor Co is mainly sourced from silicate weathering, geothermal inputs, and the redissolution of lacustrine sediments. The δ41K fractionation observed in the brines may reflect the important influence of clay mineral adsorption, with inferred K removal fractions of 0.29–0.55. Comparison of K, Li and B isotopes reveals decoupled geochemical behavior among elements and establishes a conceptual model for carbonate-type salt lakes. This study demonstrates that δ41K is an effective tracer in carbonate-type salt lake catchments. A multi-isotope approach provides a useful framework for understanding solute evolution in carbonate-type salt lakes and similar evaporitic systems.

title: Microplastics in karst groundwater: a review of current findings and methodological biases
description: Publication date: September 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology, Volume 677, Part C Author(s): Syeda Maria Zainab, Dan Lapworth, Richard Cross, Katherine Pond, Monica Felipe-Sotelo, Louise Maurice
abstract: Karst aquifers are globally important yet highly vulnerable water resources. Their rapid recharge, limited natural filtration, and conduit-dominated flow make them susceptible to contamination, including by emerging pollutants such as microplastics (MPs). While MPs are well documented in marine, freshwater, and terrestrial systems, their occurrence and behaviour in karst groundwater remain poorly understood. This review synthesises 22 published studies on MPs in karst caves, springs, wells, and boreholes, assessing comparability using a widely applied quality assessment framework and a critical evaluation of methodological influences on reported MP concentrations and characteristics. Reported concentrations vary by several orders of magnitude (0.001–911 particles/L), which is likely to reflect both karst environmental variability and methodological differences in sampling design, detection limits, contamination control, and analytical specificity. Temporal datasets remain limited, but existing studies suggest high-flow events substantially increase MP loads. No single analytical technique is quantitative across the full diversity of MPs, each being inherently selective toward sizes, shapes, or polymers. Notably, stereomicroscopy appears to overrepresent fibres, while low-density separation, such as sodium chloride solutions, miss higher-density plastics. These findings highlight the need for clear reporting of the operational definition of MPs in each study to improve cross-study comparability. We propose a harmonised sampling and analytical workflow to support future karst MP research, alongside the continued need for robust quality assurance/quality control practices, broader geographic coverage, and higher temporal resolution sampling. More work beyond simple concentration reporting is needed to investigate mechanistic processes driving MP transport and fate.

title: Experimental study on pore–permeability evolution during mineral dissolution with dynamic variations in specific surface area and tortuosity
description: Publication date: September 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology, Volume 677, Part C Author(s): Yaohui Wang, Hui Cheng, Shilin Zhang, Donghui Wang, Qingcheng He, Fugang Wang
abstract: In the evolution of groundwater systems, pore structure evolution induced by water–rock reactions significantly influences the flow properties of porous media. However, existing porosity–permeability relationship models often neglect the dynamic variations in pore-structure parameters, such as the specific surface area (SSA) and tortuosity, when describing mineral dissolution-dominated reactive transport processes. Moreover, the regulatory role of hydrodynamic conditions on the rate of pore-structure evolution lacks systematic experimental constraints. In this study, sandstone dissolution by a carbonic acid solution was investigated experimentally. The dynamic variations in SSA and tortuosity during dissolution and their effects on permeability were quantitatively characterized. The results show that increases in porosity during mineral dissolution are accompanied by significant decreases in SSA and tortuosity, and that both parameters exhibit stable, approximately linear negative correlations with porosity. As hydrodynamic conditions shift from diffusion- to advection-dominated regimes, the decreasing rates of SSA and tortuosity increase markedly, indicating that hydrodynamic conditions exert significant control on the rate of pore-structure evolution. Linear empirical relationships among SSA, tortuosity, and porosity were established and incorporated into a normalized Kozeny–Carman model to evaluate the effect of dynamic pore-structure evolution on relative permeability. Compared with a porosity-only K–C-type model, this experimentally constrained formulation better captures the observed permeability enhancement during mineral dissolution. This study provides experimental support for the representation of porosity–permeability relationships in reactive transport modeling and offers important references for groundwater flow prediction and solute transport characterization.

title: Deep learning approaches for streamflow flash drought prediction across the contiguous United States
description: Publication date: September 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology, Volume 677, Part C Author(s): Sophia Bakar, Hoang Hai Nguyen, Hyunglok Kim, Venkataraman Laskhmi
abstract: Reliable drought prediction is crucial for early warning and decision-making regarding drought-related disasters. Flash droughts, characterized by their rapid onset and severe impacts, are challenging to predict and present critical challenges to water resource management. Specifically, streamflow flash droughts (SFDs) are significant as they directly influence water supply for irrigation, industry, and domestic use. Traditional hydrologic models and drought early warning systems are primarily designed to capture slowly evolving drought conditions and often fail to represent rapid transitions in streamflow that characterize the onset of SFDs. Despite increasing attention to the identification and characterization of SFDs, their prediction remains unexplored. This study evaluates the ability of different deep learning architectures, especially the Temporal Fusion Transformer (TFT), in comparison to the widespread baseline Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) model and a two-source LSTM incorporating static catchment attributes, to predict SFDs based on streamflow percentiles. The model training and performance evaluation were conducted using hydroclimatic datasets from 671 Catchment Attributes and Meteorology for Large-sample Studies (CAMELS) catchments in the contiguous United States. Performance was evaluated using standard accuracy and event detection metrics. Results show that the TFT achieved the highest overall performance, with a median KGE of 0.87, RMSE of 0.13, MAE of 0.10, and a correlation coefficient of 0.91, outperforming the LSTM with static features (median KGE = 0.81) and the baseline LSTM (KGE = 0.78). In terms of detecting SFDs, the TFT showed the highest median detection rate and lowest miss rate across all models. These improvements were consistent across most catchments and hydroclimatic regions, indicating robust performance gains relative to LSTM-based approaches, although some regions with complex hydrologic behavior remained challenging for all models. While model performance varied across hydroclimatic regions, particularly in data-sparse or hydrologically complex areas, the integration of static attributes and attention-based mechanisms consistently improved predictive skill. These findings demonstrate that Transformer-based models can improve prediction of rapid streamflow changes associated with the onset of SFDs; however, the results are based on deterministic predictions and do not explicitly quantify predictive uncertainty. These findings contribute new insights into the spatial patterns and physical drivers of model performance under non-stationary climate conditions.

title: Reducing undercatch in the Geonor snow gauge using CFD-based shield design modification
description: Publication date: September 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology, Volume 677, Part C Author(s): Sadra Seifi, Jeffery Hoover, Pierre E. Sullivan
abstract: Wind-induced undercatch remains a major source of bias in snowfall measurements for catchment gauges used in solid precipitation. Most previous studies address this bias using empirical post-measurement corrections, whereas fewer attempts have been made to reduce the underlying aerodynamic causes through shield design. This study examines whether modest modifications to the slat-edge geometry of the single-Alter shield used with a Geonor T200B gauge can improve snowfall collection under windy conditions. A validated three-dimensional steady RANS–Lagrangian particle-tracking model is used to simulate snow particles with diameters of 0.25–5.0 mm under ambient horizontal wind speeds of 1–7 m/s. The unshielded gauge is included as a reference baseline for interpreting the aerodynamic effect of shielding. The results show that near-orifice updrafts and energetic vortical structures are the main flow features responsible for particle deflection. Among the tested geometries, the configuration with a slat-edge angle of β = 15 ∘ most effectively reduces the updraft while avoiding excessive local turbulence, increasing the overall collection efficiency averaged over the simulated wind-speed range by 11.9% relative to the standard single-Alter shield, with gains of up to 27.0% at the highest ambient wind speeds considered. Particle-deposition patterns also shift from the windward to the leeward slat surfaces; this matters because it may reduce leading-edge icing and help preserve aerodynamic performance during operation.

title: On nonlinear thermal dispersion and interfacial heat exchange in the filled fracture-matrix systems near the wellbore
description: Publication date: September 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology, Volume 677, Part C Author(s): Wenguang Shi, Quanrong Wang, Aohan Jin, Chong Ma, Fan Hu, Yanxin Wang
abstract: Numerous models have been developed to investigate heat transfer behaviors in the fracture-matrix systems. However, the thermal dispersion is either neglected or treated as linear, Fourier’s law is preferred for determining the heat exchange flux at the fracture-matrix interface, and the thermal mixing effect within the wellbore is generally ignored. We herein derive two analytical models of heat transport in filled fracture-matrix systems near the wellbore to improve existing models, in which the interfacial heat exchange flux between fracture and matrix is described by the Newton’s law of cooling and Fourier’s law, respectively. A power-exponential function is employed to describe nonlinear thermal dispersion. A time-dependent model is employed to characterize the thermal mixing effect. A comparison of the two proposed models shows nearly same temperature distributions along the fracture, whereas significant temperature differences occur in the matrix for low heat transfer coefficient ( h ) values. As h increases, the heat exchange flux between the fracture and the matrix increases, and the difference between the newly developed model based on Newton’s law of cooling and Fourier’s decreases, eventually yielding the same results. Since the thermal mixing effect model has not yet been validated with field data, it is tested in this study. Meanwhile, a simplified model is proposed to quickly evaluate whether thermal mixing effect should be considered. Compared to previous models, we find that neglecting the thermal mixing effect significantly overestimates the temperature distribution in the fracture. An increased exponent in nonlinear thermal dispersion model results in a reduction of fracture temperature. A larger thermal dispersivity decreases temperature near the injection well and increases it farther from the well. The models proposed in this study could also be applied to porous aquifer-aquitard systems. This work provides new insights for choosing models based on interfacial heat exchange processes in fracture-matrix systems.

title: MvReNowcast: Disentangling radar product features for improved nowcasting of raincloud evolution
description: Publication date: September 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology, Volume 677, Part C Author(s): Hongxu Zhu, Ji Chen, Xunlai Chen, Waikin Wong, Chao Tan, Hongyi Yao, Xianqi Jiang
abstract: Accurate radar echo extrapolation is fundamental for real-time monitoring and nowcasting severe rainfall events. However, most existing deep learning approaches tend to formulate this task in a simple manner, overlooking the physical mechanisms that govern radar echo evolution. This limitation restricts model interpretability and degrades nowcast reliability under dynamically evolving weather conditions. To this end, this study proposes a physics-informed deep learning framework that explicitly integrates prior hydrometeorological information into the radar echo extrapolation process. The evolution of radar reflectivity is decomposed into two distinct yet complementary components: advection and residual intensity evolution. By coupling both components within a unified neural architecture, the framework captures both large-scale displacement and small-scale intensity evolution of radar echoes. Numerical experiments conducted on multi-temporal radar datasets demonstrate that the proposed method outperforms the conventional data-driven benchmark model in both nowcasting accuracy and spatial consistency. The decomposition method not only reduces prediction errors but also enhances the physical interpretability of deep learning model outputs, allowing a more transparent attribution of echo evolution to dominant hydrometeorological processes. Quantitative verification confirms the MvReNowcast model’s systematic superiority over the Baseline. The performance gap widens significantly with time, reaching relative improvements exceeding 120.8 % on CSI30 and 52.9 % on CSI40 at the 120-minute forecast horizon. This study highlights the potential of physics-informed separation strategies in bridging the gap between data-driven and process-based modeling for rainfall nowcasting. The proposed approach provides a physically consistent and computationally efficient framework that can be extended to other hydrometeorological prediction tasks.

title: Dielectric properties of saline soils during freezing and a water–salinity inversion model for sandy soil
description: Publication date: September 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology, Volume 677, Part C Author(s): Qiang Meng, Junfeng Chen, Lihong Cui, Jing Xue, Qi Du, Xiaojun Yang
abstract: Monitoring soil water and salt content in seasonally frozen regions using Frequency Domain Reflectometry (FDR) sensors is essential but remains challenging due to low temperatures and complex salinity effects. In this study, variations in the real (ε′) and imaginary (ε″) components of the FDR-derived apparent dielectric constant during freezing were monitored using Hydra Probe II sensors across 45 distinct treatments (two salt types: NaCl and Na2SO4; five soil water contents: 0.07–0.36 cm3/cm3; and five salt contents: 0–0.3 g/100 g). Under unfrozen conditions, both ε′ and ε″ generally increased with water and salt contents, although the response of ε′ to salt content weakened under high water content conditions. Meanwhile ε″ was weakly sensitive to water content in low-salinity soils but increased markedly and nonlinearly with water content in high-salinity soils. As soil pore water froze rapidly, both ε′ and ε″ decreased sharply, the decline in ε′ was greater at higher initial water content, while higher salt content maintained higher ε′ and delayed the sharp decline in ε″. In addition, ε′ and ε″ showed stronger temperature sensitivity in Na2SO4 and NaCl soils, respectively. After most pore water had frozen, salt type had little effect on the soil dielectric constant. A water–salinity inversion model for sandy soil was established by modifying the Topp equation with ε″ and temperature for soil water content inversion, and by improving the Hilhorst-based framework with water content and temperature correction factors for soil salt content inversion. The model demonstrated satisfactory performance under near-freezing conditions and could relatively accurately calculate soil water content and salt content according to ε′ and ε″ near 0 °C, it was achieved higher accuracy for soil water content estimation in Na2SO4 soils and soil salt content estimation in NaCl soils. These results provided a theoretical basis for estimating soil water and salt contents in frozen soils using a low-frequency FDR sensor.

title: Electrical conductivity and groundwater elevation as parameters for continuous infiltration and inflow detection in wastewater networks
description: Publication date: September 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology, Volume 677, Part C Author(s): Behnam Motamedi, Elisangela Heiderscheidt, Axumawit Tesfamariam, Pekka M. Rossi
abstract: Extraneous groundwater infiltration and rainfall-derived inflow (I/I) undermine hydraulic capacity, raise energy costs, and dilute treatment performance in separate sewer networks. We evaluated electrical conductivity (EC) as a low-cost, conservative tracer for routine I/I diagnosis using yearlong monitoring with continuous EC sensors and groundwater elevation loggers in two Finnish catchments, a northern snow-dominated and a southern rainfall-dominated regime. Our analyses compared (I) commonly used hydrograph separation, (II) binary EC mixing (wastewater + groundwater), and (III) ternary EC–GW–SW mixing (wastewater +stormwater + groundwater). Relative to a volume-only split, incorporating EC increased the inferred infiltration share by up to ∼30 percentage points, while inflow remained secondary. Seasonal patterns aligned with meteorology; snowmelt dominated extraneous water in the north, whereas summer rainfall prevailed in the south. The binary EC-GW approach closely matched the ternary results but required no stormwater-EC sampling, favoring operational uptake. All diagnoses were cross-checked against precipitation, temperature, and snow-depth records to verify the link between weather and I/I dynamics. Pairing off-the-shelf EC and groundwater elevation sensors with simple mass-balance tools yielded accurate, season-resolved I/I budgets, targeting high-I/I zones, prioritizing rehabilitation, and building resilience under increasing freeze–thaw and rainfall variability.

title: Progressive scale convolutional network for spatio-temporal downscaling of soil moisture: A case study over the Tibetan Plateau
description: Publication date: September 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology, Volume 677, Part C Author(s): Ziyu Zhou, Keyan Hu, Ling Zhang, Zhaohui Xue, Yutian Fang, Yusha Zheng
abstract: Soil moisture (SM) plays a critical role in hydrological and meteorological processes. High-resolution SM can be obtained by combining coarse passive microwave data with fine-scale auxiliary variables. However, the inversion of SM at the temporal scale is hindered by the incompleteness of surface auxiliary factors. To address this issue, first, we introduce validated high temporal resolution ERA5-Land variables into the downscaling process of the low-resolution SMAP SM product. Subsequently, we design a progressive scale convolutional network (PSCNet), at the core of which are two innovative components: a multi-frequency temporal fusion module (MFTF) for capturing temporal dynamics, and a bespoke squeeze-and-excitation (SE) block designed to preserve fine-grained spatial details. Using this approach, we obtained seamless SM products for the Tibetan Plateau (TP) from 2016 to 2018 at 10-km spatial and 3-hour temporal resolution. The experimental results on the TP demonstrated the following: 1) In the satellite product validation, the PSCNet exhibited comparable accuracy and lower error, with a mean R of 0.881, outperforming other methods. 2) In the in-situ site validation, PSCNet consistently ranked among the top three models in terms of the R metric across all sites, while also showing superior performance in overall error reduction. 3) In the temporal generalization validation, the feasibility of using high-temporal resolution ERA5-Land variables for downscaling was confirmed, as all methods maintained an average relative error within 6% and 2% in terms of R and ubRMSE, respectively. 4) In the temporal dynamics and visualization validation, PSCNet effectively captured temporal sensitivity and fine-grained spatial heterogeneity. Overall, PSCNet provides a promising solution for spatio-temporal downscaling by effectively modeling the intricate spatio-temporal relationships in SM data.

title: Spatiotemporal dynamics of capillary rise in shallow groundwater table areas revealed by spatial TDR
description: Publication date: September 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology, Volume 677, Part C Author(s): Efthymios Chrysanthopoulos, Martha Perdikaki, Epameinondas Nondas Floros, Andreas Kallioras
abstract: Accurate quantification of soil water content (θ, cm3 cm–3) dynamics and capillary rise in shallow groundwater table areas remains a major challenge due to the limitations of conventional discrete point-scale measurements of θ. This study presents an integrated monitoring sensor system based on spatial time domain reflectometry (TDR) for retrieving high-resolution θ profiles along transmission lines. The approach combines inverse modeling of TDR waveforms using a fast–iterative physics–based transmission line model with Python-based code for automated signal processing, dynamic calibration against co-installed low-cost θ sensors and uncertainty propagation. Calibration is further constrained using soil hydraulic properties of undisturbed soil samples, enabling physically consistent scaling of θ values to soil porosity, while detailed analysis of each uncertainty source quantifies 90% confidence intervals in both θ profiles and threshold–based detection of the saturated portion of capillary fringe. Field application in a clay-rich experimental site revealed pronounced small-scale heterogeneity in groundwater table fluctuations and capillary rise dynamics. Spatial TDR measurements captured the upward–downward movement of the saturated portion of capillary fringe in response to diurnal groundwater fluctuations, providing direct observations of transient θ redistribution across the unsaturated zone. The results demonstrate that spatial TDR significantly improves the characterization of θ profile fluctuations compared to discrete measurements, resolving processes that are typically unobservable with conventional techniques. The proposed sensor system offers a robust methodology for linking groundwater dynamics with θ variability, providing a basis for precision in agricultural management, evapotranspiration estimation, and groundwater abstraction strategies. The integration of spatial monitoring with automated data processing provides a scalable pathway toward continuous, profile-scale observation of coupled surface–subsurface hydrological processes.

title: Focused recharge in engineered landscapes: Contrasting pore and fissure groundwater responses to check dams on the Loess Plateau
description: Publication date: September 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology, Volume 677, Part C Author(s): Zhenxia Ji, Alan D. Ziegler, Li Wang
abstract: Check dams are widely used across the Loess Plateau to control erosion and retain water, yet their effects on groundwater recharge remain poorly quantified. Using stable isotopes, residence-time analysis, and mixing models, we investigated groundwater recharge pathways in a check-dam catchment. Check-dam construction created two new recharge reservoirs—pond water and perched groundwater. These engineered water bodies became dominant recharge intermediaries for both pore and fissure groundwater. Together, they contributed approximately 81% of pore-groundwater recharge and about 50% of fissure-groundwater recharge. Mean residence times increased from pore groundwater (307 days) to fissure groundwater (591 days), indicating slower renewal and greater hydrological buffering in the fractured system. Seasonal isotope analyses further showed that pore groundwater receives substantial dry-season recharge, consistent with delayed infiltration from stored water behind check dams. Fissure groundwater is recharged primarily during the rainy season. These results demonstrate that check dams establish a dominant focused recharge pathway mediated by engineered surface-water storage. Meanwhile, diffuse precipitation recharge remains an important wetting component of the groundwater recharge system. The findings highlight an important but often overlooked role of check dams in groundwater regulation and hydrological-cycle modification in semi-arid landscapes.

title: A mechanistic water erosion–carbon model integrating the soil aggregate fractal dimension
description: Publication date: September 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology, Volume 677, Part C Author(s): Jinquan Huang, Yingtao Wu, Yi Zhu, Li Li, Wenjun Yang, Jigen Liu, Xiaolan Liu, Lu Zhang, Jiayu Liu, Jiapei Tian
abstract: Water erosion can serve as both a carbon source and a carbon sink in the global carbon cycle, but models often neglect soil structural dynamics, leading to biased soil organic carbon (SOC) transport predictions. We integrate soil aggregate fractal dimension (D) into water erosion–carbon model, combining controlled flume experiments with mechanistic simulations. The framework unifies aggregate protection, selective transport, threshold fragmentation, and dissolved organic carbon loss, with D as the key structural determinant of SOC dynamics. Under low-intensity erosion (0.16 m/s), runoff causes the selective removal of carbon-poor particles, resulting in a ∼ 9% enrichment in surface SOC concentration (g kg–1) (r = –0.86).
