title: Experimental investigation on mitigating the thermal contact resistance at the soil - energy geo-structure interface
description: Publication date: November 2026 Source: Geothermics, Volume 141 Author(s): Omar Elkezza, Mostafa Mohamed
abstract: Previous studies demonstrated the effectiveness of thermally enhanced backfill materials in improving borehole heat exchanger performance; however, limited experimental research studies exist on investigating the potential benefits of placing thermally enhanced soils at the soil-energy geo-structure interface to address and mitigate the thermal contact resistance. This paper presents results of a comprehensive experimental investigation on the use of thermally enhanced sands placed at the interface of energy geo-structures (EGS) such as piles and walls to improve heat transfer between energy geo-structures and the surrounding soils. The effectiveness of using of two different conductive additives named graphTHERM and carbon fibre in enhancing the thermal properties of sands was first evaluated. Subsequently, a series of tests using a relatively large-scale testing rig was performed to assess the influence of the thermally enhanced sand placed at the soil-EGS interface on the thermal performance of energy piles and walls during cooling. The results indicated that a 10% addition of graphTHERM and carbon fibres was an optimum level of additive improving the sand thermal conductivity by 62% and 35 % respectively. Placing a 100 mm of thermally enhanced sands by graphTHERM and carbon fibres at the interface between energy pile and surrounding soils was found highly effective in enhancing the heat transfer rate by 81 % and 54 % respectively. Furthermore, placing a 200 mm layer of thermally enhanced sands by graphTHERM and carbon fibres at the interface of energy walls increased the heat transfer rate by 108 % and 80 % respectively. The results demonstrated that the use of thermally enhanced sands at the soil-EGS interface was effective in expanding the thermally active soil zone without causing any increase in the lateral earth pressure acting on the EGS above those measured when the EGS was constructed in pure sand. The findings demonstrated the potential benefits of using thermally enhanced sands at the soil-EGS interface to improve heat exchange performance and contribute to the development of more efficient geo-energy systems.

title: Magnetotelluric evidence for a possible fault-guided fluid pathway beneath Tatapani hot springs in the Son-Narmada-Tapti lineament zone of Central India
description: Publication date: November 2026 Source: Geothermics, Volume 141 Author(s): Prasanta K. Patro, Ujjal Borah, Khasi Raju, S. P. Eknath Rao, K. Chinna Reddy, S. Dhamodharan, S.V. S. Sarma
abstract: The geologically and structurally controlled geothermal activity of the Tatapani hot springs region, confined within an ENE-WSW trending Son-Narmada-Tapti lineament (SONATA) zone, has been investigated by magnetotelluric (MT) studies. MT is a crucial tool for identifying geothermal reservoirs as it is highly sensitive to variations in subsurface electrical conductivity, making it one of the most significant geophysical methods for exploring geothermal resources. The Tatapani geothermal region features shallow hot water aquifers hosted in highly porous formations, while the primary thermal reservoir lies at greater depths. A detailed three-dimensional inversion of MT data reveals an ENE–WSW–trending conductive zone (<20 Ω.m) aligned with the Tatapani Fault at shallow depths, transitioning to an approximately E–W trend between 2 and 6 km depth, interpreted as the main geothermal reservoir. This cone-shaped conductive body with a narrow apex near the surface and a broad base at ∼6 km depth indicates a tectonically guided up-flow zone. This geometry reflects ascending hydrothermal fluids along deep-seated fault intersections and fracture networks, with lateral expansion within a permeable granitic basement. Infiltrated meteoric water, mostly from the Gondwana Formation, convectively circulates within the Proterozoic basement of the Chota-Nagpur Gneissic Complex, where it is heated by anomalous geothermal gradients. The causative sources for the conductive anomalies in this region are likely associated with radiogenic heat generation from basement rocks, enhanced regional heat flow and enhanced permeability along reactivated faults.

title: Genesis of low-heat flow and topography-driven geothermal field regulation at the southwestern margin of the Huangling Dome, Yangtze Craton: Insights from borehole logging and coupled hydrothermal modeling
description: Publication date: November 2026 Source: Geothermics, Volume 141 Author(s): Ziqiang Ren, Jiliang Wang, Heping Wu, Xiaoqiu Yang, Wenzhong Hao, Qi Xu, Du Liu, Long Tan, Peng Zhao
abstract: Accurate terrestrial heat flow determination is crucial for deciphering lithospheric thermal structure and deep dynamic processes. This assignment is particularly challenging in karst terrains with significant topographic relief, where groundwater flow driven by topography drastically reshapes shallow thermal regimes, obscuring deep-sourced heat flow signals. A direct consequence of this limitation is the persistent uncertainty in assessing the true thermal state of cratonic interiors. To address this, we conducted an integrated study at the southwestern margin of the Huangling Dome, Yangtze Craton. The overarching aim was to decouple the effects of hydrothermal circulation from the regional thermal state, thereby establishing a reliable background heat flow and quantifying the key mechanisms governing geothermal field heterogeneity. Through synthesis of borehole temperature logging, rock conductivity measurements, and coupled hydrothermal numerical modeling, we obtained measured heat flow values ranging from 18.1 to 40.4 mW/m². Our study concludes that values of 35.0∼40.4 mW/m² from nonsoluble rock areas robustly represent apparent regional background heat flow, which confirms the low heat flow characteristic of the study area relative to the continental average of China. Numerical simulations compellingly demonstrate that topography-driven groundwater forced convection, constituting the dominant mechanism and modulated by structural configuration and lithology, results in significant cooling and pronounced low heat flow anomalies within karst aquifers. Conversely, heat flow in nonsoluble rocks is governed by thermal refraction and lithological controls. These findings not only constrain the thermal state of the Yangtze Craton but also provide a generalized conceptual and methodological framework for reliably interpreting heat flow and assessing geothermal resources in other topographically complex terrains worldwide.

title: Reservoir response to long-term production in a low-enthalpy geothermal system: The Kızılcahamam field, Galatian volcanic province, Türkiye
description: Publication date: November 2026 Source: Geothermics, Volume 141 Author(s): Elif Yilmaz Turali
abstract: The Kızılcahamam geothermal field in Central Anatolia (Türkiye–Ankara), hosted within the Galatian Volcanic Province, has been exploited for district heating and thermal tourism since the mid-1990s. Measured production temperatures reach up to 86 °C across the field. This study integrates temperature–depth logs, water-level observations, and hydrogeochemical records to evaluate the reservoir’s thermal, hydraulic, and chemical evolution under nearly two decades of production with intermittent reinjection. Temperature–depth profiles and a 3D interpolated model reveal vertically heterogeneous gradients and convective upflow aligned with NE–SW and N–S fault systems. Water-level data combined with net extraction estimates indicate progressive depressurization, spatially variable drawdown, and heterogeneous storage behavior associated with structurally controlled flow pathways. Hydrochemical data show a temporal shift from Na–HCO₃ to Na–Cl water types, expressed by decreasing bicarbonate, increasing chloride, elevated Cl/B ratios, and strengthened reverse ion-exchange signatures—features that collectively suggest reduced shallow recharge and a relative increase in deeper, chemically evolved fluid contributions, particularly after reinjection ceased in 2011. However, bottom-hole temperature records indicate no systematic spatial or temporal increase in reservoir enthalpy despite progressive pressure decline and hydrochemical shifts. The integrated thermal, hydraulic, and geochemical evidence supports a conceptual model in which long-term production appears to favor structurally controlled deep flow while progressively reducing shallow contributions. As the analysis relies primarily on long-term monitoring records and empirical storage approximations rather than fully coupled dynamic reservoir modeling, the results should be interpreted as first-order system-scale assessments. These findings highlight the need for continuous monitoring and improved reinjection practices to ensure the sustainable management of low- to medium-enthalpy volcanic geothermal systems such as Kızılcahamam.

title: Hydrothermal system of the Middle Atlas (Morocco): Hydrochemistry, structural controls, and emplacement model
description: Publication date: November 2026 Source: Geothermics, Volume 141 Author(s): El Mehdi Jeddi, Ahmed Ntarmouchant, Maria do Rosário Carvalho, Telmo M. Bento dos Santos, Mohamed Lahtani, Brahim Mali, Salma Zerouali Masror, Nahla Ntarmouchant, Mustapha Elabouyi, My Hachem Smaili, Ayman Agharabi, Ikrame Allaoui, Youssef Driouch, Eduardo Anselmo Ferreira da Silva
abstract: Morocco's Middle Atlas offers remarkable hydro-geothermal potential through a multitude of thermal resurgences closely associated with deep regional tectonic structures, particularly the Northern, Central, and Southern Middle Atlas faults, forming a complex NE-SW-oriented structural corridor. A multidisciplinary study was conducted on eight selected thermal springs emerging along these structures, with temperatures ranging from 19 to 53.5 °C and pH values between 6.0 and 7.3. Hydrochemical analysis reveals two distinct water facies: i) Na-Cl type evolving within relatively closed hydrothermal systems sealed by impermeable marls, thereby preserving their deep geochemical signatures, and ii) Ca-HCO3 type developing in open systems within fractured limestones, where dilution by surface infiltration is favored. These results highlight the fluid circulation and interaction with reservoirs of diverse lithological nature connected by fracture networks, including Paleozoic crystalline basement, Triassic and Miocene evaporitic formations, and Jurassic carbonates. Geochemical modelling reveals that these thermal waters are oversaturated with carbonate minerals, a result of their equilibration within the Jurassic carbonate reservoir before their discharge to the surface, while their oversaturation in mafic and ultramafic minerals, as well as their concentrations of trace and rare earth elements, indicate their circulation at depth in the volcanic hydrothermal systems identified in the Middle Atlas basement. Na-Cl waters are characterised by their oversaturation in silicate and clay minerals resulting from their interaction with the Paleozoic crystalline basement. The indications provided by these waters are confirmed by the IIRG reservoir classification method. Geothermometry indicates reservoirs equilibrium temperatures between 80 and 137 °C and circulation depths from 1.9 to 3.5 km. Stable isotopic signatures (δ18O: -9.08 to -6.68‰ and δ2H: -64.3 to -37.9‰) confirm a meteoric origin of the fluids, with recharge areas located in the SW part of the Middle Atlas at elevations estimated between 1513 and 2337 m. Structural analysis shows that these thermal springs emerge at the intersection of the NE-SW and E-W to NW-SE fault systems. The NE-SW faults facilitate fluid flow from the southwestern recharge zones to the northeastern discharge zones, while the E-W to NW-SE faults correspond to thrusts and faults sealed by Triassic clays that block lateral flow and promote the vertical ascent of fluids to the surface. Thus, this study characterizes the Middle Atlas hydrothermal system as a large-scale, fault-controlled geothermal province, highlighting its considerable potential for sustainable energy development.

title: Optimization of well patterns for heat recovery in sedimentary geothermal systems: A hybrid GRA-COBRA approach
description: Publication date: November 2026 Source: Geothermics, Volume 141 Author(s): Jun Xie, Shuxing Mu, Yuxuan Liu
abstract: Engineering parameters of enhanced geothermal systems (EGS) directly govern heat recovery performance and economic viability. To address the practical engineering challenge of selecting the most robust well configuration amidst conflicting technical and economic objectives, this study develops a comprehensive evaluation and decision-making framework tailored for sedimentary geothermal systems. First, a 3D discrete fracture network model is established to simulate the thermal extraction behavior of six distinct well patterns. These configurations are evaluated through a multi-dimensional index system comprising production temperature, power generation, total heat extraction, flow impedance, and cost of electricity (COE). To systematically identify the optimal well pattern, a balance must be struck among these conflicting criteria. Consequently, we introduce a novel multi-criteria decision-making (MCDM) method, GRA-COBRA, which employs a cooperative game model for weight determination and integrates Grey Relational Analysis (GRA) with Comprehensive Distance-Based Ranking (COBRA) for evaluation. Application of the GRA-COBRA methodology identifies the single-injection-triple-production (1I3P) pattern as the optimal configuration, achieving the best equilibrium between energy output and economic feasibility. Finally, comparative analysis and sensitivity tests confirm that the proposed framework provides project developers with a more rational and robust decision-making tool compared to traditional methods.

title: Dual-porosity numerical modeling and probabilistic resource assessment of the Ulumbu geothermal field, Flores, Indonesia
description: Publication date: November 2026 Source: Geothermics, Volume 141 Author(s): Idrissa Abalhassan Jaha, Tubagus Ahmad Fauzi Soelaiman, Zuher Syihab, Ali Ashat, Tony Widiatmoro, M. Burhanuddin Aulia Asy’ari
abstract: Sustainable geothermal development requires reliable forecasts of reservoir performance and recoverable energy potential. Numerical reservoir simulation is an effective approach to achieve this, but its reliability depends on accurate calibration and quantifying uncertainties in key reservoir parameters that strongly influence power potential estimation. Accordingly, this study develops the first dual-porosity numerical model of the steam capped Ulumbu geothermal field, fully calibrated to both natural-state conditions and production history using the updated 2023 conceptual model, and applies an integrated Experimental Design-Response Surface Methodology-Monte Carlo (ED-RSM-MC) workflow to assess the probabilistic impact of reservoir-parameter uncertainty on long-term generation capacity. A three-dimensional model was developed using the TOUGH2 simulator, integrating geological, geochemical, geophysical, and well data. Calibration against pressure–temperature profiles from wells ULB-1, ULB-2, and ULB-3 yielded RMSE values of 1.9–7.1°C and 3.1–8.5 bar, successfully reproducing natural-state behavior. The close agreement between simulated and observed pressures indicates that the model represents reservoir connectivity and permeability structure realistically. Five key uncertain parameters; matrix porosity, matrix permeability, fracture volume factor, liquid saturation, and fracture spacing were systematically varied using a Box–Behnken design to construct a response surface model. The resulting proxy model, combined with Monte Carlo simulation, produced a most-likely (P50) power-potential estimate of 71.59 MW over a 30-year production period. Matrix porosity and matrix permeability were the most influential parameters controlling power output. Overall, the integrated modelling–statistical framework provides a physically consistent and probabilistically robust basis for sustainable development planning of the Ulumbu geothermal field.

title: Advancing geothermal reservoir temperature prediction in the Western Anatolia (Türkiye) using synthetic hydrogeochemical data from rank–Gaussian copulas
description: Publication date: November 2026 Source: Geothermics, Volume 141 Author(s): Füsun S. Tut Haklidir, Mehmet Haklidir
abstract: Data-driven geothermal reservoir temperature prediction can complement classical geothermometer applications in geothermal provinces with high resource potential, such as Western Anatolia (Türkiye). However, the limited availability and heterogeneous nature of hydrogeochemical datasets constrain the use of high-capacity machine-learning models and weaken their generalization to new prospective fields. In this study, a rank-Gauss copula (RGC) based synthetic data generation framework is proposed to learn the joint dependence structure among routinely measured hydrogeochemical variables and generate additional samples consistent with the observed distributions. Using a benchmark dataset of 83 hot springs and geothermal wells alongside seven commonly measured variables (pH, EC, K+, Na+, Btotal, SiO2, and Cl-), the generated synthetic data closely matched the real data’s marginal behavior and multivariate relationships (average two-sample Kolmogorov–Smirnov statistic approximately 0.04 across variables), while preserving key field-consistent correlation patterns. Two predictive settings for reservoir temperature prediction were evaluated in the study: (i) a deep neural network (DNN) ensemble pre-trained on RGC-synthetic data and fine-tuned on real samples, and (ii) NGBoost models trained on real-only versus real-plus-RGC data and test performance was consistently improved by RGC augmentation. Overall, the proposed RGC framework is data-driven, model-independent, and straightforward to implement; the Western Anatolia (Türkiye) is used as a case study, and the approach is intended to be transferable to geothermal provinces with high resource potential where routine hydrogeochemical analyses are available but reliable reservoir temperature measurements are scarce, enabling the generation of realistic synthetic datasets and improving the robustness and generalization of reservoir temperature estimation.

title: Unraveling the fluid origin, circulation and heat sources of the fault-controlled Santa Teresita Geothermal System (Pipanaco basin, NW Argentina): insights from hydrochemical, isotopic and structural analysis
description: Publication date: November 2026 Source: Geothermics, Volume 141 Author(s): Gimena M. Uran, Mariano A. Larrovere, Verena A. Campodonico, Pablo H. Alasino
abstract: The southern sector of the Pipanaco basin in NW Argentina (Eastern Sierras Pampeanas) was studied in order to comprehend its geothermal system. This study presents new detailed isotopic and hydrogeochemical data, together with a geological-structural analysis. A new comprehensive conceptual model for the Santa Teresita Geothermal System (STGS) is proposed, highlighting the role of the regional fault-system. The thermal waters of the STGS have a Na+-SO4 2−-Cl− composition, evidencing a gradual mineralization increase in the groundwater flow direction. The 222Rn concentrations measured in groundwater are consistent with waters contained in granitic fractured rocks. The stable isotopes indicate a meteoric origin with no evidence of mixing with magmatic waters. The study area presents a strong structural control over the thermal manifestations, and these are mainly concentrated on the intersection of two regional structures: the Villa Mervil – Santa Teresita reverse fault (NE-SW direction) and a dextral strike-slip fault (NNW-SSE direction). Neotectonic activity favored the development of high-permeability pathways, promoting the rise of thermal waters. The STGS corresponds to a low enthalpy geothermal system, with waters heated by the regional geothermal gradient and estimated reservoir temperatures in the range from 85 to 115 °C. It constitutes a geothermal system in the active contractional Andean broken foreland, with a reservoir depth that must exceed 3 km considering a geothermal gradient of ∼ 30 °C km−1. This study provides a robust model for future research on the geothermal potential of the region.

title: Influence of fluid-rock interactions on mechanical, thermal and transport properties of sandstone reservoir during geothermal waste fluid reinjection
description: Publication date: November 2026 Source: Geothermics, Volume 141 Author(s): Jieqin Xia, Hong Tian, Sadiq J. Zarrouk, Eylem Kaya, Jun Zheng, Bin Dou, Yan Qin, Yanting Zhao, Sen Zhang
abstract: The Guantao formation sandstone geothermal reservoir (SGR) suffers from low reinjection efficiency, severely limiting its sustainable utilization. Reinjection of geothermal waste fluid (GF) back into the SGR triggers intense fluid-rock interactions (FRIs) driven by the coupled effects of mechanical stress, mineralogical composition, and the injected fluid’s physicochemical properties. In this study, we conducted core-scale reactor experiments (25 days) and a batch numerical model (360 days) consistent with experimental parameters to explore the FRI and its influence on rock mechanical, thermal, and transport properties. Results showed that during the initial 25 days, the rock mass loss rate, diameter increase rate, and porosity all exhibited a trend of first increasing and then decreasing. Thermal conductivity varied inversely with porosity, whereas permeability declined sharply within the first 5 hours, then increased, and then declined again. The peak strength and elastic modulus of the rocks showed a fluctuating trend, initially decreasing and then increasing. The combined experimental and simulation results revealed that, before 90 days, the evolution of porosity and permeability was primarily controlled by feldspar dissolution, clay precipitation, and secondary calcite formation. Then, the FRI system gradually approached chemical equilibrium. Building upon the core scale results, a THC-coupled Near-Wellbore model was developed using well-logging data and reinjection conditions. The simulation predicted that after 50 years, reinjection of GF induced a permeability-damaged zone in the near-well region extended to approximately 50 m, while the porosity-affected zone extended to about 100 m. These findings provide valuable engineering insights for similar SGR reinjection operations.

title: Preliminary Assessment of CO 2 Compression Behavior Modified by [BMIM][AlCl 4 ] for Engineered Geothermal Working Fluids
description: Publication date: November 2026 Source: Geothermics, Volume 141 Author(s): Damian Janiga, Paweł Wojnarowski
abstract: Closed-loop geothermal systems (CLGS) benefit from engineered working fluids, and supercritical CO2 is a leading candidate due to its low viscosity and buoyancy-driven circulation. However, system performance depends sensitively on CO2 compressibility and behavior near the critical region. Ionic fluids (IFs) offer a potential route to tuning these properties, yet their interaction with CO2 under geothermal high-temperature, high-pressure (HTHP) conditions is not well understood. This study examines the mixing behavior of [BMIM][AlCl4] with CO2 using constant composition compression experiments at 30, 50 and 100 °C up to 25 MPa. The results show that [BMIM][AlCl4] alters CO2 thermodynamic response: mixtures retain substantially higher volume, near-critical compressibility peaks are strongly suppressed, and gas-like fluid-like crossover pressures shift upward. Volume-matching analysis reveals CO2 dissolution into the IF and microstructural reorganization of the halometallate phase. These findings demonstrate that [BMIM][AlCl4] acts as an active thermodynamic modifier rather than an inert additive. For geothermal applications, such IF-induced stiffening and fluctuation suppression could affect density control, circulation stability, and heat-extraction performance in CO2-based CLGS. The results provide foundational data for designing IF-CO2 working fluids tailored for next-generation geothermal systems.

title: Nigorikawa and Otake – Pioneering geothermal binary plants in Japan: Historical perspective, performance assessment, and lessons learned
description: Publication date: November 2026 Source: Geothermics, Volume 141 Author(s): Ronald DiPippo
abstract: In the 1970′s in the wake of two Oil Shocks, the countries of the world began a quest for indigenous sources of energy. In particular, alternative means were sought to generate electricity without the need to burn fossil fuels. Japan started its Sunshine Program and included, among several technologies, geothermal energy of which their country has an abundance of potential. Two pilot geothermal binary power plants were created conceptually, designed, and built at locations at opposite ends of the country, and tested for a year. These plants, the Nigorikawa and Otake pilot plants, pioneered some of the features now common at binary plants that have spread across the world, but the technical details of these plants have not yet been published in the mainstream literature. This article describes the plants in technical detail, including their locations, assesses the test results on the basis of thermodynamic First Law and Second Law principles (including exergy), and discusses the implications for future plants. As test plants, their economics was not a priority and this article does not address that facet of the projects.

title: Conceptual model of the low-temperature geothermal system in the Cuenca Alta del Río Laja basin, Central Mexico
description: Publication date: November 2026 Source: Geothermics, Volume 141 Author(s): Lucía Magali Ramírez-González, María Jesús Puy-Alquiza, Yanmei Li, Rosa María Prol-Ledesma, Jesús Horacio Hernández-Anguiano, Yasmin Hernández-Aburto, Diego Ruiz-Aguilar, Gabriela Ana Zanor, Raúl Miranda-Avilés, Viridiana Piña-González, Ashley V. Aguilar
abstract: Thermal waters in the Cuenca Alta del Río Laja are discharged from agricultural, public and recreational wells at temperatures from ∼29 to 47 °C. In this study we reviewed available surface and sub-surface information; the compilation includes geological, hydrogeological, hydrogeochemical, and geophysical data that were integrated into four cross-sections that constitute the first geothermal conceptual model of the basin. It is proposed that the heat source is driven by convection due to two main mechanisms: 1) deep convection controlled by the regional system of N-S and NW-SE normal faults; and 2) induced convection by pumping. Groundwater flows towards the center of the basin where thermal waters are sodium-bicarbonate type and they are mixed with shallower groundwater at lower temperature. Geothermometry allowed us to conceptualize the 102 °C isotherm; its position is only schematic and it is shallower in the fault zones due to convection. This study discusses the occurrence of a NW-SE buried fault and gives evidence that supports that at depth, the regional fault system enhances the vertical permeability and controls convection. We also discussed the occurrence of thermal samples unrelated to faults that may be associated to the water table drawdown as a result of overexploitation. This study has regional impact for groundwater management and geothermal exploration.

title: Field to laboratory assessment of subsurface thermal conductivity: A geothermal case study in Slovenia
description: Publication date: November 2026 Source: Geothermics, Volume 141 Author(s): Karlo Borko, Fiona M. Chapman, Jasmin Raymond, Grzegorz Ryżyński, Nina Rman
abstract: Reliable characterization of subsurface thermal properties is essential for designing efficient shallow geothermal systems and assessing the potential of Ground Source Heat Pump and Underground Thermal Energy Storage systems. The objective of this study is to evaluate the reliability of thermal conductivity estimations from different approaches by comparing three in situ methods - conventional Thermal Response Test (TRT), Enhanced Thermal Response Test (ETRT), and Distributed Thermal Response Test (DTRT) - against each other and laboratory measurements on core samples. The tests were conducted in a 100 m deep borehole heat exchanger in the Krško Basin, Slovenia. Laboratory measurements employed needle probes and an optical Thermal Conductivity Scanner (TCS), while in situ testing utilized fibre-optic Distributed Temperature Sensing (DTS) for high-resolution temperature profiling. Results show that needle probe measurements consistently underestimate thermal conductivity relative to TCS- and DTS-based methods, by 22% to 48%, mainly due to sample desaturation and limited probe contact. DTS-based ETRT revealed vertical variations and groundwater-flow-influenced zones. Cemented fibre-optic cables introduced greater uncertainty and yielded 44% higher conductivities than the ETRT with the composite cable. TCS yielded thermal conductivities most consistent with in situ measurements while providing a favourable balance of time, cost, and reliability of results.

title: Detecting and characterizing a hidden geothermal system in the Mt. Endut area, Indonesia, through integrated soil-gas component analyses
description: Publication date: November 2026 Source: Geothermics, Volume 141 Author(s): Mochamad Iqbal, Taiki Kubo, Koki Kashiwaya, Katsuaki Koike
abstract: A hidden geothermal system (HGS) is a specific, complex geothermal system that does not have surface thermal manifestations but has significant potential for energy resources. Despite the difficulty of exploration of such systems because of their concealed features, detection and development of these systems can significantly contribute to increasing geothermal power generation. This study aimed to detect and characterize an HGS in the Mt. Endut area, Banten, west Indonesia, and to clarify its relationship with the adjacent, conventional medium-temperature Cikawah Geothermal System (CGS). Mt. Endut area is classified as a hidden system because a thick low-permeability cap rock and sealed fault segments suppress surface discharge, with no evidence of a depressed water table or an overlying cold aquifer. Under such sealing conditions, moderately low-solubility CO2 and short-lived radon isotopes (222Rn and 220Rn) can migrate upward through minor fractures while liquid flow remains impeded, making them effective tracers of concealed fluid pathways. To evaluate this mechanism, an integrated soil-gas geochemical approach was employed, combining CO2 flux, δ13C-CO2, and radon isotopes measurements with interpretations from existing geophysical datasets, a complete Bouguer anomaly (CBA) map, and magnetotelluric (MT) data. The soil-gas survey revealed large variabilities in the CO2 flux (15 to 1399 g m − 2 day−1) and δ13C-CO2 (−18.71 to −9.75‰) caused by a complex mixture of biogenic and hydrothermal gas sources. The locations of high-flux zones of hydrothermal-dominated mixture (HDM) CO2 were strongly correlated with the Handeleum dextral fault having a permeable structure. The 222Rn/220Rn ratio was effective for differentiating gas source depths and attributing deep-seated 222Rn anomalies to major fault zones and advective transport. A key finding was the role of the NNE–SSW Endut normal fault as a distinct structural boundary separating the Endut HGS from the CGS, supported by a coincident gravity low and a steep MT resistivity gradient. Moreover, the results suggest that the two systems are driven by distinct heat sources, a deep magmatic body for the Endut HGS and a shallower andesitic intrusion for the CGS, and delineate three new potential areas warranting future exploration. Consequently, this study identifies robust geochemical signatures for both the concealed and conventional geothermal systems by high CO2 flux of HDM origin coexisting with shallow-source 222Rn, and underscores the effectiveness of this integrated approach in reducing exploration uncertainty for HGS detection and characterization. These result can contribute to the development of geothermal resources in Indonesia and other volcanic areas.

title: Hydraulic analysis of the GEOREAL fluid injection experiment at the KTB pilot hole, Germany
description: Publication date: November 2026 Source: Geothermics, Volume 141 Author(s): C.M. Boese, J. Kück, G. Zimmermann, G. Dresen, S. Kamrani, U. Harms, I. Sass, M. Bohnhoff
abstract: A total of 600 m 3 of fresh water was injected into the 4 km-deep KTB pilot borehole near Windischeschenbach, Germany, in November 2023. The main goal of the GEOREAL hydraulic stimulation experiment was to stimulate fractured metamorphic rocks in the vicinity of the well-characterised SE2 fault zone at 4 km depth with high flow rates and to compare rock and fluid responses to a previous one-year-long injection experiment in 2004/5 into the same formation. The intention was to quantify the potential for heat extraction at a site where temperature and pressure conditions are representative for crystalline rocks for large parts of Germany. Due to an unforeseen incident during packer deployment, however, a reduced fluid volume of 600 m 3 was injected, pressurising the entire pilot hole (KTB-VB), including the cased section to 3.85 km depth and the 150 m open borehole section below. Flow rates were variable ranging from 10 to 220 l/min. Pressure records were obtained at the well heads of KTB-VB and the main borehole (KTB-HB) at 200 m lateral distance at the surface which was also used for downhole microseismic monitoring. Hydraulic data were analysed and compared to results from 2004/5. The hydraulic parameters show similar values as in 2004/5 when no packer was blocking the borehole. Due to an unknown leak in the casing cement of the 35-year-old KTB-VB, the GEOREAL experiment had to be stopped earlier than planned. No microseismic events were detected during the injection using conventional event-detection methods. Hydraulic results for the KTB-VB injections two decades apart suggest that no significant permeability changes have occurred in the SE2 fault zone indicating that fracture healing does not play a major role in the reservoir. The pressure recordings from the KTB-HB showed no change caused by the injection into the KTB-VB, suggesting that either the injected volume was too small to cause a hydraulic response, too much fluid leaked into the formation, the hydraulic connection observed previously ceased to exist, its geometry is unfavourable for this configuration, or hydraulic diffusivity is smaller than suggested for previous experiments.

title: In-situ mechanical factors affecting hydraulic stimulation for deep-direct use heat extraction in Cambrian-Ordovician Potsdam and Beekmantown Group formations
description: Publication date: November 2026 Source: Geothermics, Volume 141 Author(s): Sean A. Fulcher, Vishesh Bhadariya, Hunjoo P. Lee, Lawrence Cathles
abstract: Heat extraction in an Enhanced Geothermal System (EGS) requires uniformly distributed fluid pathways between parallel wells. Creating uniform flow by hydraulic fracturing in low-porosity, low-permeability formations remains challenging. Bedding planes, natural fractures, and trace fossil facies are potential geomechanical barriers to hydraulic fracture propagation in the Cambrian-Ordovician age Potsdam and Beekmantown Groups of the northern Appalachian Basin where Cornell University is investigating the feasibility of deep direct use (DDU) parallel well geothermal energy extraction. To better understand these geomechanical barriers, we subjected a suite of Potsdam and Beekmantown Group outcrop samples to semi-circular bend (SCB) tests, unconfined compression strength (UCS) tests, digital image correlation (DIC) strain field mapping, and microstructure analysis. Results show Mode I fracture propagation and fracture diversion is influenced by strain concentrations in natural fractures where fracture fill transitions from full to partially infilled. Interbedded dolostone-sandstone layers do not influence fracture trajectory because the mechanical contrast between dolostone and sandstone is low, and the interface is gradational and strongly cemented. Strain mapping indicates trace fossils produce strain anisotropy during loading in the samples, but this strain anisotropy consolidates at peak load and therefore does not affect fracture propagation.

title: Insights into the formation of a low heat flow geothermal system: integrated geochemical and geophysical evidence from Anjiazhuang, China
description: Publication date: November 2026 Source: Geothermics, Volume 141 Author(s): Weizun Zhang, Yuanzhi Cheng, Meng Wang, Hui Zou, Liang Qie, Yizhuo Dong, Xiaoxiao Zhang, Jing Wang, Shuyang Wang, Qitao Ding, Jiabin Duan, Yulie Gong, Yanlong Kong
abstract: Low heat flow depressions are generally considered unfavorable for the development of shallow hydrothermal geothermal resources. However, this study identifies a promising shallow medium-low temperature geothermal resource within the boundary of the Dawenkou Basin. A borehole drilled to a depth of 350 m recorded a temperature of 52.5 °C. The formation mechanism of such geothermal systems in low heat flow settings remains insufficiently constrained. To constrain the formation mechanism of this geothermal resource, a comprehensive investigation was carried out, incorporating hydrochemical analyses, isotopic geochemistry, and controlled-source audio-frequency magnetotelluric (CSAMT) surveys. The results indicate that the geothermal water is primarily recharged by modern meteoric water originating from Mount Tai, located to the northeast of the study area. This water infiltrates along fault zones and fractures and may have undergone intensive water-rock interaction with sulfate-bearing minerals or sulfate-rich formation fluids. Consequently, the geothermal water is characterized by a SO₄·Cl-Na·Ca hydrochemical type. The geothermal system is suggested to be confined by Quaternary sediments and sandstones and shales of the Cambrian Mantou Formation. The fractured zones, together with water-rich dolomites and limestones, are interpreted as the main pathways and reservoirs for geothermal fluid migration and storage. Thermal reservoir temperature is estimated at 71–83 °C based on geothermometers, with an inferred circulation depth of approximately 2 km, subject to uncertainty in the geothermal gradient. This study supports an interpretive model of a fault-controlled medium-low temperature convective geothermal system in a low-heat-flow region, offering new insights into geothermal resource formation beyond typical high-enthalpy environments.

title: A borehole-geophysics workflow for constructing continuous thermal-property and temperature profiles from incomplete well logs: A case study from the Sichuan Basin
description: Publication date: November 2026 Source: Geothermics, Volume 141 Author(s): Feisheng Mou, Yinhui Zuo, Junlong Zhang, Luquan Zhang, Guangzheng Jiang, Yingchun Wang, Jiaxin Xie, Xinglong Wang
abstract: Reliable estimation of rock thermophysical properties is essential for subsurface temperature modelling and geothermal assessment, but laboratory measurements are commonly limited by sparse core availability. This study presents an integrated borehole-geophysics workflow for constructing continuous thermal-property and temperature profiles from conventional well logs in the Sichuan Basin. Missing sonic transit-time (AC) data were reconstructed using a CNN-LSTM model based on gamma ray (GR), density (DEN), neutron porosity (CNL), and resistivity (RT), derived log features, and normalized depth information. The model achieved excellent within-well performance in W201 and meaningful but variable cross-well performance in wells B61 and GS17, indicating that transferability remains affected by inter-well logging and geological heterogeneity. Based on reconstructed and measured AC data, radiogenic heat production was estimated using a regionally calibrated GR–A relationship, while thermal conductivity was predicted using a multi-log regression model integrating AC, DEN, CNL, RT, and GR. The predicted thermal conductivity and heat production agree well with laboratory measurements, with coefficients of determination of 0.815 and 0.854, respectively. The resulting profiles preserve lithology-controlled variations: carbonate-dominated formations generally exhibit higher thermal conductivity and lower radiogenic heat production, whereas mudstone- and shale-rich intervals display lower conductivity and elevated heat production. The log-derived thermal-property profiles were then integrated into a one-dimensional steady-state conductive temperature model that accounts for depth-dependent thermal conductivity and radiogenic heat production. The predicted temperature profile agrees well with available bottom-hole static temperature data, supporting the applicability of the workflow for well-scale to locally comparative thermal evaluation. This approach extends the use of legacy well logs and provides a practical method for thermal-property profiling and temperature prediction in data-sparse sedimentary basins, while further multi-well validation is needed before broader basin-scale application.

title: Integrating microbial induced calcium carbonate precipitation (MICP) in geothermal pavements: A coupled thermo-economic numerical evaluation
description: Publication date: November 2026 Source: Geothermics, Volume 141 Author(s): Xiaoying Gu, Alexandra Clarà Saracho, Nikolas Makasis, Monika Johanna Kreitmair, Guillermo A. Narsilio
abstract: As demand for low-carbon heating and cooling solutions grows, shallow geothermal energy systems integrated within pavements offer a promising approach for sustainable infrastructure. This study evaluates the technical and economic feasibility of microbial induced calcium carbonate precipitation (MICP)-treated geothermal pavements using a validated finite element (FE) model. Thermal performance of the embedded ground heat exchanger (GHE) system was examined across representative climates, subbase saturation levels, and subgrade thermal conductivities. Results show MICP treatment significantly enhances performance in dry conditions, particularly when subgrade conductivity is low (0.3 W/(m·K)). In a Mediterranean climate scenario, applying 4.1 wt% CaCO₃ increased annual thermal output from 177 to 290 kWh/m (64%). However, benefits diminish with higher subbase saturation or naturally high subgrade conductivity. The subbase-to-subgrade conductivity ratio emerges as a critical design parameter, with higher ratios generally improving thermal output but limiting the marginal gains from MICP. Economically, under optimal dry soil conditions, MICP treatment yields a net present value (NPVT) exceeding 300 AUD/m, offsetting over 70% of typical road construction costs. Sensitivity analysis shows MICP material cost as the dominant factor affecting NPVT. These findings emphasise the importance of balancing technical gains with economic considerations to optimise the application of MICP in geothermal pavements.

title: Monitoring the gravel packing process during completion of a geothermal well using distributed fiber optic sensing
description: Publication date: September 2026 Source: Geothermics, Volume 140 Author(s): J. Hart, M.P. Lipus, C. Wollin, A. Saadat, C. Cunow, S. Kranz, T. Reinsch, C.M. Krawczyk
abstract: An efficient, safe, and sustainable geothermal energy supply depends on reliable well completion and monitoring technologies. Gravel packing is a process in well construction where the space between the filter screen and the formation is filled with gravel. This process can be crucial for producing sand-free fluid with minimal head loss. However, conventional wireline monitoring methods, such as manual bathometers or density logs, provide only discrete or post-placement information, leaving real-time downhole processes unobserved. This lack of continuous feedback creates operational uncertainties and leads to suboptimal decisions that can threaten well construction and reduce the well's efficiency. Here, the gravel packing of a 450-meter-deep exploration well designed for High-Temperature Aquifer Thermal Energy Storage (HT-ATES) in Berlin, Germany, was investigated using a fiber-optic sensing cable attached to the production casing. The study first evaluates the feasibility of simultaneous Distributed Temperature Sensing (DTS) and Distributed Dynamic Strain Sensing (DDSS, also known as Distributed Acoustic Sensing, DAS) for real-time gravel pack monitoring. Building on this, a combined interpretation of temperature cooling fronts, pump-induced wavefield reflections, vibrational energy anomalies, and low-frequency strain transients is used to identify the thermal and acoustic signatures of operational downhole processes such as fluid circulation and gravel pack placement, as well as of operational hazards such as caving, gravel bridging and collapse, screen clogging, and artesian fluid inflow. In situ observation of these theoretical concepts demonstrates the value of continuous fiber-optic measurements for improved understanding of downhole processes during well completion. The lightweight processing required to retrieve these data products makes the workflow suitable for edge deployment, enabling timely feedback to support proactive interventions that minimize operational risks and enhance well efficiency.

title: Biogeochemical control of potential toxic elements mobility in mining sediments: The role of Arthrobacter -mediated Mn precipitation in the Mar Menor alluvial plain
description: Publication date: 10 September 2026 Source: Science of The Total Environment, Volume 1047 Author(s): O. González-Fernández, B. Fernández-Gómez, E. Marguí, I. Queralt
abstract: This study deciphers the complex biogeochemical interactions governing metal mobility within a deep soil core from the Cartagena-La Unión mining district (SE Spain), a Mediterranean semiarid area under severe environmental stress. We integrated geochemical, mineralogical, and microbiological analyses to elucidate the vertical distribution and fate of Potentially Toxic Elements (PTEs) across the alluvial plain. Results reveal extreme accumulations of Lead (Pb, ∼4 wt%) and Zinc (Zn, ∼3 wt%) throughout the 3-m core. A critical geochemical horizon was identified at 260 cm, characterized by peak concentrations of Calcium (17%), Sulfur (10%), and Manganese (2%). While physicochemical gradients partially dictate these patterns, phylogenetic sequencing revealed a predominant presence of the Arthrobacter genus at these depths. This suggests that microbial-mediated Mn oxidation acts as a biological engine for secondary mineral precipitation, effectively conditioning the partitioning of metals in the subsurface. Furthermore, the identification of marine-derived DNA sequences in deep terrestrial layers provides novel biological evidence of the historical shoreline fluctuations and the broader geographical extent of the Mar Menor Lagoon. Our findings demonstrate that microbial signatures not only serve as essential proxies for understanding geochemical evolution but also offer critical insights into the long-term stabilization of metals in mining-impacted alluvial systems.

title: Thermochemical processing of sewage sludges: Comparative analysis of hydrochars and biochars for sustainable phosphorus recovery
description: Publication date: 10 September 2026 Source: Science of The Total Environment, Volume 1047 Author(s): Mozhdeh Alipoursarbani, Hossein Asadi, Christian Abendroth
abstract: Securing sustainable phosphorus (P) resources from municipal sewage sludge is critical for circular nutrient management. This study investigates the effects of hydrothermal carbonization (HTC, 180 °C) and pyrolysis (450 °C and 600 °C) on two different sewage sludges: Stabilized Sewage Sludge (SSS) derived from an extended aeration activated sludge (EAAS) system, and Sludge Cake (SC) obtained from an anaerobic–anoxic–oxic (A/A/O) treatment process. Feedstock origin strongly governed phosphorus speciation, transformation pathways, and char properties during thermochemical processing. The two raw sludges were influenced by their original treatment, with SSS showing higher total phosphorus (TP = 39.04 mg g−1) but a lower Ca/P molar ratio (0.20) compared with SC (TP = 26.10 mg g−1, Ca/P = 0.50), indicating distinct P partitioning between mineral and organic fractions. Hydrochars (SH from SSS, CH from SC) showed moderate total P concentrations (TP) and retained some organic P (OP), whereas pyrolysis produced biochars with higher TP: 59.7 mg g−1 in SB600 (SSS) and 46.0 mg g−1 in CB600 (SC). OP decreased significantly from 6.38 mg g−1 (SSS) and 8.15 mg g−1 (SC) to below 2.5 mg g−1, while inorganic P (IP) became dominant. In SSS biochars, apatite phosphorus (AP) was the main fraction, while in SC biochars, non-apatite inorganic P (NAIP) remained significant. These contrasting behaviors are attributed to feedstock-dependent mineral compositions, where Fe- and Al-associated fractions in SSS promoted conversion of NAIP into AP, whereas the higher initial Ca content in SC favored NAIP retention. Solid-state 31P NMR confirmed that orthophosphate (Ortho-P) is the main P species, highlighting its bioavailability and thermal stability. Pyrolysis increased carbonization, decreased H/C and O/C ratios (down to 0.44 and 0.33 at 600 °C), and generated highly porous, thermally stable chars. Overall, these results demonstrate that both sludge type and thermochemical pathway critically influence char properties and phosphorus forms.

title: Source attribution of polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons and dioxins in soil and dust following compound climate events in legacy-contaminated environmental justice areas
description: Publication date: 10 September 2026 Source: Science of The Total Environment, Volume 1047 Author(s): God'’sgift N. Chukwuonye, Zain Alabdain Alqattan, Miriam Jones, Mónica D. Ramírez-Andreotta
abstract: Communities with histories of industrial contamination may face heightened exposures when compound climate events interact with persistent organic pollutants. Limited multi-matrix data exist are available to evaluate how sequential wildfire and flood disturbances may influence contaminant distribution in environmental justice (EJ) communities. This study characterized polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons (PAHs) in nonresidential soil/sediment (n = 75), residential surface soil (n = 35), control soil (n = 24), and residential indoor dust (n = 35), and polychlorinated dibenzo-p-dioxins/dibenzofurans (PCDD/Fs) in selected 2–15 cm nonresidential and control soils, in the Globe-Miami area of Arizona, USA following the 2021 Telegraph and Mescal wildfires and subsequent flash floods. PAH diagnostic ratios classified 91–100% of samples across matrices as pyrogenic, while residential soils showed strong correlations among high molecular weight PAH co-correlations (r = 0.87–0.97) consistent with co-deposition/redistribution of combustion-derived particles. Residential soil ΣPAH16 ranged from 0.017 to 15,860 μg kg−1 and benzo[a]anthracene and benzo[a]pyrene exceeded USEPA soil-to-groundwater soil screening levels (SSL) in 40% and 20%, respectively. Indoor dust ΣPAH16 ranged from 1.667 to 167.5 μg m−2, with greater lower-molecular-weight contributions than outdoor soil, suggesting indoor-specific sources and partitioning processes in addition to possible outdoor-to-indoor transport. For PCDD/Fs, 16 of 17 congeners detected in flooded, nonresidential soils compared with 13 in controls; however, total PCDD/F concentrations and overall congener composition did not differ significantly (p = 0.22). Nonresidential soil toxic equivalency quotient (TEQ) values ranged from 0.192 to 29.6 ng kg−1, with the highest value observed at Icehouse Canyon, consistent with localized legacy dioxin contamination, including historical Agent Orange-related herbicide application as one plausible contributor. All samples exceeded the 2,3,7,8-Tetrachlorodibenzo-p-dioxin USEPA soil-to-groundwater SSL of 0.059 ng kg−1. Overall, findings support a layered-source interpretation in which combustion-derived PAHs and persistent legacy PCDD/Fs may coexist and be redistributed through post-fire runoff and flooding in these climate-vulnerable EJ communities.

title: Cross-lag interaction between temperature and PM 2.5 reveals hidden windows of cardiovascular mortality risk in a tropical megacity
description: Publication date: 10 September 2026 Source: Science of The Total Environment, Volume 1047 Author(s): Phichet Khunthong, Sitthichok Puangthongthub
abstract: Background Climate change and PM2.5 co-occur in tropical megacities, yet their joint effects on cardiovascular mortality remain poorly resolved. Prior studies assess aligned-lag interactions, although PM2.5 may prime susceptibility to later thermal stress. We mapped the temperature-PM2.5 cross-lag surface to identify excess risk. Methods We conducted a time-series study in Bangkok regions (2014–2022), linking daily cardiovascular deaths to temperature and PM2.5. Quasi-Poisson generalized additive models evaluated 8 × 8 cross-lag pairs (lags0–7) using a tensor-product interaction term, adjusted for humidity, time trends, and COVID-19. Interactions were predicted relative to minimum-mortality references, with subgroup analyses. Results 179,455 cardiovascular deaths were included, with mean temperature, PM2.5, and relative humidity of 29.14 ± 1.66 °C, 26.49 ± 15.37 μg/m3, and 68.29 ± 8.96%, respectively. PM2.5 itself showed a relative risk (RR) (95%CI) of lag1 = 1.029(1.018–1.040). The heat peaked at lag0 = 1.017(1.002–1.033); cold at lag4 = 1.044(1.031–1.058). Minimum-death references were 27.5 °C and 9.6 μg/m3. For visualization, the interaction-component surface at temperature lag3 × PM2.5 lag0 showed a significant interaction surface of 74.79% and a maximum RR of 1.206(1.111–1.309) at 23.98 °C and 76.23 μg/m3. In the 64 lag-pair analysis, positive interaction patterns were concentrated around temperature lags 2–4 and PM2.5 lags 0–2, rather than being restricted to a single lag pair. Peak RR was higher in females, 1.316(1.145–1.513), than in males, 1.173 (1.066–1.292), but smaller positive surface (23.44% vs. 73.38%). Greater in the younger age group (<65), 1.292(1.120–1.489), than in the older age group (≥65), 1.174(1.064–1.295), but a smaller surface (30.82% vs. 78.43%). Ischemic heart disease showed a stronger RR peak, 1.285(1.119–1.476), than cerebrovascular disease, 1.162(1.028–1.312), yet with a smaller surface (29.45% vs. 65.94%). Conclusions Co-exposure was asymmetric; PM2.5 preceded temperature effects. Females and ischemic heart disease had higher risks; older age and cerebrovascular mortality showed broader vulnerability. Cross-lag evidence supports time-based warning for future research on early-warning interactions and targeted protection.

title: Water vapour as a carrier of mould metabolites in indoor air: an explanation for the sick building syndrome and severe morbidity
description: Publication date: 10 September 2026 Source: Science of The Total Environment, Volume 1047 Author(s): Kirsi Vaali, Michael Sulyok, Jari Louhelainen, Marika Mannerström, Tuula Heinonen, Rudolf Krska, Leena A. Räsänen, Arto Visala, Panu Harmo, Mirja Salkinoja-Salonen
abstract: Indoor air quality (IAQ) is a possible but unproven culprit for sick building syndrome (SBS). We earlier showed that emitted mould exudates are carried into ambient air by water clusters. When nine students (7–12 years) moved from the damaged school to reference schools, their symptoms attenuated but reappeared, within the same day, when transferred to schools with known IAQ problems. A self-made experimental recording of glass chambers and sensors of volatile organic compounds (VOC) and non-volatiles, relative humidity, CO2 and CN/sulphide were applied to mimic IAQ of the school. Mortar samples of the damaged school wall, when cultured on malt agar, grew alternative oxidase fungi (aox-fungi), which emitted exudates. Exudates were analysed by LC-MS/MS and tested on human BJ cells. LC-MS/MS analysis of the cultivated mortars showed that the mould-derived droplets hanging underneath culture lids transferred in water, being the same as the exudates' contents on top of mould growths. Boric acid added to the mortar cultivation, promoted the emission of mould metabolites, which were shown to be lethal to BJ cells. The results support presence of aox-fungi in the mortars, which was closest to the damaged area of the building. Cytotoxicity of the mould exudates in cultivation varied time-dependently, within two weeks, as indicated by BJ cells. The present results and earlier reported cytotoxic water vapour of this school air are the contact points between the mould exudates, damaged building and clinical symptoms: the missing link in the mystery of SBS. Analysing water vapour will reveal piggy-bagged toxic substances.

title: Cyanobacteria relative biomass modulates the contrasting effects of species richness and evenness on phytoplankton resource use efficiency in a mesocosm experiment
description: Publication date: 10 September 2026 Source: Science of The Total Environment, Volume 1047 Author(s): Yafang Qin, Chaoyue Cheng, Shangsheng Sun, Ruyi Li, Misha Zhong, Yuwei Wang, Yihan Wang, Zengliang Jian, Chaokun Wang, Yulian Chu, Jianfeng Chen, Haojie Su
abstract: Understanding the complex relationship between biodiversity and ecosystem functioning (BEF) in freshwater ecosystems under multiple stressors remains a critical challenge. While species diversity and functional diversity are key components, their relative importance on functions like phytoplankton resource use efficiency (RUE) under stressor regimes is inadequately resolved. Here, through a six-month mesocosm experiment simulating multiple stressors, we investigated how phytoplankton community structure (specifically species richness, functional richness, species evenness, functional evenness, and cyanobacterial relative biomass) is associated with RUE. In such a system, where experimental conditions are artificially controlled, we have discovered that both species richness and functional richness were positively associated with RUE, while species evenness and functional evenness were negatively associated with RUE. In addition, cyanobacterial relative biomass emerged as a significant positive predictor of RUE, suggesting that cyanobacteria-dominated communities exhibit higher nutrient use efficiency. Among these predictors, species evenness and species richness were the strongest determinants of RUE variation, exceeding the predictive power of functional diversity metrics. Piecewise structural equation modeling (pSEM) supported pathways in which species evenness was associated with RUE both directly and indirectly via functional evenness, whereas species richness showed a direct association with RUE. These findings underscore the statistical associations of both biodiversity components (richness and evenness) and cyanobacterial dominance with phytoplankton resource use under multiple stressors, highlighting the particular importance of monitoring and managing cyanobacterial proliferation in impacted freshwater systems.

title: Temporal 2G–5G RF-EMF exposure assessment in ten European countries during one year
description: Publication date: 10 September 2026 Source: Science of The Total Environment, Volume 1047 Author(s): Han Van Bladel, Adriana Fernandes Veludo, Nicolas Loizeau, Martin Röösli, Milena Maule, Zsuzsanna Vecsei, Orsolya Molnár, Tanja Vrijkotte, Kinga Polanska, Piotr Politański, Paweł Mamrot, Shanshan Wang, Joe Wiart, James Grellier, Anastasiia Kovalenko, Paige M. Hulls, Frank De Vocht, Nina Vaupotiĉ, Mònica Guxens, Wout Joseph
abstract: Due to the rapid evolution and densification of mobile communication networks, there is an increased interest in the long-term assessment of environmental exposure to radiofrequency electromagnetic fields (RF-EMF). While numerous studies have investigated RF-EMF exposure using short-term or spatial measurement campaigns, the number of comprehensive analyses capturing temporal variability across multiple frequency bands and countries remain limited. This pilot study aims to establish a multi-country sensor network to collect data on long-term RF-EMF exposure, including 5G, and to investigate whether temporal trends occur. Twenty frequency-selective sensors were deployed at fixed indoor and outdoor locations in ten European countries, continuously measuring E-field (electric field) strengths in four mobile communication frequency bands (806 MHz, 942 MHz, 1842 MHz, and 3625 MHz) over a period of 17 months with a temporal resolution of 1 s. The raw measurement data were calibrated and analyzed to describe RF-EMF exposure levels, temporal patterns, and variability across environments and spatial characteristics. A strong and recurring diurnal pattern was observed across the four frequency bands. The highest day-night contrasts occurred in the 806 MHz and 1842 MHz bands, where nighttime values decreased by 35.1% and 48.4%, respectively compared to daytime values. Milder contrasts were observed between weekdays and weekends with the most pronounced decrease of 16.6% for the 1842 MHz band. Temporal variability, quantified using the R-factor (i.e. the ratio of the median field strength to the maximum field strength measured during the period of interest), varied substantially across frequency bands and locations, with lower R-factors observed for higher-frequency bands (with a median R-factor of 0.45 for 3625 GHz), indicating a greater variability. Given the scope and duration of this study, it aims to serve as a pilot study for long-term exposure monitoring at fixed sites in multiple countries.

title: Accelerating wastewater-based SARS-CoV-2 surveillance using a mobile laboratory in mixed infrastructure regions
description: Publication date: 10 September 2026 Source: Science of The Total Environment, Volume 1047 Author(s): Amirmohammad Sakhaei, Soroosh Torabi, Mohammad Dehghan Banadaki, Alexus Rockward, William D. Strike, Soroush Farahbakhsh, David Graf, August Bodin, Amanda Muzzey, Riley Lang, Sara Ignoffo, Sean Haley, Will Theodore, Jarret Stiles, Ann Noble, Blazan Mijatovic, Savannah Tucker, Matthew Liversedge, James W. Keck, Lin Xiang
abstract: Wastewater-based epidemiology (WBE) is a powerful tool for early infectious disease detection, but its effectiveness depends on rapid sample processing to prevent RNA degradation and maximize detection lead time for public health responses. To address delays and logistical constraints in regions with limited laboratory infrastructure, we deployed a mobile laboratory to enable on-site, near–real-time sample processing and analysis. Evaluation of this approach for on-site wastewater processing and RNA extraction showed a significant reduction in time-to-results compared to centralized laboratory workflows. A comparison of two RT-qPCR processes (a mobile system vs. a conventional instrument) revealed that while a concentration difference was observed between the two RT-qPCR platforms, the mobile system dramatically improved turnaround time without compromising detection capability, demonstrating the potential of decentralized WBE.

title: Health risk profiles of heavy metals and radionuclides in geothermal waters and groundwater, Kanchanaburi Province, Thailand: An interannual comparative baseline assessment
description: Publication date: 10 September 2026 Source: Science of The Total Environment, Volume 1047 Author(s): Amara Apilux, Patchawee Nualkhao, Puwis Amatyakul, Thitaporn Tusai, Natthanit Nuanla-Or, Thawatchai Itthipoonthanakorn, Saroh Niyomdecha, Naeimah Doloh, Sumana Kladsomboon
abstract: Geothermal systems of Kanchanaburi Province in western Thailand constitute important hydrothermal resources yet represent potential reservoirs of geogenic contaminants. Despite increasing utilization, the combined health risks posed by heavy metals and naturally occurring radionuclides under variable hydrogeochemical conditions remain poorly understood. This study presents an integrated, interannual comparative assessment of trace constituents in major geothermal springs and adjacent groundwater, based on datasets collected in November 2023 and November 2024. The analytical results indicate persistent localized contamination, with mercury (Hg) and radium-226 (Ra-226) exceeding Thai regulatory standards and WHO drinking water guidelines at specific thermal sites. Health risk modeling for adult receptors revealed a distinct interannual shift in the risk profile. In 2023, non-carcinogenic risks were unacceptable (Hazard Index >1), primarily driven by Hg toxicity. Conversely, in 2024, while non-carcinogenic risks declined, carcinogenic risks (CR) increased to unacceptable levels (CR > 1 × 10−4), driven by the elevated presence of arsenic (As). These findings demonstrate that static, single-point assessments may inadequately characterize for managing geochemically complex systems. Consequently, periodic monitoring strategies are essential to safeguard public health against such interannual variations in toxicological threats.

title: Oxidative damage and cholinesterase activity in maternal and umbilical cord blood from an agricultural region in southern Brazil
description: Publication date: 10 September 2026 Source: Science of The Total Environment, Volume 1047 Author(s): Graziela Rodrigues Ródio, Isac George Rosset, Hela Rodrigues Aparecida, Marise Fonseca dos Santos, Priscila Soares Oliveira, Kádima Nayara Teixeira, Gabrielle Caroline Peiter, Ana Paula Carneiro Brandalize
abstract: Pesticide exposure during pregnancy, particularly to organophosphates and carbamates, has been associated with oxidative stress imbalance and adverse maternal and neonatal outcomes. This study aimed to evaluate cholinesterase activity and oxidative stress biomarkers in maternal peripheral blood and umbilical cord blood from mother and newborn pairs residing in an agricultural region of southern Brazil with environmental pesticide exposure. A total of 98 third-trimester pregnant women were recruited. Biomarkers of oxidative stress (MDA, GST, protein carbonyls, and 8-OHGua) and cholinesterase activity (AChE and BChE) were assessed in maternal and cord blood at delivery. Sociodemographic, clinical, and behavioral data were also collected. AChE activity was significantly reduced in cord blood (0.305 ± 0.15 μmol/min/mg) compared to maternal blood (0.612 ± 0.27 μmol/min/mg; p < 0.0001), with inhibition observed in 95% of neonatal samples. Elevated 8-OHGua levels were detected in 87% of maternal and 90% of neonatal samples. GST activity was significantly reduced in 65% of cord samples (p = 0.0001). Exploratory MCA analyses identified association patterns between biomarkers and maternal or neonatal variables. In cord blood, low birth weight showed the highest contribution in Dimension 3 (32.6%), followed by normal GST activity (20.9%). However, no significant associations were observed between biomarkers and major perinatal outcomes. The findings suggest relevant biochemical alterations in the maternal–newborn dyad, involving cholinesterase inhibition and oxidative imbalance. However, the absence of direct pesticide quantification requires cautious interpretation of the findings.

title: Agroecological transitions reveal trade-offs and synergies among ecosystem services
description: Publication date: 10 September 2026 Source: Science of The Total Environment, Volume 1047 Author(s): Mathieu Delandmeter, Bruno Basso, Jérôme Bindelle, Benjamin Dumont
abstract: The management of agroecosystems not only shapes the ecosystem services they provide – e.g., food production and soil carbon (C) sequestration – but also determines the environmental impacts they generate – e.g., nitrate leaching and greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions. Here, using soil-crop simulations from the validated STICS model, we compare eight crop rotations over 541,800 ha in southern Belgium. Starting from a conventional and intensive crop rotation, we examined the impacts of progressively adopting various agroecological levers in crop rotations. They range from efficiency improvements – reducing nitrogen (N) fertilization, to agroecosystems redesign – increasing crop diversity and integrating pastures and livestock under different modalities. Results show that reduced N fertilization lowers GHG emissions and nitrate leaching, but also reduces productivity and hence soil organic carbon. Deeper agroecosystem transformations – crop diversification and, to a further extent, integrated crop-livestock systems (ICLS) – further amplify the reductions of GHG emissions and nitrate leaching, while also enhancing SOC and increasing the stability of the productivity. While the primary environmental benefits of crop diversification stem from reduced N fertilizer use, ICLS are crucial for overcoming the traditional trade-off between C storage and N supply. However, the advantages of ICLS largely depend on how pastures are managed regarding to grazing or mowing practices. Our study measures over large spatio-temporal scales the trade-offs between maximizing productivity and minimizing environmental impacts. By quantifying the environmental benefits and economic losses of gradually adopting these agroecological practices, it shows that broader adoption would require financial support for farmers and/or internalizing the environmental costs of agroecosystems.

title: Legacy persistent organic pollutants in Mytilus galloprovincialis from the Sochi River estuary (Russian black sea coast): A mussel watch monitoring study
description: Publication date: 10 September 2026 Source: Science of The Total Environment, Volume 1047 Author(s): Aleksandra D. Borovkova, Maksim M. Donets, Maksim A. Belanov, Tatyana V. Boychenko, Kristina R. Masaleva, Vasiliy Yu. Tsygankov
abstract: This study presents current data on POP levels in the soft tissues of Mytilus galloprovincialis from the Sochi River estuary on the Russian Black Sea coast. Our results revealed a predominance of degradation products (β-HCH, DDE, and DDD), indicating the long-term environmental persistence of these substances. However, the presence of parent pesticide compounds (lindane, o,p’-DDT, and p,p’-DDT) in some samples could suggest a possible recent local influx. Among PCBs, highly chlorinated congeners (PCBs 118, 153, and 138) were prevalent, implying a historical contribution of these xenobiotics. Significant intersex differences in ∑PCB accumulation were found, with males accumulating higher levels than females, which may be attributed to reproductive traits and the elimination of lipophilic compounds with gametes. An inverse relationship between mussel shell size and ∑PCB tissue concentrations was established, attributable to the growth dilution effect in actively growing young individuals. A comparative analysis showed that current POP levels in the study area are lower than the historical maxima recorded in the Black Sea in the late 20th century. However, the contaminant profile, characterized by a high proportion of HCH isomers, differs from those typical of other contemporary Black Sea studies (e.g., in Bulgaria and Turkey), where DDT metabolites dominate. This mixed profile shows a qualitative resemblance to findings from some developing nations in the Asia-Pacific region, although cross-study comparisons are complicated by methodological differences. These findings underscore the necessity for further monitoring of POPs in this area and highlight the need for wider spatial surveys along the Russian Black Sea coast.

title: Development of a ranking of barriers to the adoption of green roofs in Brazil using Delphi methodology
description: Publication date: 10 September 2026 Source: Science of The Total Environment, Volume 1047 Author(s): Daniela de Ávila Modesto Barcelos, Peter Ludvig, Eduardo Romeiro Filho, Cristiane Machado Parisi Jonov, Adriano de Paula e Silva, Ricardo Filipe Mesquita Silva Mateus, Hélvio Júnio Barcelos
abstract: Green roofs can contribute to mitigating urban heat islands, managing stormwater, and improving the environmental performance of buildings, however, their adoption in Brazil remains incipient. Although previous studies have examined green roof barriers in different countries, the Brazilian context remains insufficiently characterized in terms of expert-based prioritization, particularly given the absence of official market statistics, the lack of a dedicated national technical standard, and the early-stage development of public policies and incentives. This study produces an empirically validated context-sensitive ranking of green-roof adoption barriers in Brazil by combining a structured literature search based on the ProKnow-C protocol with an iterative Delphi panel of Brazilian experts conducted until simultaneous convergence criteria were met. Its contribution lies in situating the prioritization within the specific institutional, technical, and informational conditions that constrain green roof diffusion in Brazil, and in enabling structured comparison with international evidence to distinguish universally reported obstacles from context-amplified constraints. Prioritization was estimated using the Relative Importance Index, and consensus was verified through pre-defined thresholds for median, interquartile range, coefficient of variation, and Kendall's concordance coefficient. Twenty barriers were identified and grouped into five categories. The results indicate that adoption is predominantly constrained by informational deficits and economic and institutional barriers. The five highest-ranked barriers were gaps in public knowledge, lack of public incentives and governmental support, increased design and construction costs, low environmental awareness, and insufficient performance data. Comparison with international studies reveals convergence regarding the role of costs and incentives, but informational barriers assume greater centrality in Brazil, reflecting the early diffusion stage of the technology and limited local performance evidence. These findings provide an empirical basis for public policy design, professional training strategies, and applied research agendas targeting the priority constraints on green roof adoption in Brazil.

title: Hospital wastewater as a reservoir of environmental hazards for humans: Implications for public and occupational safety and health in the era of One Health
description: Publication date: 10 September 2026 Source: Science of The Total Environment, Volume 1047 Author(s): Linda Ferrea, Paolo Durando, Rosanna Tindara Micale, Anna Maria Spagnolo, Francesco D'Agostini, Sebastiano La Maestra
abstract: Hospital wastewater (HWW) represents a complex and increasingly relevant source of environmental contamination. These effluents contain a wide range of pollutants, including pharmaceuticals, disinfectants, pathogenic microorganisms, antimicrobial resistance genes, heavy metals, radionuclides, and emerging contaminants such as micro- and nanoplastics (MNPs). Within the evolving European regulatory framework for urban wastewater treatment, HWW is now recognised as a critical matrix requiring targeted management strategies. This review critically examines current evidence on the composition of HWW, highlighting the role of MNPs as vectors for bioactive, toxic, and potentially genotoxic substances. Special attention is devoted to different processes that markedly influence the environmental fate, bioavailability, and toxicity of associated contaminants. Growing experimental evidence indicates that MNPs can enhance the persistence, mobility, and biological effects of hazardous compounds, amplifying potential risks to both environmental and human health, and focusing on the occupational risks associated with HWW for wastewater treatment plant operators and hospital maintenance workers. These workers may be exposed to complex mixtures of chemical and biological agents through aerosols, sludge, and direct contact, with possible oxidative, inflammatory, and genotoxic effects. The limitations of conventional wastewater treatment processes in removing emerging contaminants and MNPs are discussed, together with the potential of advanced technologies such as membrane bioreactors, advanced oxidation processes, and hybrid systems. In conclusion, the review highlights the urgent need for integrated monitoring strategies that combine chemical, biological, and toxicological assessments within a One Health framework to better protect environmental, public, and occupational health and to support future policy development and technological innovation.

title: Modeling soil solution electrical conductivity across Europe
description: Publication date: 10 September 2026 Source: Science of The Total Environment, Volume 1047 Author(s): Mohammad Aziz Zarif, Amirhossein Hassani, Mehdi H. Afshar, Panos Panagos, Inma Lebron, David A. Robinson, Dani Or, Nima Shokri
abstract: Soil salinization, referring to the excessive accumulation of soluble salts in soils, adversely influences nutrient cycling, biodiversity, soil structure, crop production, soil health, and ecosystem functioning. Accurately assessing soil salinity via electrical conductivity (EC) is key to mitigating its impacts. Thus, developing predictive tools for soil EC at regional and continental scales is essential for sustainable soil management. Here, we apply machine learning models to predict soil EC in the European Union (EU) and United Kingdom (UK) soils using different environmental factors like soil, climate, topography, and satellite data as predictors. The model is trained by ≈40,000 soil EC data points from the 2015 and 2018 Land Use/Cover Area Frame Survey data (LUCAS) surveys, complemented by the EC observations from World Soil Information Services (WoSIS) dataset. To improve the model performance, a forward feature selection technique was used resulting in selection of 17 covariates out of initially 34 predictors. The final selected XGBoost model achieved R2 values of 0.68, 0.6, and 0.63 for the training, internal testing, and independent validation datasets, respectively. For the year 2018, we estimate ≈21.7 Mha of EU + UK land exceeds an EC of 0.6 dS/m (at a 1:5 soil to water ratio, the so-called EC1:5). This estimate should be interpreted as elevated predicted EC1:5, rather than a direct estimate of soils meeting protosalic diagnostic criteria. The output of the predictive model consists of a gridded dataset that illustrates the spatial distribution of EC1:5 throughout the study area for the year 2018, along with an associated uncertainty map with a spatial resolution of 1 km.

title: Microbiota under bloom stress: A review and meta-analysis of bloom-associated cyanopeptides, environmental stressors, and microbial shifts in free-living and host gut microbiomes
