The resulting internally validated empirical models provide screening-level estimates of 210Po occurrence within the range of Canadian freshwater conditions represented in this dataset. Furthermore, observed activity concentration ranges provide comparative context for future monitoring and site-specific assessments.

title: A compact, platform-agnostic system for underwater radioactivity detection
description: Publication date: August 2026 Source: Journal of Environmental Radioactivity, Volume 298 Author(s): Christos Tsabaris, Efrossyni G. Androulakaki, Ioanna Kora, Stylianos Alexakis
abstract: This work presents the development and evaluation of a compact underwater radioactivity detection system, named Mini KATERINA, designed to be integrated in platform-agnostic mobile robotic vehicles operating in controlled aquatic environments to identify radioactive sources. It employs a 2″ × 2″ NaI(Tl) scintillation crystal coupled to a silicon photomultiplier (SiPM), achieving reduced size, weight, and power consumption. The system was characterized in laboratory conditions using calibrated reference point sources and dedicated simulants (volume sources), enabling training and validation for the identification of suspicious objects. Initial performance assessment was conducted in a water tank to investigate detection capabilities as well as to perform calibrations in terms of energy, energy resolution and full energy peak efficiency. The calculated efficiency of the system for distances between source and detector surface at 4.5, 8.5 and 12.5 cm was 0.0038, 0.0016 and 0.00051, respectively. The limit of detection (LD) of the system at 662 keV for distances between source and detector surface at 4.5, 8.5 and 12.5 cm was 8, 17 and 54 Bq, respectively. Subsequently, field tests were performed in a marine environment to evaluate the limit of detection of a point source using a known radioactive simulant housed in a dedicated enclosure. The Limit of Detection of a point source (LD) of the system in this field configuration in the marine environment resulted a value of 43 Βq when the system is in a distance of 6 cm from the 137Cs point source. The results demonstrate the system's effectiveness for underwater radiation monitoring and its potential integration into diverse mobile underwater platforms.

title: Investigation of the migration behavior of 237 Np, 238 Pu, and 90 Sr in unsaturated silty loam sediment
description: Publication date: August 2026 Source: Journal of Environmental Radioactivity, Volume 298 Author(s): Chen Chao, Xu Cheng-Long, Liang Peng-Liang, Zhu Jun
abstract: Laboratory migration experiments investigating 237Np, 238Pu, and 90Sr were conducted over a period of 1073 days (approximately 3 years), corresponding to the predetermined duration of the study project, using large-scale undisturbed unsaturated silty loam soil columns to compare their migration behaviors under identical conditions. Results revealed distinct patterns: after 1073 days, 237Np and 90Sr exhibited single, symmetrical concentration peaks without tailing, with peak concentrations of 1688 Bq·g−1 and 398 Bq·g−1 migrating downward by 3.25 cm and 9.75 cm, respectively. The significant difference in migration distance between these nuclides primarily stems from variations in their chemical speciation, adsorption characteristics, and interaction mechanisms within the soil. Conversely, 238Pu displayed a distinct bimodal distribution, with a high-concentration peak (423 Bq·g−1) retained near the surface at 0.25 cm due to strong initial adsorption, and a secondary lower-concentration peak (408 Bq·g−1) formed at 4.04 cm. This pattern indicates partial desorption of 238Pu under leaching conditions, leading to accelerated downward migration and subsequent re-adsorption deeper in the profile. Numerical simulations using HYDRUS-1D, incorporating colloidal effects, showed that both equilibrium and non-equilibrium adsorption models adequately described 237Np and 90Sr transport. For 238Pu, a non-equilibrium model featuring a first-order adsorption-desorption rate constant (β) effectively captured the leading-edge tailing of the secondary peak. However, reproducing the full bimodal distribution required a more sophisticated conceptualization using a two-region or dual-porosity model.

title: Radiological dose assessment of waterborne radon and Monte Carlo–based evaluation of lifetime excess cancer risk in uranium mining regions of South Africa
description: Publication date: August 2026 Source: Journal of Environmental Radioactivity, Volume 298 Author(s): Abubakar Adekunle Muritala, Idowu Richard Akomolafe, JJ van Zyl, Naven Chetty
abstract: Radon (222Rn) is a naturally occurring radioactive noble gas found in groundwater, particularly in regions with uranium-rich geology and extensive mining, such as South Africa. This study presents a multi-site comparative assessment using a unified methodology and represents one of the first South African investigations to explicitly integrate ingestion and water-to-air inhalation pathways within a probabilistic lifetime excess cancer risk (LECR) framework. Using a RAD7 radon monitor, we measured radon concentrations in 80 boreholes across Carletonville, Wedela, Mokopane, Beaufort West, and Sutherland to calculate the total effective dose and lifetime excess cancer risk. Radon concentrations ranged from 18 ± 2 to 369 ± 96 B q L − 1 , with an overall mean of 127 ± 32 B q L − 1 , resulting in total effective doses (ingestion + inhalation of waterborne radon released into indoor air) ranging from 0.09 ± 0.02 to 1.87 ± 0.50 m S v y − 1 . The calculated mean radon concentration exceeds the World Health Organization (WHO) reference level of 100 B q L − 1 . Although the mean total effective dose remains below the International Commission on Radiological Protection (ICRP) public dose limit of 1 m S v y − 1 , the result indicates a non-negligible public health concern that warrants mitigation. Monte Carlo simulation (100,000 iterations, water-only pathway) yielded a mean lifetime excess cancer risk (LECR) of 2.58 × 1 0 − 3 and a median of 2.36 × 1 0 − 3 , both above the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency (USEPA) acceptable risk threshold of 1 × 1 0 − 4 . These translate to approximately 2580 and 2360 additional cancer cases per million people exposed over a 70-year lifetime, respectively, with 100 % of simulated iterations exceeding the USEPA threshold. The reported risk reflects only the waterborne pathway; soil-gas and building-material contributions, which typically dominate total indoor inhalation dose, were not measured. Even so, the waterborne component alone exceeds international risk benchmarks across the entire simulated distribution and at every site sampled, supporting the case for explicit national radon-in-water regulation, systematic monitoring, and complementary indoor-air radon assessment.

title: Artificial radionuclide levels in land cover of radiological warfare agent test site ‘4’
description: Publication date: August 2026 Source: Journal of Environmental Radioactivity, Volume 298 Author(s): N.V. Larionova, V.V. Bozhko, A.V. Panitskiy, P. Ye Krivitskiy, M.V. Skripnikov, A.V. Toporova, V.N. Monayenko, A. Ye Kunduzbayeva, A.O. Aidarkhanov, V.V. Baklanov
abstract: Assessing the environmental legacy of historical test sites for nuclear weapons and radiological warfare agents (RWAs) is critical for understanding long-term isotopic evolution and evaluating land safety. This study evaluates artificial radionuclide levels (241Am, 137Cs, 90Sr and 239+240Pu) in the land cover of Site ‘4’, a historic RWA testing ground in the Republic of Kazakhstan. Within the 37 km2 area analysed via pedestrian and discrete gamma spectrometric surveys, 14 radioactively contaminated locations with gross gamma count rates exceeding the experimentally established baseline of 180 cps were identified, totalling ∼0.37 km2. Soil analysis revealed 90Sr activity concentrations exceeding those of other artificial radionuclides by several orders of magnitude, with the highest values at all sampling points recorded in the upper soil layer (0–10 cm). From the vertical 90Sr distribution within the soil profile, two distribution patterns were identified: (1) high migration into the 10–20-cm layer and below, and (2) high activity concentrations in the 0–10-cm layer, followed by a sharp decrease in the 10–20-cm layer. This differing distribution pattern is attributed to the use of liquid vs. powdered RWA formulations. The maximum total dose rate of the investigated artificial radionuclides to herbaceous vegetation reached 220 μGy/day, driven primarily by 90Sr exposure. This study fills a critical research gap in the radioecological monitoring of this area and provides precise geographical and radioecological data necessary for the rehabilitation of these lands.

title: Up-scaling of radon migration in rock media based on multi-resolution CT pore modeling and volume averaging method
description: Publication date: August 2026 Source: Journal of Environmental Radioactivity, Volume 298 Author(s): Yuan-Chao Chen, Dong Xie, Zhong-Luo Liao, Jun Zeng, Qian-Ran Jia
abstract: The macroscopic radon migration behavior in rock media is inherently dominated by its microscopic pore structure and transport properties. However, the lack of accurate correlation methods between microscopic transport characteristics and macroscopic parameters has long been a bottleneck in revealing radon migration mechanisms. To address this issue, this study proposes an integrated approach combining multi-resolution CT pore modeling and the Volume Averaging Method. 3D pore models of rock specimens were constructed at resolutions of 48.9 μm/voxel, 7.3 μm/voxel, and 1.1 μm/voxel using CT scanning and 3D visualization and analysis software. Through thresholding, connectivity analysis and REV analysis, key pore structure parameters (porosity and connectivity) and optimal REV sizes were determined. The results indicated that connected pore channels in the Z direction were only formed at the highest resolution (1.1 μm/voxel) with a connected porosity of 1.92%. On this basis, radon diffusion and seepage simulations were performed on the identified REVs to obtain the radon migration parameters. The Volume Averaging Method was innovatively adopted to realize the up-scaling of REV parameters to macroscopic ones, yielding the up-scaling diffusion coefficient (9.57 × 10−9 m2/s) and permeability (2.19 × 10−15 m2) in the Z direction, while parameters in disconnected directions were close to 0. Furthermore, the up-scaling parameters were extended to unsaturated and non-isothermal conditions by coupling the unsaturated non-isothermal radon diffusion coefficient model and Brooks-Corey model. Experimental verification showed that the deviation between the up-scaling radon diffusion coefficient and the experimental value was only 1.83% at 20 °C, and the deviation between the simulated radon exhalation rate (based on the up-scaling parameters) and the experimental value ranged from 10.38% to 31.12% when water saturation varied from 0% to 70%. This study presents a feasible technical approach for the accurate up-scaling of radon migration parameters in rocks, which helps to narrow the disconnect between microscopic and macroscopic research.

title: Treatment of barium-contaminated wastewaters using adsorption: a review
description: Publication date: August 2026 Source: Journal of Environmental Radioactivity, Volume 298 Author(s): Nathan Vinícius Martins da Silva, Amanda Magliano Pontes, Clascídia Aparecida Furtado, Ana Cláudia Queiroz Ladeira
abstract: Barium-containing wastewaters are produced on a large scale by various industries, including electronics, pigment, and ceramics manufacturing. They are also generated by the nuclear industry, where barium chloride is used to precipitate and remove Ra-226. Improper disposal of these wastes can potentially cause various adverse effects on the biosphere because the metal can be toxic to humans and other life forms, depending on the dosage. Therefore, choosing the best available treatment technology that is economically achievable is essential to ensure the safety of both the environment and human health. Among the various methods available for this purpose, adsorption is considered one of the most promising because it offers benefits like low cost, simple design, and high efficiency. This review discusses the use of adsorption for decontaminating industrial wastewaters containing barium. It highlights the adsorptive performance of various materials and explores key factors influencing adsorption, including optimal pH, contact time, and the impact of competing species. The adsorption capacities of various adsorbents ranged from less than 5 mg/g to over 500 mg/g. Adsorption mechanisms such as ion exchange and complexation were described. Surface modifications have been found to significantly improve the performance of some adsorbents. Similarly, nanotechnology has enabled the design of materials with enhanced properties, such as increased surface area and porosity, as well as the ability to be functionalized. Nature-derived adsorbents, in turn, offer the advantages of high environmental compatibility and wide availability, although some of these exhibited poor adsorptive performances. Finally, suggestions for future work include the incorporation of the adsorbents into macrostructures to facilitate their removal after adsorption.

title: Indoor radon exposure in Serbia – A critical review
description: Publication date: August 2026 Source: Journal of Environmental Radioactivity, Volume 298 Author(s): Predrag Kuzmanović
abstract: The aim of this study was to provide the first comprehensive assessment of indoor radon levels in Serbia based on long-term monitoring data and available studies, including a critical review of methodological limitations. The analysis, conducted using activated charcoal canisters, includes 875 buildings (2011–2024) across seven cities in Serbia, with radon concentrations ranging from 5 to 1609 Bq/m3, an arithmetic mean value of 119 ± 149 Bq/m3, and a geometric mean value of 76 ± 3 Bq/m3. About 38% of buildings exceed 100 Bq/m3, while 7% exceed 300 Bq/m3. Comparison with other national studies shows a much wider range (1–13,400 Bq/m3 in residential and commercial buildings and 10–1130 Bq/m3 in schools and kindergartens), depending on building type, geology, and measurement methodology. Higher values were observed in southern Serbia and in Kosovo and Metohija, with a log-normal distribution and pronounced local variability. Effective dose estimates indicate moderate average exposure, but also localized areas of elevated risk (average < 4 mSv/y, maximum up to 40 mSv/y). The critical analysis highlights key limitations, including data heterogeneity, dominance of short-term measurements within monitoring campaigns, inconsistent national criteria compared with WHO guidelines, and insufficient spatial coverage. In particular, there is a lack of epidemiological studies and insufficient integration of radon data with geological and building material sources. The conclusion is that Serbia exhibits moderate average indoor radon levels, but with pronounced local radiation risks. Standardization of measurement methods, long-term monitoring aimed at developing a more comprehensive radon map compared to the current one, expansion of the monitoring network, and development of epidemiological studies are necessary to improve public health protection.

title: Analytical determination of radium isotopes in water: current capabilities, challenges and future directions
description: Publication date: August 2026 Source: Journal of Environmental Radioactivity, Volume 298 Author(s): M. Gongora, J. Martínez, A. Peñalver, C. Aguilar, F. Borrull
abstract: Radium isotopes in water remain a significant analytical challenge due to their low environmental activity concentrations, chemical similarity to alkaline-earth elements, and strict regulatory limits. Accurate determination of 226Ra and 228Ra requires efficient preconcentration and selective radiochemical separation prior to detection. This review evaluates contemporary methodologies for radium isotope determination in water, with particular emphasis on developments reported since 2014. Special attention is given to preconcentration strategies, radiochemical isolation procedures, source preparation and measurement techniques, as well as to how these steps influence analytical performance in terms of ingrowth time, counting time, recovery and minimum detectable activity concentration. Overall, this review provides a critical framework for selecting appropriate analytical methods for environmental monitoring and regulatory applications, by critically comparing complete analytical workflows and highlighting the parameters which control analytical performance.

title: Evaluation of radon progeny mitigation techniques (HEPA filtration, ionization, electrostatic deposition) and their potential use in caves
description: Publication date: June 2026 Source: Journal of Environmental Radioactivity, Volume 297 Author(s): J.E. Martínez, B. Juste, G. Verdú
abstract: Radon and its short-lived progeny are recognized as significant contributors to the radiological dose received indoors and are associated with increased lung cancer risk. This study evaluates the effectiveness of various air purification technologies—including HEPA filtration, ionization, electrostatic deposition, and combined systems—in reducing airborne concentrations of radon progeny (PAEC, 218Po, and 214Po) in a controlled, non-ventilated environment. Measurements were carried out using active and passive detectors over multiple campaigns with and without air purifiers. Statistically significant reductions were observed for all purification methods tested, with the greatest decrease found for 214Po and PAEC, and more moderate reductions for 218Po. The combination of HEPA filtration and ionization proved most effective, achieving reductions exceeding 40% in PAEC. The results confirm that air purification systems, particularly those using ionization and electrostatic principles, can play a crucial role in mitigating radon progeny exposure in enclosed spaces. These findings support the practical implementation of air purification strategies in high-risk environments such as underground workplaces, shelters, and laboratories.

title: Gamma emissions from NORM in building materials: A position paper on national transposition of the Euratom basic safety standard
description: Publication date: June 2026 Source: Journal of Environmental Radioactivity, Volume 297 Author(s): M. Dodek, R.E. Djabou, C. Sainz, I. Fuente, L.L. Vintró, O. Hanley, J. Goggins, M. Foley
abstract: This position paper examines how the Euratom Basic Safety Standards (EU-BSS), Council Directive 2013/59/Euratom) on gamma radiation from building materials have been transposed into national regulation across selected EU Member States. It focuses on Austria, Belgium, the Czech Republic, Denmark, Finland, France, Germany, Ireland, Italy, Poland, Portugal, Netherlands, Spain, and Sweden. Drawing on national legislation, technical guidance and direct correspondence with regulators and researchers, the paper compares who is responsible for characterising Naturally Occurring Radioactive Material (NORM) in building materials, and how compliance with the 1 mSv/year reference level is demonstrated. Across the countries studied, regulation is broadly convergent with the Gamma Index being widely used as a screening tool. Responsibility for measurements generally lies with manufacturers or suppliers using accredited laboratories with regulatory attention primarily focused on natural igneous and pozzolanic stones, alum-shale–related products, and construction materials containing industrial residues such as fly ash, phosphogypsum, slags and red mud. At the same time, there are notable differences in the existence of long-term national datasets, the degree of integration with construction-product approval systems, and whether NORM above exemption levels is treated as radioactive waste or managed under a more flexible “existing exposure” regime. The paper provides a current snapshot of this evolving European regulatory landscape and is intended to inform the further development of proportionate NORM regulation and monitoring strategies for building materials and recycled building materials in Europe. Its added value lies in bringing dispersed national sources into a single comparative framework and in identifying recurring implementation models, practical divergences and emerging issues for recycled and secondary materials.

title: Seasonal patterns in the relationship between gamma emitters in the ground-level atmospheric layer and total atmospheric precipitation in southern Poland (Kraków), 2022 - 2025
description: Publication date: June 2026 Source: Journal of Environmental Radioactivity, Volume 297 Author(s): Sylwia Błażej, Jerzy W. Mietelski, Renata Kierepko, Mikołaj Wielgat
abstract: Atmospheric physical and chemical processes significantly influence the presence of radionuclides, affecting their production (for cosmogenic isotopes), horizontal and vertical transport, and resuspension. This study presents weekly gamma-spectrometric measurements of aerosol and monthly measurements of atmospheric precipitation collected in Krakow (southern Poland) during the years 2022-2025, which is a continuation of studies initiated in 1990. For both types of samples, time series and correlations between observed activity concentrations of 40K, 210Pb, 7Be, 22Na and 137Cs for the whole period and in sub-sets of four seasons. Most observed trends correspond to seasonal patterns characteristic of temperate climate zones and to prevailing atmospheric phenomena during the study period. Due to increasing solar activity during the 25th solar cycle a decreasing trend for both cosmogenic radionuclides is observed, however with a strong seasonal variation. No traces of 131I were found either in aerosol form or in gaseous form.

title: From zonal containment to spot recovery: Multi-platform geostatistical reassessment of radiation risk boundaries in Fukushima (2019–2024)
description: Publication date: June 2026 Source: Journal of Environmental Radioactivity, Volume 297 Author(s): Imam Ghazali Yasmint, Yo Ishigaki, Kayoko Yamamoto
abstract: This study provides a spatiotemporal reassessment of the radiological landscape within the Difficult-to-Return Zone (DTRZ) surrounding the Fukushima Daiichi Nuclear Power Plant (FDNPP), integrating airborne, car-borne, and walk-borne survey data from 2019 to 2024 through Empirical Bayesian Kriging (EBK) to generate high-resolution (50-m) dose-rate surfaces. Applying the official Japanese government occupancy threshold of 3.8 μSv·h−1 (equivalent to 20 mSv·y−1), the 2019 DTRZ boundary demonstrated complete radiological containment, with all threshold-exceeding grid cells located within the zone boundaries in both monitoring years, but exhibited pronounced internal over-restriction: 96.2% of the 337.34 km2 DTRZ area comprised grid cells that did not exceed the threshold in 2019, rising to 98.4% by 2024 as the threshold-exceeding area contracted by 56.8% from 12.74 km2 to 5.50 km2. Radiological assessment of the seven Specified Reconstruction and Revitalization Base Areas (SRRBA) (digitized from published cartography) revealed that mean dose rates across all patches declined from 6.45 mSv·y−1 to 3.08 mSv·y−1 (−52.2%), with all patches recording doses below the 20 mSv·y−1 policy threshold and threshold-exceeding area contracting by 86.1%. Forest classes (Deciduous Broadleaf Forest [DBF], Deciduous Needleleaf Forest [DNF], Evergreen Broadleaf Forest [EBF], Evergreen Needleleaf Forest [ENF], and Bamboo forest) accounted for 60.2% of threshold-exceeding cells in 2019, declining to 56.5% in 2024, with a notable compositional shift from DBF (39.6% to 25.8%) toward ENF (15.1% to 22.8%) reflecting differential radioecological recovery rates. These findings empirically validate the radiological justification for the SRRBA designation and the broader transition from broad zonal restriction toward spot-based recovery management.

title: Degradation pathways in mediterranean coastal groundwater dependent ecosystems: A process based review toward an integrated conceptual framework
description: Publication date: August 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology: Regional Studies, Volume 66 Author(s): Luigi Alessandrino, Nicolò Colombani, Micòl Mastrocicco
abstract: Study region The Mediterranean Basin hosts a diverse array of coastal groundwater dependent ecosystems, here defined as coastal environments that rely on groundwater to sustain hydrological regimes and associated biogeochemical processes. These systems include lagoons, coastal lakes, marshes, river delta wetlands, sabkhas, and artificial wetlands distributed along approximately 46,000 km of coastline. Located within a recognized climate change hotspot, Mediterranean coastal groundwater dependent ecosystems are exposed to intensifying climatic seasonality, chronic water scarcity, and long-standing anthropogenic pressures, making their functioning particularly sensitive to alterations in groundwater recharge, storage, and subsurface connectivity. Study focus This review examines 267 peer-reviewed studies (2000–present) on Mediterranean coastal groundwater dependent ecosystems through a site-based bibliographic approach that combines satellite-derived site identification with targeted literature searches. The studies were classified according to spatial, temporal, and conceptual dimensions, with particular emphasis on dominant degradation processes and on the extent to which groundwater is incorporated into interpretative frameworks. New hydrological insights: Lagoon systems account for the majority of the reviewed literature (183 studies), reflecting both their widespread occurrence and the existence of well-established research traditions. Research is geographically concentrated in Italy, Spain, and France, whereas North Africa and the eastern Mediterranean remain comparatively underrepresented. Groundwater is most commonly conceptualized as an implicit component (147 studies) or a mediating factor (83 studies), and only rarely as a primary driver (37 studies). Salinization, nutrient enrichment, hydrological alteration, and contaminant accumulation emerge as the principal degradation pathways, governed by nonlinear interactions between climatic and anthropogenic pressures. A five-phase process-based framework is proposed to integrate hydrogeological, biogeochemical, and ecological analyses, providing a transferable basis for diagnosing degradation mechanisms and supporting adaptive management strategies across diverse coastal groundwater dependent ecosystems settings.

title: From canopy to creek: A systematic review of the hydrological trade-offs of Mediterranean forest expansion
description: Publication date: August 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology: Regional Studies, Volume 66 Author(s): Safae Jourani, Pierre-Alain Ayral, Matthieu Vignal, Didier Josselin
abstract: Study region The Mediterranean region, identified as a global climate change hotspot, faces a critical hydrological paradox: while forest expansion is promoted for carbon sequestration and soil conservation, it potentially threatens water availability in water-scarce catchments. Study focus This article presents a systematic synthesis of peer-reviewed literature (2010–2024) to evaluate the mechanistic trade-offs between Mediterranean forest recovery and hydrological fluxes. Using a PRISMA-compliant protocol, we analysed 59 studies to disentangle the effects of spontaneous reforestation, afforestation, and land abandonment on runoff, infiltration, and evapotranspiration. New hydrological insights for the region The synthesis reveals that forest expansion consistently reduces annual water yield by approximately 20–30% in headwater catchments. This decline is primarily driven by increased interception and transpiration rates that override infiltration gains. Unlike in temperate regions, the "sponge effect" in Mediterranean environments is frequently compromised by high evaporative demand, leading to significant baseflow reductions during summer droughts. However, forests play an irreplaceable role in stabilizing sediment fluxes and buffering flood peaks. The analysis highlights that these hydrological responses are non-linear, scale-dependent, and increasingly amplified by climate warming. We identify a critical gap in current modelling approaches, which often fail to couple dynamic vegetation responses with extreme climatic events. Consequently, we argue that passive reforestation policies must be replaced by adaptive forest management strategies, such as targeted density reduction, to reconcile ecosystem services.

title: Managing the Nile under climate change: A systematic review of hydrological shifts and adaptive strategies for transboundary water security
description: Publication date: August 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology: Regional Studies, Volume 66 Author(s): Nahom Mena, Joseph Awange, Xiaolong Mi
abstract: Study Region: The Nile River Basin (NRB), spanning 11 countries in East Africa and supporting over 300 million people. Study Focus: This study synthesizes three decades of research using an AI-enhanced PRISMA review to assess impacts of climate change, land-use change, and infrastructure on water availability and risks across the basin. New Hydrological Insights for the Region: The review reveals pronounced spatial heterogeneity in hydrological responses. In the Blue Nile, discharge trends are mixed and often statistically insignificant, with recent changes increasingly linked to land-use dynamics rather than climate alone. In the White Nile, hydrology shows multi-decadal variability rather than consistent long-term trends. A major regime shift in 1961, associated with a positive Indian Ocean Dipole (IOD), raised Lake Victoria by about 2 m and increased baseline outflows. Flows declined through the 1990s, dropped sharply in the early 2000s due to dam operations, and reached record highs in 2020 following IOD-driven extreme rainfall. Attribution studies indicate climate change has likely contributed to increased White Nile flows in recent decades, although uncertainties remain regarding the roles of climate, land use, and human interventions. Future rainfall and river flow projections show wide divergence, ranging from − 10 % to + 25 % for rainfall and − 20 % to + 40 % for discharge by late century, highlighting uncertainty in future water availability and increasing pressure on transboundary water management.

title: Monitoring groundwater and terrestrial water storage with GRACE/GRACE-FO across MENA and the Gulf Cooperation Council countries: A regional review
description: Publication date: August 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology: Regional Studies, Volume 66 Author(s): Omar Alsenjar, Mohamed Mostafa Mohamed
abstract: Study region This review focuses on the Middle East and North Africa (MENA) and the Gulf Cooperation Council (GCC) countries as the primary regional evidence base. Nile Basin, Mediterranean, and South-Central Asian arid/semi-arid studies are used only as methodological benchmarks where they share comparable water stress, groundwater-use conditions, and GRACE-scale basin characteristics. Study focus We synthesize GRACE (2002–2017) and GRACE Follow-On (GRACE-FO, 2018–present) applications for terrestrial water-storage anomalies (TWSA), groundwater-storage anomalies (GWSA), basin water-budget closure, downscaling, reconstruction, and decision-oriented groundwater monitoring. The review is based on 274 screened records and a coded core set of 73 studies, of which 58 were used in structured regional evidence maps. The manuscript cites 63 references overall, including methodological, product, and benchmark references. Selection, coding, and evidence-strength ratings follow a PRISMA-informed workflow. This review provides a region-centered, uncertainty-aware synthesis rather than a new basin-scale retrieval. New hydrological insights for the region Across MENA/GCC case studies, the strongest evidence indicates basin-integrated TWSA/GWSA decline in intensively managed aquifers, but inference strength varies with basin size, product lineage, leakage/scaling treatment, component separation, validation data, and reference-period choices. We propose minimum reporting and validation requirements for decision-ready GRACE-based groundwater assessment, including product disclosure, anomaly-baseline definition, leakage/scaling correction, TWSA-to-GWSA partitioning, uncertainty propagation, and independent validation using wells, discharge, altimetry, GNSS/InSAR, or documented water-use data.

title: Agricultural drought: A comprehensive review of research trends, monitoring indices, modeling frameworks, knowledge gaps, and future pathways
description: Publication date: August 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology: Regional Studies, Volume 66 Author(s): Rajkumar Guria, Manoranjan Mishra, Pijus Hatui, Satya Sundar Samantaray, Biswaranjan Baraj, Richarde Marques da Silva, Celso Augusto Guimarães Santos, Rabin Chakrabortty, Manjula Ranagalage, Yuji Murayama
abstract: Study region Agricultural drought (AD) poses persistent risks to global food systems, with severe consequences for climate-sensitive regions such as South Asia, China, Africa, and drought-prone agroecosystems worldwide. These regions experience increasing soil-moisture deficits, vegetation stress, crop-yield losses, and heightened socio-economic vulnerability. This review, although global in scope, gives particular emphasis to drought-affected agricultural landscapes, including semi-arid, monsoon-dependent, and rain-fed farming regions where drought impacts are most pronounced. Study focus This study provides a broad assessment of AD research spanning 1960–2024 through scientometric analysis (2294 Scopus publications) combined with a systematic literature review. It synthesizes global trends in drought indices, satellite-based monitoring, machine learning (ML) and artificial intelligence (AI) applications, hydrological and crop modeling frameworks, socio-economic vulnerability assessments, and early warning systems. The review evaluates major methodological developments—ranging from optical, thermal, and microwave remote sensing to composite drought indicators, advanced ML techniques and hybrid models. It also examines critical gaps in data quality, model interpretability, sensor limitations, multi-source data fusion, and the lack of region-specific calibration. New hydrological insights This review highlights several emerging directions: (i) increasing reliance on multi-sensor satellite data for soil moisture, evapotranspiration, and vegetation-health diagnostics; (ii) the growing importance of explainable AI, graph neural networks, and digital-twin frameworks for capturing spatiotemporal drought propagation; (iii) improved understanding of lag relationships between meteorological triggers and agricultural impacts; and (iv) recognition of socio-ecological feedbacks as fundamental components of drought risk. Findings reveal that AD research is rapidly transitioning toward integrated, data-rich, and context-specific monitoring systems. Future priorities include enhanced calibration standards, cross-regional model transferability, integration of socio-economic vulnerability, sensor–model fusion, and real-time drought advisory systems to support adaptation and policy planning.

title: Propagation of precipitation errors to streamflow: A large-sample evaluation of IMERG V06 and V07 in southern China
description: Publication date: August 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology: Regional Studies, Volume 66 Author(s): Wen Liu, Naili Zhao, Yonghua Zhu, Haishen Lü, Qingyi Yang, Jianbin Su
abstract: Study region 312 small- and medium-sized watersheds across humid southern China. Study focus Using the Xinanjiang (XAJ) model together with an effective automatic calibration algorithm, this study systematically evaluates the streamflow simulation performance of the Integrated MultisatellitE Retrievals for Global Precipitation Measurement (IMERG) Version 06 (V06) and Version 07 (V07) Final Run products across 312 small- and medium-sized watersheds (SMWs). Hydrological impacts of two types of IMERG precipitation error characteristics are quantified through parallel experiments and sensitivity analyses. New hydrological insights for the region Simulation skill varied markedly among products and regions. The calibrated IMERG V07 product achieved the highest median Nash–Sutcliffe efficiency (NSE) during calibration, but its validation performance deteriorated because of the anomalous overestimation associated with the Global Precipitation Climatology Centre (GPCC) after 2019. After removal of this temporal anomaly, the calibrated IMERG V07 and V06 products achieved median NSE values of 0.61 and 0.58, respectively, over the full period. Recalibrating the XAJ model accommodated the modest underestimation of the uncalibrated IMERG V07 product in eastern watersheds, whereas severe underestimation in western high-elevation watersheds still resulted in substantial streamflow-volume underestimation and degraded simulation skill. This study provides baseline streamflow simulation performance for IMERG precipitation in humid southern China. More broadly, it demonstrates that precipitation-error magnitude and temporal anomalies can constrain streamflow simulation under model recalibration.

title: Transient bidirectional flow in Yangtze River Estuary: Driving mechanisms and spatiotemporal variations
description: Publication date: August 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology: Regional Studies, Volume 66 Author(s): Chi Zhang, Jicai Zhang, Guansuo Wang
abstract: Study region The Yangtze River Estuary, China, located at the confluence of the Yangtze River and the East China Sea. Study focus This study combined observations and numerical modeling to investigate the occurrence, driving mechanisms, impacts, and spatiotemporal characteristics of transient bidirectional flow (TBF) events in the Yangtze River Estuary. New hydrological insights for the region In the Yangtze River Estuary, we identified TBF events characterized by instantaneous surface-seaward and bottom-landward currents that persisted over multiple tidal cycles. This differs from classical estuarine exchange flow, whose instantaneous flow field is usually vertically unidirectional under tidal dominance. Although similar instantaneous bidirectional flow structures have been observed previously in estuaries, their impacts, governing mechanisms, and spatiotemporal characteristics remain insufficiently understood. Our results show that TBF significantly influenced water column stratification and enhanced the net transport of water and salt. Momentum analysis and sensitivity experiments revealed its driving mechanisms: during ebb tides, strong northerly winds enhanced saltwater intrusion, generating a persistent landward baroclinic pressure gradient that reversed the bottom ebb current landward; during flood tides, the combined effect of river discharge and the salt wedge raised the upstream water level, producing a strong seaward barotropic pressure gradient that reversed the surface flood current seaward.

title: Investigating climate change-induced extreme floods: Insights from super-high-resolution climate datasets using Rainfall-Runoff-Inundation (RRI) model
description: Publication date: August 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology: Regional Studies, Volume 66 Author(s): Sophal Try, Jackson Hian-Wui Chang, Sovannara Uk, Mengshan Lee, Huan-Yu Shiu, Carlos García Castro, Yong Jie Wong
abstract: Study region Characterized by steep mountainous terrain, short river systems, and frequent typhoon-induced rainfall, the river basins of Taiwan are highly susceptible to flooding. Despite the expected intensification of extreme precipitation under climate change, regional hydrological assessments using super-high-resolution climate projections remain limited. Study focus This study investigates the impacts of future climate change on extreme streamflow and flood hazards across 15 hydrological stations representing major river basins in Taiwan. Super-high-resolution climate projections from the Meteorological Research Institute Atmospheric General Circulation Model (MRI-AGCM3.2S HighResMIP) and the Database for Policy Decision Making for Future Climate Change (d4PDF) under the 4°C warming experiment were coupled with a Rainfall-Runoff-Inundation (RRI) model to simulate flood responses. Annual peak discharges were estimated for near-future (2020–2040), mid-future (2050–2070), and far-future (2080–2100) periods under 10-, 100-, and 1000-year return periods. New hydrological insights for the region The simulations indicate that projected annual peak discharges under the 4°C warming scenario consistently exceed those under the present climate across all return periods, indicating an increased probability of extreme flood events throughout Taiwan. The magnitude of change varies among river basins, demonstrating strong regional heterogeneity in hydrological responses to climate change. These findings provide new evidence that super-high-resolution climate projections improve the representation of future flood extremes and offer valuable regional-scale information for flood risk assessment, climate adaptation planning, and the design of resilient water resources and flood management strategies in Taiwan.

title: Spatiotemporal changes and flow–sediment associations of planform adjustment in the wandering reaches of the upper Tarim River
description: Publication date: August 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology: Regional Studies, Volume 66 Author(s): Bo Feng, Xuewei Fan, Zhexin Zhang, Wenhong Dai
abstract: Study regions The wandering reaches of the upper Tarim River. Study focus Under the combined effects of mountain meltwater recharge, changing flow and sediment conditions, and human activities, planform adjustment in the upper Tarim River poses risks to bank stability and water conveyance. Using multi-temporal remote sensing images from 2005 to 2023, this study delineated channel water boundaries and centerlines, and quantified channel width, sinuosity, lateral migration rate, and water-boundary expansion and contraction. Hydrological and sediment records were further used to construct high-flow metrics, and hierarchical clustering and correlation analysis were applied to identify interannual adjustment types and their associated flow and sediment conditions. New hydrological insights for the region Planform evolution showed clear downstream differences. Reach R1 exhibited slowly increasing sinuosity and persistent bend-scale centerline oscillation. Reach R2 was wide, shallow, and relatively stable, with limited sinuosity variation. Reach R3 showed increasing sinuosity, bend development, and stronger local main-channel oscillation. Interannual adjustment was classified into three types, including strong migration with main-channel oscillation, expansion and widening with bank retreat, and contraction adjustment with bend development. These types corresponded to different high-flow and sediment conditions. Multi-stage water-boundary overlay analysis identified persistently expanding and contracting active bank sections, which were further assigned to the three adjustment types. The results provide a basis for risk identification and segmented, type-specific management of wandering reaches in arid inland rivers.

title: Hydrological response to drought-flood and flood-drought transitions in the Geul River basin, Netherlands
description: Publication date: August 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology: Regional Studies, Volume 66 Author(s): Srividya Hariharan Sudha, Elisa Ragno, Ruud van der Ent, Oswaldo Morales-Nápoles
abstract: Study Region: The study examines the Geul River basin in the southern Netherlands, a small (343 km 2 ), hilly, rain-fed catchment characterised by a rapid rainfall-runoff response and exposure to both floods and droughts. Recent extremes, including the July 2021 flood and multiple dry summers, make the basin a relevant case study for understanding transitions between these opposite hydrological conditions. Study Focus: Transitions between drought-flood and flood-drought events were analysed using observations and hydrological simulations for 1982–2018. Floods and droughts were defined from meteorological thresholds and extended by an empirically derived catchment response time to capture hydrological effects. The role of antecedent precipitation, temperature, streamflow, soil moisture, and groundwater storage on subsequent event’s hydrological response was assessed using correlation and distribution (Kolmogorov–Smirnov) analyses. New Hydrological Insights for the Region: Antecedent droughts were associated with lower flood peaks, likely reflecting greater absorption of rainfall by dry soils prior to runoff generation. In contrast, antecedent floods were not associated with a consistent mitigation of streamflow response during subsequent droughts, consistent with continued streamflow recession from prior high flows. Groundwater showed a slower and more gradual adjustment than surface fluxes at the event scale, consistent with sub-seasonal storage buffering. Overall, opposite antecedent conditions in the Geul basin tend to moderate, rather than amplify, subsequent extremes. These findings emphasise the importance of considering antecedent catchment conditions and longer-term subsurface storage when evaluating flood and drought interactions in regional water management.

title: Coupled hydrological–hydrodynamic modelling of GLOFs triggered by extreme precipitation in the Western Himalayas
description: Publication date: August 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology: Regional Studies, Volume 66 Author(s): Deepali Gaikwad, Daishisha Iawphniaw, Vikas Singh Jadoun, Reet Kamal Tiwari, Biswajeet Pradhan
abstract: Study region Western Himalayas (Himachal Pradesh). Study focus Glacial Lake Outburst Floods (GLOFs) are increasingly recognized as a major cryosphere-related hazard in the western Himalayas, where accelerated glacier retreat, elevation-dependent warming, and intensifying extreme hydro-meteorological events collectively amplify downstream flood risk to settlements and infrastructure. Most existing GLOF hazard assessments treat lake outburst processes and extreme rainfall-induced flooding independently, potentially underestimating worst-case flood magnitudes and inundation extents. To address this critical gap, the present study integrates Extreme Rainfall Events (EREs), including Probable Maximum Precipitation (PMP), into a coupled hydrological–hydrodynamic modelling framework to assess compound GLOF–flood hazards in glacier-fed Himalayan basins. New hydrologic insights Two high-risk glacial lakes in the Beas and Sutlej river basins were analysed using coupled HEC-HMS and HEC-RAS models under multi-return-period flood scenarios (2–100 years) and the Probable Maximum Flood (PMF). PMF discharges peaked at 17,086 m³ /s at Pandoh Dam and 23,478 m³ /s at Bhakra Dam, with model validation showing strong performance (Nash–Sutcliffe Efficiency > 0.65 and > 0.75). Incorporating PMP-based discharges into GLOF simulations enabled worst-case combined GLOF-PMF modelling, yielding peak flows of 17, 356 m³ /s (Beas) and 24,723 m³ /s (Sutlej). Inundation mapping revealed major risks to hydropower projects, religious sites, and over 680 structures. Given the projected intensification of extreme precipitation under climate change, this integrated approach is readily transferable to other glacierized basins across the Himalayas.

title: Hydrological controls on seasonal nitrate reduction and microbial community dynamics in the hyporheic zone of Songjiho lagoon, South Korea
description: Publication date: August 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology: Regional Studies, Volume 66 Author(s): Chanyoung Jeong, Soo Min Song, Woo-Hyun Jeon, Soo Young Cho, Sung Pil Hyun, Hee Sun Moon
abstract: Study region Songjiho lagoon, located on the east coast of Korea, is a coastal freshwater-seawater transition system in which seasonal water-level fluctuations shape hyporheic biogeochemical conditions. Study focus We investigated how seasonal changes in water level and salinity affect nitrate reduction and microbial community structure in the hyporheic zone of Songjiho Lagoon, South Korea. New hydrological insights for the region Managed sandbar breaching during the wet season maintained relatively saline conditions, whereas subsequent water-level decline increased groundwater influence and freshened the upper sediments. This hydrological shift altered porewater salinity profiles and coincided with elevated organic carbon and nitrogen concentrations, particularly at 20 cm depth, where potential denitrification was also highest. Potential denitrification rates were consistently greater under saline than freshwater conditions, reaching 85.1 ng N₂O-N g⁻¹ h⁻¹ . Putative nitrate-reducing taxa also varied with salinity, with genus Shewanella associated with saline conditions and genus Pseudomonas more abundant under fresher conditions. These results indicate that seasonal hydrological variability regulates nitrate-reduction potential by modifying salinity gradients, groundwater-surface water interactions, and associated microbial assemblages. Under drawdown-driven freshening, nitrate-reduction potential may decline, increasing the likelihood of nitrogen retention in lagoon sediments.

title: Influences of meteorological factors on stable isotopic fractionation of evaporating water bodies: Insights from experiments and simulations of the evaporation pans
description: Publication date: August 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology: Regional Studies, Volume 66 Author(s): Xiong Xiao, Yong Zhang, Xinping Zhang, Jinzhao Liu, Zhu Liu
abstract: Study region A typical subtropical monsoon region. Study focus Parallel evaporation pan experiments under rain-excluded and rain-included conditions were conducted. The Rayleigh fractionation (RL), Craig-Gordon (C-G), and Isotope and Water Mass Balance (IWB) models were used to simulate residual water isotopes (δL), aiming to reveal how meteorological factors control isotopic fractionation. New hydrological insights for the region The δL were negatively correlated with the residual water fraction (f), with larger amplitude variations in f induced correspondingly larger fluctuations in δL. The C-G model showed better performance than the RL model in the δL simulation, with RMSE values of only 1.6‰ for δ2H and 0.7‰ for δ18O, and the integration of the IWB model on rainy days improved the simulation accuracy of both models; High temperature and low relative humidity decreased the slope of the evaporation line systematically, which was attributed to the asymmetric reduction of kinetic fractionation coefficients for 18O and 2H and the preferential depletion of 2H in evaporative vapor, with relative humidity acting as the dominant controlling factor; Simulation accuracy was highly sensitive to parameterization schemes rather than merely depending on model structure, and arithmetic averages of meteorological factors yielded better δL series than weighted averages in high-humidity environments of our evaporation pan experiment. These findings deepen the understanding of isotopic variation and fractionation processes of evaporating water bodies in humid subtropical regions.

title: Navigating the energy-ecology-carbon nexus: A multi-objective reservoir operation framework for greener hydropower development
description: Publication date: August 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology: Regional Studies, Volume 66 Author(s): Zhenxiang Xing, Pengyu Shi, Han Zhang, Yue Guan, Wenlong Tang, Yuanyang Li, Yinan Wang
abstract: Study Region The Nirji Reservoir is located in the Nenjiang River Basin, Northeast China. Study Focus Navigating the energy–ecology–carbon nexus is a critical challenge for the sustainable development of hydropower under China’s dual-carbon strategy. The failure of carbon emission mitigation by traditional reservoir operations has led to a shift in reservoirs from being carbon sinks to carbon sources and the deterioration of ecological performance. To address this issue, this study proposes a hydropower generation–ecology–low-carbon coordinated multi-objective reservoir operation framework (HECC-RO) that integrates inflow forecasting, carbon-emission accounting, Pareto-based multi-objective optimization, and multi-criteria decision analysis to evaluate alternative operation schemes under different management preferences. New Hydrological Insights Results show that the proposed framework improves the balance among hydropower generation, ecological performance, and carbon reduction in the Nirji Reservoir. Relative to the current engineering-practice baseline, the Carbon-optimal scheme reduces carbon emissions by 29.6% and EcoDev by 85.9%, with only a 12.3% loss in hydropower generation, and CEI decreases to 115–125 g/kWh. These findings provide regional hydrological insight into how monthly operation of a large upstream control reservoir in the Nenjiang River Basin can better coordinate hydropower production, downstream flow regulation, and low-carbon performance.

title: Using geochemical signatures to identify subsurface flow pathways in the intermittent reach of the Yusheng Creek in Taiwan
description: Publication date: August 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology: Regional Studies, Volume 66 Author(s): Tsung-Yu Lee, Hsiu-Hao Yeh, Yen-Wei Pan, Shao-Yu Hsu, Yung-Chia Chiu, Jr-Chuan Huang
abstract: Study region Yusheng Creek is a mountain stream in central Taiwan where the critically endangered Formosan landlocked salmon (Oncorhynchus masou formosanus) has been reintroduced but remains vulnerable to intermittent streamflow. Study focus Subsurface flow pathways and groundwater-stream interactions were investigated using end-member mixing analysis (EMMA). Monthly water samples were collected from four observation wells, stream water, and tributaries during two monitoring periods (January–November 2017; October 2021–August 2022). Geochemical parameters and stable isotopes (δ¹⁸O and δ²H) were analyzed to trace water sources. New hydrological insights Results reveal contrasting hydrological connectivity between dry and wet years. During dry years, the hyporheic zone persisted within the streambed but remained disconnected from groundwater, while upstream stream water infiltrated and migrated downstream through subsurface pathways. In wet years, the hyporheic zone and groundwater formed a hydraulically connected system, as indicated by similar geochemical signatures. These results highlight the critical role of the hyporheic zone in maintaining longitudinal connectivity in intermittent mountain streams, providing new insights into subsurface flow dynamics in humid subtropical regions.

title: Contributions and driving factors of multi-pathway nutrient loss from gully slope of the Loess Plateau
description: Publication date: August 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology: Regional Studies, Volume 66 Author(s): Lili Wang, Guanghui Zhang, Qingfeng Chen, Pingzong Zhu, Lin Liu
abstract: Study region This research was carried out in the Zhifanggou small watershed on the Chinese Loess Plateau. Gully slopes in this area feature fragile ecological condition and serve as the primary source of soil erosion and nutrient loss. Study focus Clarifying multi-pathway nutrient loss characteristics is essential for soil erosion and nutrient management. Current research lacks systematic understanding of the contribution and driving mechanisms of multi-pathway nutrient loss on gully slopes. So we conducted a comprehensive study based on eight natural rainfall events in 2021. Runoff plots (3 m × 1 m) were installed on six typical plant communities and one bare land (BL), to monitor carbon (C), nitrogen (N), and phosphorus (P) losses via runoff, sediment and litter export pathway, and key environmental factors were quantified. New hydrological insights for the region Plant communities produced runoff, sediment yield, and litter export mass ranges of 1.94–7.31 L m-², 2.57–5.18 g m-², and 0.26–0.78 g m-², respectively. Grasslands had higher C, N and P losses through runoff and sediment than shrublands, and litter-related nutrient losses in grasslands ranked as AG > CL > AS > BI. Sediment was the dominant nutrient loss pathway for BL, while shrublands mainly lost nutrients via litter export (43.66%-84.76%) rather than sediment pathway (3.85%-14.36%). Dominant nutrient loss pathways differed greatly among grassland communities. Soil total carbon (STC) and soil organic carbon (SOC) content significantly inhibited sediment-mediated C, N, and P loss (p < 0.05), while STC content significantly enhancing litter-mediated total C and P loss (p < 0.05). Runoff reduced nutrient loss via runoff and litter pathways, while significantly promoted sediment-mediated C, N, and P loss (p < 0.05). Overall, grassland communities exhibited better performance in reducing total nutrient loss across all three pathways. Soil surface carbon content and runoff were the main drivers of the loss pathways. The findings provide critical insights for designing soil conservation and nutrient loss control strategies.

title: Projecting 21st-century glacier change in the Qilian Mountains: A dynamic modeling approach of Laohugou Glacier No.12 with Elmer/Ice and CMIP6
description: Publication date: August 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology: Regional Studies, Volume 66 Author(s): Yushuo Liu, Xiang Qin, Yuzhe Wang, Zizhen Jin, Jiawen Ren
abstract: Study region The Laohugou Glacier No.12 (LHG12) located at the west Qilian Mountains. Study focus Glaciers in the Qilian Mountains constitute a critical freshwater reservoir for the Hexi Corridor. In recent decades, their accelerated retreat has introduced new challenges to water resource applications downstream. As the largest valley glacier in the region, LHG12 holds considerable significance. However, dynamical modeling studies targeting this glacier remain limited and require further development. This study employs the Elmer/Ice model to perform a 3-D dynamical simulation of LHG12. Using measured ice thickness data as primary input, diagnostic simulations were conducted. Subsequently, AWS and downscaled CMIP6 data were used to project the evolution of LHG12 up to 2100 CE under the current climate baseline, the SSP1–2.6 and the SSP5–8.5 scenarios. New hydrological insights for the region The simulation results indicate a maximum basal temperature of −0.7 ℃, which is consistent with observations, suggesting that the base of LHG12 at surface elevations below 4 500 m a.s.l. is at or near the pressure melting point. Under the current baseline climate, the SSP1–2.6 and the SSP5–8.5 scenarios, the eastern and western branches of LHG12 are projected to separate around 2085 CE, 2069 CE and 2058 CE, respectively; by 2100 CE, the glacier area reduces by 6.33%, 10.68% and 59.17%, respectively; and the glacier volume decrease by 11.70%, 37.13% and 82.30%, respectively.

title: Salinity effects on water surface and phreatic evaporation in arid regions: Evidence from controlled experiments
description: Publication date: August 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology: Regional Studies, Volume 66 Author(s): Mi Lei, Yanfeng Liu, Jinlong Zhou, Zixuan Qi, Ruiliang Jia
abstract: Study region Changji Groundwater Balance Experiment Station, located on the northern foothills of the Tianshan Mountains in Xinjiang, China. Study focus Evaporation from high-salinity water and shallow groundwater was investigated through controlled experiments across a TDS gradient (0.8–250 g·L⁻¹), groundwater depths (0.5, 1.0, and 3.0 m), and vadose-zone lithologies (fine sand and silty clay). Salinity suppressed water-surface evaporation following a negative exponential relationship, with inhibition rates ranging from 6.4% to 37.4%. For phreatic evaporation, higher salinity reduced evaporative flux, particularly at shallow depths (0.5 and 1.0 m). During the freezing period, freezing-point depression and snow insulation enhanced evaporation under saline conditions, whereas non-freezing periods showed consistent suppression. New hydrological insight A critical salinity threshold (TDS=30 g·L⁻¹) was identified where osmotic potential reversed, shifting from evaporation promotion to inhibition. Conversion coefficients for water-surface evaporation (Kₛ) and phreatic evaporation (Kₘ), and an evaporation response coefficient (R=1 −K) were established to facilitate estimation of saline evaporation from freshwater data. Additionally, a capillary rise limit in fine sand (<3.0 m) was revealed, and high salinity was demonstrated to sustain evaporative flux during freezing by overcoming ice‑barrier blockage. These findings suggest a revision to the traditional view that evaporation in deep, frozen zones is negligible and could provide practical tools for water-salt management in saline-affected agricultural regions.

title: A deep U-Net framework for flood hazard mapping using hydraulic simulations of the Wupper catchment, in the North Rhine-Westphalia region, Germany
description: Publication date: August 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology: Regional Studies, Volume 66 Author(s): Christian Lammers, Fernando Arévalo, Leonie Märker-Neuhaus, Daniel Heinenberg, Christian Förster, Karl-Heinz Spies
abstract: Study region: The research was performed for the Wupper Catchment, in the North Rhine-Westphalia region, Germany. Study focus: The increasing frequency and severity of global flood events highlights the need for the development of rapid and reliable flood prediction tools. This process traditionally relies on hydraulic models, which are used to generate flood hazard maps. However, the process of generating hydraulic simulations is computationally expensive, and has a significant latency. Due to the latency, these models are used as offline analysis tool for flood hazard. This research proposes a framework to develop deep-learning-based surrogated models to approximate hydraulic models for the generation of flood maps with a low latency. Moreover, we detailed a data generation procedure using a patch generation and data augmentation strategies. The framework was tested using hydraulic simulations of the Wupper catchment. The trained models were compared with holdout simulations from a calibrated hydraulic model, obtaining comparable results. Moreover, due to the approach’s low latency, it can be used in (near) real-time applications. New hydrological insights for the region: The results showed a final RMSE of 0.0227 m and a significant computational time speed-up of 21.5 times compared to the available hydraulic models. Moreover, the framework can be replicated to develop surrogate models for other catchments, which is of great importance to other water associations of the region and of other countries.

title: Evaluation of vegetation drought resistance and resilience across central Asian drylands under water limitation and heat extremes
description: Publication date: August 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology: Regional Studies, Volume 66 Author(s): Shiran Song, Xi Chen, Akylbek Kurishbayev, Chanjuan Zan, Chuan Wang, Philippe De Maeyer, Shukhrat Shokirov, Imanmadi Duman, Luqmon Samiev, Tie Liu
abstract: Study region Arid Central Asia is one of the largest dryland systems in Eurasia and has experienced amplified warming, increasing drought, and intensifying heat extremes. Yet ecosystem drought stability and its hydroclimatic controls remain insufficiently resolved. Study focus We quantified vegetation drought resistance and resilience across arid Central Asia during 2000–2021 using the transpiration-to-evapotranspiration ratio (TET), a functional indicator of vegetation-regulated water use. Drought events were identified using SPEI3, and heatwaves were characterized by frequency, duration, and cumulative heat. Event-based resistance and post-drought resilience were derived from TET responses to isolated drought events, and machine-learning models coupled with SHAP were used to assess the relative associations of hydroclimatic, edaphic, vegetative, and heatwave-related factors with spatial variation in drought stability. New hydrological insights for the region Drought resistance and resilience showed a significant but relatively weak negative association (r = -0.21, p < 0.001). Forests demonstrated the highest resistance (mean Rt = 0.379), whereas sparse vegetation exhibited the highest resilience (mean Rs = 0.059). Ecohydrological attributions revealed that surface soil moisture was the top-ranking predictor associated with resistance. Conversely, resilience was most closely associated with heatwave duration, precipitation, and soil organic carbon. Heatwave associations differed by dimension: heatwave frequency was positively associated with resistance, whereas longer, more intense heatwaves were negatively associated; resilience showed opposite patterns.

title: Estimation of extreme rainfall using intensity-duration-frequency curves for Ashanti Region, Ghana
description: Publication date: August 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology: Regional Studies, Volume 66 Author(s): G.A. Torsah, M. Maranan, V. Akyeampong, K.A. Adjei, L.K. Amekudzi, A.H. Fink
abstract: This study addresses the challenge of constructing Intensity-Duration-Frequency (IDF) curves in Ghana’s Ashanti Region, where sparse gauge networks limit high-resolution extreme rainfall analysis. A 36-station-year annual maximum series (AMS) was developed by concatenating 14 sub-daily stations from the Kumasi Meso Rain Gauge Network (KMRGN), creating a continuous regional reference series. The validity of this concatenation approach was supported by L-moment-based regional frequency analysis, confirming statistical homogeneity of the network despite localized variability in higher-order moments. Temporal consistency analysis further indicates no statistically significant trends or change-points in the AMS, supporting the assumption of stationarity for extreme-value modelling. The AMS of the benchmark concatenated sub-daily series is modeled within a Generalized Extreme Value (GEV) framework, complemented by intercomparison with Gumbel, Pearson Type III, and Log-Pearson Type III distributions under a multi-criteria model selection approach. The distributions of each model are validated using Chi-square and Kolmogorov-Smirnov tests, and are applied to construct and compare IDF curves. Results from the multi-criteria framework indicate that the Log-Pearson Type III distribution provides the most balanced performance in terms of goodness-of-fit, bias, and stability of extreme estimates. This benchmark is used to evaluate AMS derived from disaggregated daily records from the Ghana Meteorological Agency network. Results show that the concatenated sub-daily AMS reliably captures short-duration rainfall intensities while atte station-specific anomalies. However, disaggregated daily AMS underestimated short-duration (12 min-1 h) intensities by up to −18%, particularly during the convectively active minor rainy season, reflecting smoothening of peak rainfall. Performance improves at longer durations, and when concatenated into a 220 station-year homogeneous regional series, the disaggregated data closely reproduce the regional intensity structure across durations and return periods. Uncertainty analysis reveals strong duration dependence, with the highest sensitivity at short durations primarily controlled by the nonlinear scaling exponent of the disaggregation procedure. Comparison of disaggregated curves with existing 2016 IDF curves from the Ghana Meteorological Agency under the Gumbel distribution, similarly adopted by the agency, indicates systematic positive biases, ranging 20–40% on average across all durations for each return period and more than 50% increase in rainfall intensity at longer return periods across the respective durations and return periods, suggesting intensification of extremes. However, the absence of statistically significant trends in the AMS suggests that these increases are largely attributable to extended sampling, improved temporal representation, and methodological differences rather than definitive climatic non-stationarity. These findings establish the concatenated sub-daily series as a robust regional reference and highlight the necessity of high-resolution data or seasonally adjusted correction methods for reliable flood risk assessment, infrastructure design, and climate adaptation planning in the region.

title: A novel framework for estimating probable maximum precipitation events by integrating extreme value theory and storm transposition
description: Publication date: August 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology: Regional Studies, Volume 66 Author(s): Zixin Yang, Jia Wang, Jiahong Liu, Hao Wang, Chao Mei, Fengping Li, Xinyi Chen
abstract: Study region Beijing Municipal Administrative Center (Beijing MC), China. Study focus To improve the applicability of Probable Maximum Precipitation (PMP) in urban flood protection, this study proposes the concept of Potential Probable Maximum Precipitation Events (PMPE) and develops a dual-pathway estimation framework. Based on rainfall-pattern classification, Extreme Value Theory (EVT) is used to derive statistical extreme-rainfall scenarios, while the WRF model transposes historical extreme storms from neighboring regions to generate physically consistent scenarios. By integrating statistical extremity and atmospheric-process consistency, the most adverse scenario in terms of peak intensity and total rainfall is selected for each rainfall pattern as the final PMPE. New hydrological insights for the region Extreme rainfall in the Beijing MC exhibits strong rainfall-pattern dependence, with historical storms classified into six patterns. The most hazardous PMPE features a short-duration, high-intensity structure, with a total rainfall of 326.2 mm, a maximum 1-hour intensity of 84.8 mm, and a duration of 7 h. EVT and storm transposition exhibit complementary strengths, with the former better capturing statistical extremes and the latter producing more severe scenarios when atmospheric dynamics and topographic effects dominate. These findings indicate that urban precipitation extremes arise from both statistical and physical mechanisms. PMPE therefore extends traditional design rainfall estimates to physically plausible extreme-rainfall processes, providing a more reliable basis for urban flood-risk assessment and infrastructure resilience planning.

title: Explainable deep learning for predicting lake expansion in the Siling Co Endorheic basin: Unraveling driver shifts and hydro-climatic tipping points
description: Publication date: August 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology: Regional Studies, Volume 66 Author(s): Xiangnan Jing, Rao Zhu, Yunfa Miao
abstract: Study region The Siling Co Endorheic Basin (SCEB) on the central Tibetan Plateau is a critical terminal closed-flow catchment within the Asian Water Tower. Highly sensitive to hydro-climatic water balances, the basin has undergone rapid, cryosphere-fed lake expansion. This expansion coincides with significant regional warming and wetting. Study focus To clarify alpine lake evolution mechanisms and overcome the black-box limitations and phase lags of traditional models, this study forecasts the monthly total lake area sequence of the SCEB (2000–2021). We developed the CAF(PINN) framework, a physics-informed approach that embeds the water balance principle over a hybrid architecture consisting of a 1D-CNN, an attention mechanism, and a frequency-domain multi-layer perceptron. Additionally, we quantified interrelationships within lacustrine hydrological processes and physical tipping points using PLS-SEM and Transformed Generalized Additive Models (TGAM). New hydrological insights The CAF(PINN) framework achieved a high Nash–Sutcliffe Efficiency of 0.91, outperforming benchmark models while preserving physically consistent behavior. The model identified a distinct hydrological transition in 2013, suggesting a regime shift toward a meltwater-dominated system. Prior to 2013, lake variations were largely associated with precipitation fluctuations while the cryosphere buffered thermal inputs. Post-2013, however, rising temperatures were closely linked to increased glacier melt and permafrost thaw as primary contributors to lake recharge. This transition suggests an intensifying, non-linear coupling between cryospheric change and regional hydrology, highlighting the expanding influence of thermal factors on water cycles within the Asian Water Tower.

title: Spatiotemporal dynamics and key drivers of potential evapotranspiration across the Yangtze River Basin from 1975 to 2018
description: Publication date: August 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology: Regional Studies, Volume 66 Author(s): Ting Chen, Feiyu Wang, Huiyuan Liu, Lei Zou, Zhiwei Wang, Ying Fan
abstract: Study region The Yangtze River Basin (YZRB). Study focus As a key indicator of atmospheric evapotranspiration capacity, potential evapotranspiration (ET 0) plays a fundamental role in water-energy exchange processes. This study investigated the spatiotemporal variability and underlying mechanisms of ET 0 in the YZRB. Based on a long-term ET 0 dataset, the sensitivity analysis was conducted to assess the response of ET 0 to meteorological factors influencing its temporal variability, and the Multiscale Geographically Weighted Regression (MGWR) model was implemented to identify the drivers shaping the spatial variability of ET 0. New hydrological insights The mean annual ET 0 in the YZRB from 1975 to 2018 was approximately 930 mm, exhibiting a significant increasing trend of 0.63 mm/yr, with a clear upward shift in mean values after 2003. Temperature (T) dominated the spatial heterogeneity of ET 0 in most seasons except spring, with MGWR spatial regression coefficients (SRC) of 0.466 at the annual scale and exceeding 0.60 at seasonal scales. Besides, solar radiation (RS) had the greatest effect on the temporal variation of ET 0, especially in summer when the temporal sensitivity coefficients (TSC) of ET 0 to RS generally exceeded 1.00. These results highlight the distinct roles of temperature and radiation in shaping the spatiotemporal variability of ET 0 and provide valuable insights for large-scale water resources management under climate change.

title: Reconstructing Holocene high-magnitude outburst floods in the Lancang River (Upper Mekong) Grand Cayon, Southeastern Tibetan Plateau: Implication for hazard assessment
description: Publication date: August 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology: Regional Studies, Volume 66 Author(s): Yongqiang Guo, Yonggang Ge, Peini Mao, Tao Liu
abstract: Study area Lancang River (Upper Mekong) Grand Canyon, situated on the southeastern Tibetan Plateau, represents a high mountain canyon of Three Parallel Rivers Region. Research focus This study integrates sedimentary, geomorphic, chronological, and hydraulic evidence from outburst flood events in the Lancang River Grand Canyon. Our investigation identified three primary palaeoflood records: fine-grained slackwater deposits, gravel bar deposits, and boulder deposits. These flood deposits with similar geochemical composition implies a same flood source. Outburst floods induced by the upstream two landslide dams were dated to 11.9–6.4 ka. New hydrological insights for the region Holocene outburst flood magnitudes were estimated to 39,500–45,900 m³ /s, exceeding the largest observed flood by 7.5–10 times. Such discharges were generated by partial landslide dam failures that eroded more than 50% of the dam height. Hydrodynamic variations and channel morphology result in lateral accretion and backwater-eddy effects during floods. Bedrock channel erosion occurred preferentially at local topographic features within narrow meander bends. High-magnitude outburst floods generate high shear stress (0.4–1.1 kPa) and unit stream power (4.5–10.5 kW/m²) and play a critical role in the geomorphic evolution of the upper Lancang River. Depth-velocity (DV) metrics from palaeoflood‑based worst‑case scenarios indicate highest hazards (DV> 240 m2/s) for bridges versus backwater flooding (DV< 65 m2/s) for roads/villages. This study provides valuable insights into the assessment of similar cascading flood hazards in the southeastern Tibetan Plateau.

title: Stable snowmelt supply dominates enhanced runoff stability in the Tianshan Mountains of Central Asia
description: Publication date: August 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology: Regional Studies, Volume 66 Author(s): Xueyan Qin, Xiuliang Yuan, Rafiq Hamdi, Jie Bai, Philippe De Maeyer, Hossein Tabari
abstract: Study region This study focuses on 89 basins in the Tianshan Mountains (TMs). Study focus The strength of seasonal cycle (R) from recently developed Directional Statistics method was employed to quantify the changes in runoff stability (Rrunoff) in the TMs during 1980–2019. ERA5-Land daily and monthly runoff data were validated against station observations and the Tianshan Watershed Streamflow dataset (TSWS) at basins-scale, respectively. Random Forest model (RF) coupled with SHapley Additive Explanations (SHAP) was applied to identify the dominant drivers of Rrunoff changes. New hydrological insights for the region Our results revealed a widespread increase in runoff stability, indicated by a decreasing trend of Rrunoff, across 82% of the basins, with approximately 24% showing significant (p < 0.05) trends. Enhanced runoff stability was characterized by a more uniform intra‑annual runoff distribution and reduced intensity and frequency of runoff extremes. A more even seasonal distribution of snowmelt dominated enhanced runoff stability, as evidenced by decreasing Rsm across 68% of the basins. Rain-to-runoff conversion efficiency declined in 97% of basins, 39% of which exhibited significant declines. This decline was attributed to enhanced actual evapotranspiration associated with vegetation greening. These changes reduced runoff extremes, highlighting the buffering capacity of vegetation in hydrological regulation in arid regions and offering important implications for improving water resources management in the arid TMs.

title: Uncertainty-informed regionalization of sub-daily rainfall extremes in northwestern Italy using Bilinear Surface Smoothing with credible-interval-based data screening
description: Publication date: August 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology: Regional Studies, Volume 66 Author(s): Nikolaos Malamos, Paola Mazzoglio, Theano Iliopoulou
abstract: Study region This study focuses on the northwestern part of Italy, where accurate spatial characterization of sub-daily rainfall extremes is essential for hydrological design, flood risk assessment, and infrastructure planning. Observational data are drawn from the I2-RED dataset, comprising approximately 820 rain gauges with records spanning 1927–2020. The region is characterized by complex terrain and substantial spatial variability in rainfall extremes. Study focus The Bilinear Surface Smoothing with Explanatory variable (BSSE) framework is applied to regionalize mean annual maximum rainfall depths at 1, 3, 6, 12, and 24 h timescales. Elevation is incorporated as an explanatory variable.
