ET-related parameters exhibit physically consistent relationships with soil types and vegetation cover, indicating improved representation of underlying surface heterogeneity. Long-term simulations reveal pronounced spatial gradients, with precipitation and runoff decreasing from northwest to southeast, ET increasing from west to east, and TWSC showing relatively limited spatial variability. Overall, spatially distributed dual-objective calibration improves both the accuracy and spatial consistency of water cycle simulations, providing a robust framework for hydrological modeling in heterogeneous basins.

title: Statistical evaluation of multi-satellite precipitation products: Performance, uncertainty, and sensitivity analysis against ground observations and climatic trends in the Omo-Gibe transboundary basin, Ethiopia
description: Publication date: August 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology: Regional Studies, Volume 66 Author(s): Temesgen Desta, Moltot Zewdie, Tewodros Assefa, Tewodros Tesfaye
abstract: Study region The Omo-Gibe River Basin in south-western Ethiopia is a hydrological significant East African basin characterized by complex terrain, high climatic variability, and sparse rain-gauge coverage. These constraints increase reliance on gridded precipitation datasets, yet their catchment-scale reliability, uncertainty, and trend consistency remain insufficiently evaluated. Study focus This study evaluates five widely used satellite- and reanalysis-derived precipitation datasets (CHIRPS, PERSIANN-CDR, CFSR, ERA5, and ERA5-Land) against long-term rain-gauge observations across the Omo-Gibe River Basin (1990–2020). Station-based gridded precipitation extracted from Climate Engine was evaluated at daily, monthly, and seasonal scales using statistical (CC, RMSE, ME, Bz) and categorical (POD, FAR, CSI) metrics, with uncertainty and precipitation trends assessed using Sen’s slope and the Mann–Kendall and modified Mann–Kendall tests. New hydrological insights for the region CHIRPS showed the highest overall agreement with observations (CC up to 0.85; Bz: 0.97–1.07), while CFSR exhibited the largest biases ((Bz: 0.47–2.16). and ERA5-Land consistently outperformed ERA5. Monthly estimates were less accurate (RMSE up to 78 mm/day), though categorical scores improved seasonally. Significant positive trends were found for CHIRPS (Z = 1.8) and ERA5-Land (Z = 1.7). Precipitation uncertainty and trends were strongly controlled by topography and seasonality, highlighting the importance of terrain-specific validation for reliable hydro climatic analyses and water-resources management in data-scarce mountain basins.

title: A national overview of historical floods in Romania over the past 800 years
description: Publication date: August 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology: Regional Studies, Volume 66 Author(s): Cristian C. Stoleriu, Andrei Urzică, Alin Mihu-Pintilie, Dan C. Lesenciuc
abstract: Study region Romania is located in the lower sector of the Danube hydrographic basin, and approximately 98% of its hydrographic network is tributary to the Danube. Romania's national territory covers an area of 232,193 km2, and its hydrographic network has a length of 115,000 km. This hydrographic network is managed on a basin basis through 11 hydrographic basin administrations (HBAs), which were used in our analysis. Study focus This study focuses on mapping historical hydrological events that occurred on the territory of Romania between 1234 and 2024. A geospatial database, named ROmanian Flood Event Database (RO-FED), has been created that incorporates information regarding the period, intensity, and magnitude of these hydrological events. This database can be used as an analytical tool at both national and international levels to understand flood patterns. New hydrological insights for the region The final version of the database contains 1084 hydrological events. Based on the analysis of the dataset, we can conclude that Romania is facing an increase in floods, with summer floods being the most predominant. The Carpathian Mountain system influences the occurrence of spring floods in the river basins of western Romania. Furthermore, the most affected HBAs are RO10 (Siret HBA) and RO3 (Olt HBA), while the highest number of casualties were recorded in RO7 (Mureș HBA) and RO10 (Siret HBA).

title: Extreme minimum temperature and precipitation indices drive the shortening of snow cover duration in China
description: Publication date: August 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology: Regional Studies, Volume 66 Author(s): Hang Wu, Qiuli Yang, Yuhao Feng, Xiaoyong Wu, Haoxuan Liu, Yuping Li, Changchun Xu
abstract: Study region This research focuses on China's stable snow cover regions, encompassing the Mid-Temperate Arid, Semi-Arid, and Semi-Humid Zones, alongside the Plateau Temperate Semi-Arid Zone. Spanning 1980–2019, this domain constitutes a critical component of global hydrological and energy cycles, demonstrating pronounced susceptibility to recent warming trends. Study focus To address the insufficient quantification of snow characteristic (SC) responses to extreme climate, we analyzed snow onset date (SOD), snow end date (SED), and snow cover duration (SCD). Using an integrated framework of trend analysis, Random Forest, and Structural Equation Modeling (PLS-SEM), we disentangled the interplay between SC and extreme indices while accounting for mean warming. New hydrological insights for the region The analysis reveals pervasive snow contraction, with SCD shortening by −2.56 days/5a. The annual minimum daily minimum temperature (TNn) and continuous dry days (CDD) emerge as primary drivers. Other factors regulate snow by modulating these extremes: Leaf Area Index for low vegetation (LAI-LV) influences TNn to delay snow phenology, while nitrous oxide (N2O) affects CDD to advance SED and truncate the snow season. These findings decode complex driver-climate interactions, supporting refined snow modeling under climate warming.

title: Tracking lakeshore wetland changes in China using Sentinel satellite data from 2019 to 2023
description: Publication date: August 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology: Regional Studies, Volume 66 Author(s): Yajie Chen, Zongming Wang, Ling Luo, Yanzhu Fu, Dehua Mao
abstract: Study region The lakes with area larger than 100 km2 in China Study focus A novel method integrating time-series Sentinel imagery (2019–2023) with an inundation frequency-based classification algorithm was developed to obtain the spatial distribution of lakeshore wetlands (LSWs). By applying the developed method, a spatial distribution dataset of China's LSWs with a 10-meter spatial resolution for the period of 2019–2023 was established. The spatiotemporal patterns of China's LSWs were further investigated based on the dataset and the driving mechanism of variations in LSWs under the extreme climatic conditions was discussed. The research findings were expected to support water environment management, biodiversity conservation, and watershed sustainable development. New hydrological insights Mapping results revealed that LSWs exhibit distinct spatial heterogeneity, with denser distributions in humid southeastern China. A net LSWs area loss of 2769.50 km² occurred during the study period, primarily resulting from dramatic lake shrinkage in the Eastern Plains (EP) ecoregion. Basin runoff constituted the primary controlling factor nationwide, while temperature and snowmelt exerted stronger influences in cold zones, and precipitation–evaporation dynamics dominated in arid regions. Alternating droughts and floods can lead to more frequent changes in hydrologic processes and an increase in the magnitude of water level changes in LSWs. The variations of LSWs caused by the hydrological changes would cause notable ecological effects including changes in waterbird habitat and greenhouse gas emissions.

title: Urban–rural flood risk inequality in Pakistan: Coupling social vulnerability and flood susceptibility
description: Publication date: August 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology: Regional Studies, Volume 66 Author(s): Lihong Yang, Jing Tan, Xin Yao, Zhangjie Li, Zhiqiang Xie, Shiyin Liu, Zhiqun Hou
abstract: Study region Pakistan, South Asia Study focus Against the backdrop of global climate change, rapid urbanization, and persistent urban–rural development disparities, Pakistan has experienced a sustained increase in flood frequency and the magnitude of associated losses. However, the spatial distributions of the country’s Social Vulnerability Index (SVI) and Flood Susceptibility Index (FSI), along with their coupled interactions, remain insufficiently characterized, thereby constraining the design of targeted disaster prevention and mitigation strategies. To this end, we developed an urban–rural flood risk assessment framework (URSV-FS). First, we constructed the urban–rural SVI using principal component analysis (PCA) and estimated the FSI using an Extreme Gradient Boosting (XGBoost) model. We then integrated SVI and FSI to derive flood risk and examined the spatial coupling between the two indices. Finally, nighttime light (NTL) remote-sensing data capturing the 2022 extreme flood event were used to validate the risk results and assess urban–rural flood resilience. New hydrological insights for the region The results indicate that: (1) Rural SVI was significantly higher than urban SVI. The proportion of rural districts with very high SVI was 25.4%, and the spatial variability was closely related to socioeconomic development level. (2) The XGBoost model performed well, with an AUC of 0.948 and an accuracy of 0.877. Soil type (SHAP = 0.833), NDVI (SHAP = 0.662), and slope (SHAP = 0.634) were the most influential predictors of FSI. The model classified 24.4% of the study area as high FSI, primarily along river corridors on the Indus Plain and in highly urbanized areas. (3) Flood risk was widespread in rural areas: 13.9% of rural districts were classified as very high risk, and 12.09% of the districts simultaneously exhibited high SVI and high FSI; both proportions were significantly higher than in urban areas. (4) During the flood disaster period, the decline in NTL in rural areas was 2.4 times larger than that in urban areas. However, after the disaster, the recovery of NTL in urban was 2.7 times larger than that in rural, suggesting a weaker recovery capacity in rural areas.

title: Soil erosion under climate and land-use change scenarios: An integrated modelling approach for the Upper Blue Nile Basin
description: Publication date: August 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology: Regional Studies, Volume 66 Author(s): Legese Abebaw Getu, Sándor Szegedi, Hailu Kendie Addis, Zoltán Túri
abstract: Study Region The study was conducted in the Gumara–Maksegnit watershed of the Upper Blue Nile Basin, Ethiopia, an erosion-prone landscape that drains into Lake Tana, a hydrologically and ecologically critical freshwater system. The region is characterized by steep escarpments, highly erodible soils, and rapidly expanding agriculture, making it a hotspot of sediment generation and land degradation within the basin. Study Focus This study assessed past (2003), present (2023), and future (2083) soil erosion by integrating the RUSLE model with ANN-based LULC simulations, Bayesian Model Averaging of five CORDEX RCMs, and bias-corrected rainfall projections. Land-use analysis showed agricultural land expanding from 53.6% (2003) to 68.7% (2023) and projected to reach 72.1% (2083), with corresponding declines in forest and grazing areas. Rainfall erosivity increased from a range of 565–647 to 613–689 MJ mm ha⁻¹ h⁻¹ yr⁻¹ , and is projected to rise to 756–853 (RCP4.5) and 809–907 (RCP8.5) by 2083. Mean annual soil loss increased from 30.1 t ha⁻¹ yr⁻¹ in 2003 to 39.2 t ha⁻¹ yr⁻¹ in 2023, and is projected to reach 42 t ha⁻¹ yr⁻¹ under land-use change alone, 43.4 and 45.9 t ha⁻¹ yr⁻¹ under RCP 4.5 and RCP 8.5 climate scenarios, and 46.3 and 49.2 t ha⁻¹ yr⁻¹ when both drivers are combined. New Hydrological Insights for the Region Future soil loss will increase by up to 63.5% under the combined LUC + RCP8.5 scenario, with steep northern and northeastern slopes remaining persistent erosion hotspots. Topography (LS: 39.6%) is the dominant erosion driver, while high C and P values on cultivated slopes intensify sediment generation. The results show that climate change has a stronger marginal impact than land-use change and that their interaction amplifies erosion non-linearly, underscoring the need for slope-focused, climate-adaptive soil and water conservation to protect the hydrological stability of Lake Tana.

title: Divergent responses of hysteresis loops and sediment sources to rainfall regimes in karst small watersheds of Southwest China: A multi-method integrated framework for classifying erosive rainfall patterns
description: Publication date: August 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology: Regional Studies, Volume 66 Author(s): Xianwen Zhang, Kunqian Yue, Jiacheng Lan, Rui Li, Yongxiang Jiang, Ruitao Mao, Ya Zhang, Hui Dong
abstract: Study region A typical karst small watershed in Southwest China. Study focus Rainfall patterns regulate runoff–sediment dynamics, yet the mechanisms linking specific patterns to hydro-sedimentary regimes and sediment sources remain unclear. This study utilized a multi-method approach—including Pearson correlation, Random Forest(RF), and Partial Least Squares Regression(PLSR)—to identify the dominant rainfall variables driving runoff–sediment yield from 79 erosive rainfall events (2018–2022). Erosive rainfall patterns were classified to evaluate the subsequent responses of hydro-sedimentary processes and sediment source contributions. New hydrological insights for the region The results indicate that rainfall amount (P), rainfall duration (Dr), and rainfall erosivity (R) are the primary drivers influencing runoff–sediment yield. Using K-means clustering, rainfall events were classified into three patterns (A, B, and C). Pattern A (short duration, moderate erosivity) occurred most frequently (79.75%) and accounted for the highest cumulative runoff–sediment yield. Conversely, Pattern B, though less frequent (7.59%), generated the maximum runoff–sediment yield per event. Hysteresis loop analysis revealed significant variations across rainfall regimes: Pattern A exhibited clockwise loops, Pattern B showed complex loops, and Pattern C displayed counterclockwise loops. Notably, 68% of events exhibited clockwise or complex hysteresis loops, indirectly infers that the subsurface riverbed and conduits are the primary sediment sources. This study provides a theoretical framework for targeted soil erosion control and watershed management in karst regions.

title: Failure mode and effects analysis as a screening tool for urban drainage systems failures: A comparison with hydrodynamic modelling in Feldbach, Austria
description: Publication date: August 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology: Regional Studies, Volume 66 Author(s): F. Funke, S. Reinstaller, K. Kearney, D. Muschalla, T. Ertl, M. Kleidorfer
abstract: Study region The case study is the small city of Feldbach, Austria, a semi-urban catchment recently affected by flooding. Study focus Malfunctions in urban drainage infrastructure significantly increase flood risk, however resource-constrained municipalities often lack the means for complex hydraulic analysis. This study assesses the consistency of an adapted Failure Mode and Effects Analysis (FMEA), a qualitative, expert-driven tool, by comparing its severity ratings against outputs from a coupled 1D-2D hydrodynamic model. The comparison is limited to environmental and neighbouring system severity dimensions, as occurrence, detectability, and infrastructure-level severity lie outside the scope of model-based assessment. We analysed 25 failure scenarios across both centralized (grey) and decentralized (blue-green) infrastructure to assess whether expert-based FMEA severity ratings are consistent with quantitative model outputs for a range of failure types. New hydrological insights for the region Results indicate that failures in centralized "grey" infrastructure cause substantially greater system-wide impacts than malfunctions in decentralized elements within this catchment, a finding that reflects the grey-dominated structure of Feldbach. FMEA severity ratings show strong consistency with quantitative model outputs for high- and low-severity failures, though divergence remain at mid-range severity. These findings support the use of FMEA as a practical first-stage screening tool for small municipalities. We propose a tiered management strategy: utilizing FMEA for broad screening and reserving resource-intensive hydrodynamic modelling for the in-depth analysis of critical infrastructure failures.

title: Compound dry and hot events in subregions of mainland China and the evolving dynamics from synoptic to sub-seasonal perspective
description: Publication date: August 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology: Regional Studies, Volume 66 Author(s): Yali Zhu, Xianghui Kong, Yang Liu, Huopo Chen, Jianqi Sun, Xiao Tang
abstract: Study region This study focuses on ten climate-geographical subregions of China, using daily 30-day Standardized Precipitation-Evapotranspiration Index (SPEI) and daily maximum temperature data (1961–2018). Compound dry and hot events (CDHEs) are more frequent in western northeastern China, South China, eastern northwestern China, and Northeast China. Study focus While previous studies have emphasized seasonal or monthly scales, this research addresses the critical gap in understanding CDHEs at the synoptic-subseasonal scale—directly relevant to hydrological disaster prediction and early warning—by analyzing dry/hot/CDHE metrics and evolving processes of long-lasting events with emphasis on land-atmosphere interactions and atmospheric circulations. New hydrological insights for the region Hot days increased nationwide, but CDHE days show no significant trend in most subregions due to compensating dry day reductions, challenging simplistic assumptions about compound extremes under global warming. Mechanistically, distinct land–atmosphere pathways dominate across hydroclimatic zones: latent heat flux (LH) governs energy partitioning in humid/semi-humid areas while sensible heat flux (SH) prevails in arid/semi-arid areas. For large-scale circulations, southeastward migration of anomalous anticyclones dominates northern subregions pre-CDHE, whereas local anomalous anticyclones are more critical in southern subregions. These findings fill key knowledge gaps in synoptic-subseasonal CDHE dynamics, offer novel evidence for heterogeneous regional hydrological responses to global warming, and provide actionable insights for advancing short-to-medium-range hydrological disaster prediction and region-specific water resource management strategies.

title: Regional hydraulic controls on flood wave propagation post-impoundment: Insights from the Three Gorges Reservoir for regulated river systems
description: Publication date: August 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology: Regional Studies, Volume 66 Author(s): Yancheng Han, Wenguang Luo, Jun Xia, Jinxiao Zhao, Yanjun Zhang, Liping Zhang, Jie Liu
abstract: Study region The Three Gorges Reservoir (TGR), a large channel-type reservoir on the Yangtze River, extends 595.6 km from Cuntan to the dam and is strongly influenced by longitudinal backwater. Study focus This study investigated how impoundment alters flood-wave propagation and travel time in the TGR, using a calibrated 1D hydrodynamic model combined with a physically based wave celerity framework under multi-scenario conditions. New hydrological insights for the region Impoundment shifted the dominant control of flood propagation from discharge (kinematic-wave behavior pre-impoundment) to reservoir water level (dynamic-wave behavior under backwater). Near-dam wave celerity increased to ∼19 m/s at high levels, reducing mean travel time from ∼39 h (pre-impoundment) to ∼15 h at 175 m. The proposed celerity formulation agreed well with model results (R² = 0.61), and improved significantly (R² = 0.90) when using model-derived pre-impoundment celerity. These findings provide a physical basis for flood travel time estimation in regulated rivers and support forecasting and reservoir operation.

title: A data-based method to identify anthropogenic impacts on hydrological drought evolution: A case study for the Grande River basin, São Francisco River, Brazil
description: Publication date: August 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology: Regional Studies, Volume 66 Author(s): Carlos E.S. Lima, Cleiton S. Silveira, Alexandre C. Costa, Germano G. Ribeiro Neto
abstract: Study region Grande River Basin (GRB), Brazil, an important tributary of the São Francisco River Study focus Evaluate the impact of anthropogenic changes on the onset, development and recovery of hydrological droughts, considering different drought states and their transition probabilities New hydrological insights A new data-based method was proposed to evaluate the impact of anthropogenic changes on the evolution of hydrological drought called “Drought Roulette Analysis” (DRA). By applying the DRA in the GRB, we identified a significantly slower hydrological recovery during the human-modified period, characterized by increases in the probability of transitioning from hydrometeorological to hydrological drought (+14.04%) and a significant reduction in the probability of transitioning to the ND state (−24.83%). The DRA proved to be a simple and efficient tool, providing greater flexibility for drought-propagation analysis in human-modified basins.

title: Composite flood generation driven by a warm atmospheric River in a southern Andean basin, Chile
description: Publication date: August 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology: Regional Studies, Volume 66 Author(s): Francisco Manquehual-Cheuque, Álvaro Cruces-Zárate, Mario Lillo-Saavedra, Diego Rivera, Alfonso Fernandez, Marcelo Somos-Valenzuela
abstract: Study region Ñuble Alto basin, Chile. Study focus Analyze and characterize the interaction among meteorological variables, hydrological state variables, and hydrological flux variables before, during, and after the landfall of a Zonal Atmospheric River (ZAR), that caused flooding events between June 22 and 26, 2023, in Ñuble Alto basin in south-central Chile (71.25° W, 36.68° S). We analyzed and characterized the simulated hydrological state and flux variables using a physically-based distributed hydrological model. To improve the initial conditions (ICs), we enhanced the spatiotemporal characterization of precipitation by using a Random Forest model to merge observed data and precipitation products. To increase the reliability of our results, we performed a sensitivity analysis on the input data, ICs, and parameters. In addition, we quantified the uncertainty in the ICs. Finally, we developed a workflow for forecasting streamflow up to 10 days in advance. New Hydrological Insights for the Region The results showed that the event was dominated mainly by liquid precipitation (snowmelt contribution = 0.03), with 75% of the precipitation on the day of the peak event converted to runoff and a soil moisture ratio of 0.97, confirming that extreme liquid precipitation and highly saturated soils jointly controlled the magnitude of the June 2023 floods. In addition, our forecast was able to predict peak streamflow five days in advance.

title: Machine-learning-based regionalization and CMIP6 ensemble projections of precipitation extremes across Pakistan
description: Publication date: August 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology: Regional Studies, Volume 66 Author(s): Muhammad Abbas, Hamd Ullah, Firdos Khan
abstract: Study region Pakistan is a topographically diverse region influenced by both the South Asian monsoon and westerly disturbances. The interaction of these climatic systems produces pronounced spatial and temporal climate variability, and recent decades have witnessed a significant increase in the occurrence and intensity of hydroclimatic extremes. Study focus This study examines historical and future changes in precipitation extremes using an optimized climate modeling framework. Homogeneous climatic regions are identified through a machine learning–based clustering approach that combines elevation, geographical coordinates, and long-term precipitation records. A weighted multi-model ensemble of CMIP6 simulations is constructed using K-fold cross-validation (KFCV) to improve the robustness and regional reliability of climate projections, while Quantile Delta Mapping (QDM) is employed for bias correction. Precipitation extreme indices are evaluated for the historical baseline period (1985–2014) and projected under SSP2–4.5 and SSP5–8.5 scenarios to quantify future changes in extreme precipitation characteristics. New hydrological insights for the region The findings reveal that there is significant spatial and scenario-dependent variability in precipitation extremes across Pakistan. Arid southwestern regions are subjected to more continuous dry days and less overall precipitation, signifying a high risk of drought. In contrast, northern and monsoon-influenced regions reveal significant growth in heavy and very heavy precipitation indices (R20mm, R25mm, R95p, R99p, RX1day, and RX5day), especially with SSP5–8.5, which indicates high floods and flash flood hazards. Trend analysis shows a remarkable increase in extreme rainfall intensity alongside prolonged dry spells in arid areas. From a hydrological perspective, these projected changes imply increasing challenges for reservoir operation, irrigation planning, flood risk management, and drought preparedness. These findings provide region-specific insights to support climate-resilient water management, agricultural planning, and disaster risk reduction in Pakistan.

title: The evaluation, attribution and ecological implications of downstream flow regime changes in a large transboundary basin in Central Asia
description: Publication date: August 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology: Regional Studies, Volume 66 Author(s): Liuxin Xu, Xiaoyan Wang, Huanghe Gu, Yijia Liu, Yi Cao
abstract: Study region The Ili River is a typical transboundary river between China and Kazakhstan. Study focus This study applied the Indicators of Hydrologic Alteration to investigate downstream discharge changes after Kapchagay Reservoir (KR) impoundment. Then a hybrid model was proposed to reconstruct the downstream flow under the hypothetical condition of no human activities in the KR interval catchment (HAKR), and the contribution of HAKR to change in downstream discharge was quantified. New hydrological insights for the region Significant decreases in annual maximum streamflow and summer streamflow were detected during the FS (former-Soviet) period at both stations, where substantially increased annual minimum streamflow at short- and medium- durations and winter streamflow during the PS (post-Soviet) period were observed. The hybrid model increased the Nash-Sutcliffe efficiency by 0.05–0.08 (calibration) and 0.04–0.06 (validation) over extreme gradient boosting (XGBoost). HAKR led to the homogenization of the intra-annual runoff. However, the degree of discharge homogenization induced by HAKR varied with time. Mean annual discharge reduction during the FS period was mainly driven by HAKR at both stations, whereas increased annual streamflow during the PS period was primarily attributed to other factors such as climate change and upstream inflow. HAKR dominated the decrease in summer streamflow regardless of time period or hydrological station. This study can support sustainable water management and provide insights for local ecological restoration in the Ili River.

title: Effects of meteorological reconstruction on hydrological and deep learning streamflow models in Lanyang Watershed, Taiwan
description: Publication date: August 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology: Regional Studies, Volume 66 Author(s): Nhat Thanh Tran, Yuan-Fong Su
abstract: Study region The Lanyang River watershed in northeastern Taiwan, a steep mountainous basin characterized by strong climatic gradients and frequent discontinuities in meteorological observations. Study focus To evaluate how different meteorological reconstruction methods influence watershed scale streamflow simulation using SWAT+ and deep learning models, and to quantify how variable specific reconstruction errors propagate through hydrological forecasts across multiple testing intervals. New hydrological insights for the region Maximum and minimum temperature variables can be reconstructed reliably across stations, whereas precipitation remains the variable with the highest level of uncertainty even when supported by the high-resolution background fields provided by the Taiwan Climate Change Projection Information and Adaptation Knowledge Platform. Reconstruction quality directly affects hydrological behavior, as different machine learning reconstruction approaches modify streamflow timing, seasonal coherence, and event scale variability in distinct ways. Deep learning models, especially Long Short-Term Memory, outperform SWAT+ in temporal efficiency and variability reproduction, typically improving coefficient of efficiency (CE) by about 10–35% compared with SWAT+ model, demonstrating the value of combining improved meteorological reconstruction with advanced forecasting approaches to enhance hydrological reliability in this data scarce mountainous basin.

title: Compound flood hazard and exposure in the Limpopo River Basin: A copula-based climate risk assessment for disaster risk reduction
description: Publication date: August 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology: Regional Studies, Volume 66 Author(s): Marcio Fernando Mathe, Andreas Persson
abstract: Study region The Limpopo River Basin (LRB) is a transboundary catchment in Southern Africa spanning South Africa, Botswana, Zimbabwe, and Mozambique. The lower basin, particularly the Chókwè–Xai-Xai floodplain in Mozambique, is highly flood-prone due to flat topography, climate variability, and rapid agricultural and settlement expansion. Study focus This study presents a climate-informed framework for assessing compound flood hazards in the LRB by coupling a process-based hydrological model with two-dimensional hydraulic simulations and copula-based multivariate statistics. Bias-corrected late-century (2065–2099) climate projections under RCP 4.5 and RCP 8.5 drive hydrological simulations that provide boundary conditions for 2D hydraulic modelling of flood depth, velocity, and duration. Copula functions quantify dependencies among these variables and are used to derive probabilistic compound-hazard classes, which are intersected with land-cover data to assess exposure. New hydrological insights for the region Results reveal moderate, symmetric dependence among flood depth, velocity, and duration, best captured by a Gaussian copula, indicating joint intensification without strong tail asymmetry. Compound hazards increase sharply with return period and emissions pathway, with the Chókwè–Xai-Xai corridor consistently identified as the primary hotspot. Under RCP 8.5, high compound-hazard areas expand non-linearly, approaching ∼48,000 ha for 100-year events, compared with ∼5500 ha under RCP 4.5. Agricultural land shows the greatest exposure, while urban exposure peaks at intermediate return periods. The framework provides decision-relevant evidence for climate-resilient floodplain zoning, infrastructure design, and early-warning prioritisation.

title: Future projections of reference evapotranspiration in semi-arid areas: CMIP6 bias correction, climate trends, and implications for irrigation in the Chichaoua agricultural basin in Morocco
description: Publication date: August 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology: Regional Studies, Volume 66 Author(s): Afaf Bounajra, Abdelhamid Amahouch, Kamal El Guemmat, Khalifa Mansouri
abstract: Study Region The study was conducted in the Haouz plain of Morocco, focusing on five rural municipalities in the province of Chichaoua (Saidate, Sidi M’Hamed Dallil, Majjat, Lamzoudia, and Ahdil), a semi-arid agricultural region located in the foothills of the western High Atlas. Study Focus Climate change is increasing pressure on water resources in semi-arid regions where irrigated agriculture remains essential to food security. This study provides a detailed analysis of future changes in reference evapotranspiration and the meteorological parameters governing it using a bias-corrected CMIP6 multi-model ensemble. Fourteen CMIP6 models were first evaluated over the historical period 1981–2014, and five best-performing models were selected to generate future projections under the SSP245 and SSP585 scenarios. Climate variables were interpolated at the barycenters of 37 agricultural plots distributed across the five municipalities and bias-corrected against ERA5-Land using an empirical non-parametric quantile mapping method. Monthly ET₀ was computed following the FAO-56 Penman-Monteith formulation. Future anomalies and temporal trends were analyzed using Mann-Kendall tests and Sen slope estimators, while the relative contribution of climatic drivers was quantified using standardized multiple regression. New hydrological insights for the region The projections indicate a robust increase in ET₀ across all municipalities, with stronger anomalies during spring and summer and under the SSP585 scenario. Average ET₀ is projected to increase by about 3.5 mm month⁻¹ (≈2.7%) for 2031–2060 under SSP245 and up to about 8.3 mm month⁻¹ (≈6.4%) by 2071–2100 under SSP585. Trend analyses reveal significant positive annual and seasonal trends, intensifying toward the end of the century. Attribution analysis shows that air temperature is the dominant driver, explaining approximately 40–60% of the projected increase in ET₀, while decreasing relative humidity further amplifies atmospheric evaporative demand. These changes imply increasing irrigation water requirements and growing pressure on water resources in the Haouz plain. The results provide scientific evidence to support water planning, crop calendar adjustments, irrigation optimization, and agroclimatic adaptation strategies in semi-arid agricultural systems.

title: Nonlinear trend decomposition for reconstructing terrestrial water storage anomalies across the GRACE/-FO data gap in Mainland China
description: Publication date: August 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology: Regional Studies, Volume 66 Author(s): Shengkun Nie, Wei You, Xiangyu Wan, Xinchun Yang, Ruiqi Zhao, Dongming Fan
abstract: Study region Mainland China. Study focus Bridging the nearly one-year data gap between the Gravity Recovery and Climate Experiment (GRACE) and its Follow-On mission (GRACE-FO) remains a key challenge in terrestrial water storage anomaly (TWSA) studies. However, the adequacy of trend separation in TWSA reconstruction has received limited attention. To address this, a nonlinear trend decomposition framework was developed to isolate continuous, low-frequency trends directly from TWSA time series. Using this framework, we reconstructed the TWSA driven by various hydro-climatic variables (including precipitation, temperature, evapotranspiration, runoff, and CLSM_TWSA), and subsequently conducted comprehensive comparisons and applications. New hydrological insights for the region The nonlinear framework enhances reconstruction accuracy at both basin and grid scales. Across more than 15,000 grid cells nationwide, it outperformed the piecewise linear method, increasing the Pearson correlation coefficient (CC), Nash-Sutcliffe efficiency (NSE), and Kling-Gupta efficiency (KGE) by 2.1%, 4.3%, and 28.4%, respectively, while reducing the normalized root mean square error (NRMSE) by 40.0%. Relative to linear decomposition, the CC, NSE, and KGE improvements reached 5.4%, 10.3%, and 59.3%, respectively, with a 50.0% reduction in NRMSE. Furthermore, the reconstructed TWSA successfully captures a major flood in May 2018 within the gap, and effectively quantifies the relative contributions of human activities and natural climate variability. These prominent advantages achieved in TWSA reconstruction firmly demonstrate the global generalizability and robust application potential of this nonlinear framework.

title: Multi-factor impacts identification and runoff forecasting based on ensemble model: A case study of the source region of Yellow River
description: Publication date: August 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology: Regional Studies, Volume 66 Author(s): Hanxiao Liu, Denghua Yan, Tianling Qin, Xizhi Lv, Shanshui Yuan, Jianming Feng, Jie Lu, Shu Xu, Yuhui Yang, Haoyue Gao
abstract: Study region The Source Region of Yellow River (SRYR), China. Study focus To further enhance the performance and reliability of runoff prediction models base on signal processing, this study incorporated Frequency Analysis (FA) techniques into the ensemble model. By combining FA with the advantages of Variational Mode Decomposition (VMD) and Convolutional Long Short-Term Memory (ConvLSTM) network in feature extraction and multi-factor prediction, the study constructed an ensemble model capable of uncovering the spatiotemporal contribution of various factors to the runoff process and combining the joint effects of multiple hydrological factors. New hydrological insights for the region Based on the observational data from local hydrological and meteorological stations, along with reanalysis dataset, the VMD-FA-ConvLSTM model reached the best prediction result with NSE and KGE of 0.92 and R2 of 0.93, displaying better performance than many traditional models. This affirms that the proposed ensemble model yields higher precision and greater applicability with hydrological signals. Additionally, the study forecasts the future runoff trends in the study area for the next 20 years based on four Shared Socioeconomic Pathway (SSP) scenarios. The results indicate that the average runoff in SRYR from 2021 to 2040 decreases by about 1.55% under the SSP1–2.6 scenario compared with that from 2001 to 2020, whereas the forecasted runoff increases by about 5.22%, 10.77%, and 6.42% under the SSP2–4.5, SSP3–7.0, and SSP5–8.5 scenarios, respectively.

title: Ecosystem service mismatches in a socio-ecological system under chronic hydrological stress: A Water-Energy-Food nexus approach in the Segura River Basin, Spain
description: Publication date: August 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology: Regional Studies, Volume 66 Author(s): Celina Aznarez, Francisco José Segura-Méndez, Anna Sperotto, Adrián López-Ballesteros, Juan Pablo Pacheco, Javier Senent-Aparicio
abstract: Study region Segura River Basin, south-eastern Spain. Study focus This study examines synergies, trade-offs and mismatches in the supply and demand of ecosystem services (ES) in the semi-arid Segura River Basin, a region marked by intense competition among water, energy, and food (WEF) demands. Focusing on four key ES (sediment retention, carbon sequestration, food provisioning, and water provisioning), we applied a spatially explicit, integrative modelling framework that combines the Soil and Water Assessment Tool (SWAT+) for hydrological simulation with the ARIES platform (via k.LAB) for AI-driven semantic modelling of ES. New hydrologic insights Our findings reveal clear synergies and trade-offs shaped by land-use patterns and ecosystem condition. Natural areas, particularly forested and protected zones, function as ES hotspots, critical for regulating services like sediment retention and carbon sequestration, underscoring their importance in WEF sustainability and conservation. Conversely, agricultural and urban areas showed pronounced mismatches: intensive agriculture exacerbates soil degradation and carbon loss, while urban areas place pressure on rural ecosystems where their high demands for provisioning ES are constrained by a limited capacity for regulating ES. By identifying spatial hotspots of intervention this research highlights the value of spatially explicit assessments for understanding ES interactions. These findings demonstrate how land-use intensity and spatial configuration shape hydrological–ecosystem interactions in water-limited regions and provide region-specific insights for managing trade-offs and reinforcing synergies within WEF nexus decision-making under climate and socio-economic pressure.

title: A data-driven approach for assessing future resilience of Trasimeno Lake in central Italy under CMIP6 climate scenarios
description: Publication date: August 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology: Regional Studies, Volume 66 Author(s): Jacopo Dari, Alessia Flammini, Arash Rahi, Renato Morbidelli, Piergiorgio Manciola, Francesco Leopardi, Carla Saltalippi
abstract: Study region Trasimeno Lake, located in central Italy. Study focus After depicting trends currently detectable by historical water level records, an LSTM (Long Short-Term Memory) modeling framework is exploited to produce forecasts up to 2100 of water level fluctuations on the basis of input rainfall and temperature data. Future resilience of the Trasimeno Lake under four representative CMIP6 (Coupled Model Intercomparison Project - Phase 6) scenarios is discussed. Moreover, the impacts on water level forecasts of uncertainties associated with future projections of precipitation and temperature data are quantified. New hydrological insights for the region The lower performance thresholds achieved for RMSE (Root Mean Square Error), BIAS , r (Pearson correlation coefficient), MAPE (Mean Absolute Percentage Error), and MPE (Mean Percentage Error) are 0.30 m, 0.04 m, 0.72, 9.76%, and 1.70%, respectively. The optimized model is subsequently applied to assess future lake-level dynamics under the SSP1–2.6, SSP2–4.5, SSP3–7.0, and SSP5–8.5 scenarios. Projections indicate that water level decline rates may increase by approximately a factor of 2 (SSP2–4.5), 4 (SSP3–7.0), and 7 (SSP5–8.5) compared with the historical trend of −0.008 m/year observed over 1961–2024. Across these scenarios, navigability is expected to become an increasingly recurrent concern, while hydrological conditions comparable to those recorded during the severe 1958 drought are projected to occur by the end of the century. Forecast results are presented together with a quantitative evaluation of the associated uncertainties.

title: Quantifying the potential of cloud water resource exploitation to mitigate water scarcity in Xinjiang
description: Publication date: August 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology: Regional Studies, Volume 66 Author(s): Zepeng Tong, Yong Zeng, Mamtimin Ali, Jing Liu, Yi Chang, Jiangang Li, Xuefeng Cao, Zhanshan Ma
abstract: Study region Xinjiang, Northwest China. Study focus Water scarcity severely constrains Xinjiang’s ecological and socio-economic development. While exploiting cloud water is a strategic solution, quantifying its grid-scale impact on the Water Scarcity Index (WSI) is difficult due to complex land-surface feedbacks. This study develops an integrated gridded framework using a novel Supply-Demand Match Index (SDMI) to quantify the spatial alignment between cloud water potential and water scarcity pressure. By coupling reanalysis data with multi-scenario simulations, the framework establishes a quantitative benchmark for evaluating water allocation efficiency in arid regions. New hydrological insights for the region Scarcity peaks in spring and summer, with high-stress zones (WSI > 2) covering ∼45% of Xinjiang, primarily in the south. We identified a 15–20% precipitation enhancement threshold as critical. At this intensity, mitigation efficiency is optimal in northern Xinjiang during spring and summer, where ΔWSI reaches 1.3–1.7, whereas efficiency is lower in the south and during cold seasons. While summer Cloud Water Path (CWP) varies (0.02–0.13 mm), favorable supply-demand matching (SDMI ≥ 0.7) is concentrated in the north. Findings demonstrate that cloud water exploitation significantly alleviates engineering-induced shortages and ecological water competition, supporting climate adaptation and sustainable water management.

title: Machine learning gap-filling of hydrometeorological time series in south-central Chile: Streamflow, temperature and precipitation
description: Publication date: August 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology: Regional Studies, Volume 66 Author(s): Paul Sandoval-Quilodrán, Guillermo Barrientos, Johan Valdés, Isadora León-Soto, Piero Mardones, Efrain Duarte, Pedro Arriagada, Mauricio Aguayo, Rafael Rubilar
abstract: Study Region This study was conducted in south-central Chile, between 34°S and 41°S, encompassing a hydroclimatically diverse region extending from the Pacific coast to the Andes Mountains. Study Focus We evaluated the non-parametric MissForest algorithm for gap-filling daily hydrometeorological time series from 1980 to 2022 across 57 streamflow, 19 temperature, and 97 precipitation stations with < 20% missing data. Performance was assessed under point and continuous-gap validation schemes using the modified Kling–Gupta Efficiency (KGE), root mean square error (RMSE), and, for precipitation, wet-day occurrence diagnostics. For meteorological variables, ERA5-Land was also evaluated both as an auxiliary predictor within the MissForest framework and as input to a linear regression baseline. New Hydrological Insights for the Region MissForest improved moderately incomplete hydrometeorological records; however, performance depended on variable type and gap structure. Point gaps were reconstructed more accurately than continuous gaps, with median observation-based KGE decreasing from 0.89 ± 0.11–0.66 ± 0.43. Temperature exhibited the most stable performance, whereas precipitation remained sensitive to wet-day occurrence and event timing. Streamflow showed the greatest variability under continuous validation, particularly during high-flow conditions. ERA5-Land enhanced meteorological gap-filling primarily under point validation, yielding near-optimal KGE values for temperature and precipitation while reducing false wet days. Overall, MissForest is most suitable for short, isolated gaps and general daily variability, whereas caution is needed for extremes events and long continuous gaps.

title: An analytical study on the influence of initial soil moisture and meteorological anomalies on flash droughts
description: Publication date: August 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology: Regional Studies, Volume 66 Author(s): Vishal Singh, Tushar Apurv
abstract: Study region The study focusses on 13 major watersheds of India. Study focus Rapid depletion of soil moisture during flash droughts is influenced by complex interactions between initial soil moisture and anomalies in meteorological variables. In this study, numerical experiments are conducted on an analytical land-atmospheric model to gain a conceptual understanding of the influence of initial soil moisture (SM) and meteorological anomalies on flash droughts. The analytical model is calibrated using reanalysis dataset and validated with remotely sensed surface soil moisture. Numerical experiments are conducted on the calibrated model by perturbing the soil moisture at the onset of flash drought events and its impact on flash drought severity are analysed. New hydrological insights for the region It is found that the influence of meteorological anomalies decreases with initial soil moisture in majority of monsoon season flash droughts in humid, sub-humid and semi-arid regions. In these flash droughts, precipitation anomalies are the major contributors to flash droughts. On the other hand, the influence of meteorological anomalies increases with initial soil moisture in flash droughts of arid regions. In these flash droughts, soil moisture depletion is primarily driven by precipitation anomalies in dry antecedent conditions and jointly by precipitation and potential evapotranspiration anomalies in wet antecedent conditions. The insights gained from the analysis highlight the need to use region- and season-specific predictors for accurate prediction of flash drought severity.

title: A hybrid modeling approach for analyzing the risk propagation of water quality deterioration associated with water transfer during flood season
description: Publication date: August 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology: Regional Studies, Volume 66 Author(s): Rui Yang, Wenlong Chen, Yiping Li, Qiong Wu, Xudong Li, Shiqiang Wu, Chen Zhang
abstract: Study region The Nansi Lake is a key storage reservoir for the Eastern Route of the South-to-North Water Diversion Project in China. Study focus As a new practice in existing water diversion projects, inter-basin water transfer during flood season poses new challenges to water quality deterioration risk management. Risk propagation analysis is crucial for risk management, which constitutes a critical determinant for the success of flood-season water transfer operations. Commonly used risk propagation analysis models in water quality deterioration, such as the hydrodynamic-water quality model or data-driven models, either fail to quantify the probability and magnitude of risk propagation, or are limited by insufficient risk associated records. Therefore, a new hybrid modeling approach is designed to overcome the limitations, coupling a Hydrodynamic-water quality model, a C-Vine Copula function, Sine functions, and a Markov chain. It can depict the physical and stochastic processes of water quality deterioration risk, further deciphering its spatial evolution pattern. New hydrological insights for the region The results show that 33∼67% of the lake area is highly likely (97.5%) to suffer water quality deterioration when water transfer scheduled during flood season, and the middle and northern regions of the lake are the hotspots of high risk. Moreover, the risk propagation route is from rivers to the lake and from the south to the north in the lake. From the spatial risk evolution perspective, it maintains low-risk or medium-risk propagation in the south, while exhibiting risk-enhanced propagation in the middle, and maintaining high-risk propagation in the north. Thus, rivers flowing into the north and middle of the lake are the priorities for the risk management. Overall, the study quantitatively reveal the spatiotemporal evolution patterns of water quality deterioration risk, identifying risk hotspots in the lake and the priority areas for risk management. These results provide decision-makers with a scientific basis for optimizing water environment management strategies.

title: The Altered Water Balance: An analysis of urban shallow groundwater level dynamics using a high-density groundwater level observation network for Aalborg, Denmark
description: Publication date: August 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology: Regional Studies, Volume 66 Author(s): Søren Thorndahl, Per Møldrup, Ida Kemppinen Vester, Jesper Ellerbæk Nielsen, Morten Westergaard, Anja Sloth Ziegler
abstract: Study Region: The research is conducted in the Kærby district of Aalborg, Denmark (0.6 km 2 ). Study Focus: Urban areas with shallow groundwater levels face increasing challenges related to groundwater flooding, infrastructure damage, and sewer system infiltration under changing anthropogenic climatic conditions. This study aims to quantify and analyze components of the water balance through a comprehensive, observation-based assessment of shallow urban groundwater variability, using high-resolution data from both citizen science initiatives and automated groundwater level monitoring. New Hydrological Insights for the Region: Over a 4.5-year period, groundwater levels are monitored, revealing seasonal fluctuations of approximately ± 0 . 5 m, and rapid dynamic responses to individual rainfall events, with observed groundwater level increases up to 6 times the corresponding rainfall depth. Cross-correlation analysis links fluctuations to antecedent precipitation and groundwater recharge dynamics. Hydraulic characterization indicates high infiltrability and a narrow vadose zone (0–2 m), explaining rapid saturation and groundwater response. The study quantifies groundwater infiltration into combined sewers using a water budget, showing that in some subcatchments, annual infiltration matches precipitation and exceeds recharge, suggesting lateral inflow and anthropogenically transformed flow regimes. Geospatial interpolation reveals inverted gradients and lowered groundwater levels driven by infrastructure-induced drainage. The study reveals a natural water balance altered by urbanization. The findings highlight the importance of understanding natural and anthropogenic hydrological processes to support climate-resilient urban water management and inform solutions mitigating groundwater impacts.

title: Spatiotemporal propagation of multi-type droughts across different ecological geographical regions in China: Explaining the contributions of atmospheric teleconnection factors
description: Publication date: August 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology: Regional Studies, Volume 66 Author(s): Tingting Wang, Ni Wang, Jiancang Xie, Ganggang Zuo, Xinyue Ke, Xixi Lv
abstract: Study region The study region is China's four major ecological geographical regions Study focus Investigating the cascading propagation effects of different drought types across distinct zones and their influence by atmospheric circulation is crucial for refined regional water resource management. This study systematically characterizes meteorological, hydrological, and ecological droughts. By constructing a comprehensive analytical framework integrating Pearson correlation analysis, wavelet coherence, and interpretable machine learning, we quantified the spatiotemporal coherence of multi-type drought evolution, propagation delays, and the nonlinear driving effects of atmospheric circulation factors. New hydrological insights for the region (1)The propagation of meteorological drought to hydrological drought is significant on the long timescale, while its progression to ecological drought is concentrated on the shorter timescale. (2)Meteorological and hydrological droughts in China's northwest region have continued to worsen, while ecological drought conditions have eased. (3)Hydrological drought follows a meteorological cascade with lags ranging from near-synchronous to approximately 1.5 months. Conversely, ecological drought exhibits decoupling and weaker correlations, manifesting as quasi-instantaneous responses in islands. (4)Among atmospheric circulation factors, ENSO dominates meteorological drought, while sunspot activity emerges as a key associated factor, producing opposing effects. These findings clarify the distinct propagation lags and atmospheric forcing mechanisms across diverse drought types.

title: Integrated geophysical and hydrochemical characterization of geologically and structurally complex groundwater systems in the Mekelle area, northern Ethiopia
description: Publication date: August 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology: Regional Studies, Volume 66 Author(s): Kaleab Adhena Abera, Yonatan Garkabo Doyoro, Tesfamichael Gebreyohannes, Miruts Hagos, Gebremedhin Berhane, Abdelwassie Hussien, Marieke Paepen, Thomas Hermans, Kristine Walraevens
abstract: Study region Mekelle area, northern Ethiopia. Study focus Groundwater in sedimentary basins is influenced by lithology and structural deformation, yet these controls remain poorly understood in many sedimentary basins. This study investigates subsurface architecture and groundwater characteristics using an integrated geophysical and hydrochemical approach. Vertical electrical soundings (VES, DC resistivity method), supported by borehole lithological logs, were used to delineate subsurface units and structures. Major-ion chemistry of 107 groundwater and surface water samples was analyzed to identify hydrochemical facies, water–rock interactions, and anthropogenic influences. New hydrological insights for the region Integrated geophysical and hydrochemical results indicate a structurally controlled, heterogeneous aquifer system with pronounced hydraulic compartmentalization. Geophysical evidence shows that dolerite intrusions mainly behave as resistive units that locally restrict groundwater flow but also serve as productive aquifers where sufficiently fractured. Fault and fracture networks enhance secondary permeability and form preferential groundwater pathways that control aquifer connectivity. Hydrochemical data reflect this structural control, with shallow groundwater dominated by Ca–HCO₃ and Ca–Mg–HCO₃ facies, indicating active recharge conditions. In contrast, Ca–SO₄ facies in deeper groundwater are linked to interaction with gypsum-bearing formations. Elevated nitrate and chloride concentrations in shallow groundwater further indicate influence from surface-derived contamination. These findings demonstrate the strong influence of lithology and structural features on groundwater systems and support improved groundwater management in complex sedimentary basins.

title: Understanding temperature-driven drought intensification in Northeast Asia through multiple drought indices
description: Publication date: August 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology: Regional Studies, Volume 66 Author(s): Ghani Rahman, Umar Farooq, Subin Kang, Joo-Heon Lee, Hyun-Han Kwon
abstract: Study region Northeast Asia encompasses diverse hydroclimatic conditions across nine Köppen climate zones. Study focus This study investigates the spatiotemporal dynamics of drought intensification in Northeast Asia (NEA) using the Standardized Precipitation Index (SPI), the Standardized Precipitation-Evapotranspiration Index (SPEI), and the Evaporative Demand Drought Index (EDDI). We apply a multi-index framework with General Linear Modeling (GLM) to assess the effects of climatic variables on drought severity. Drought characteristics are assessed at 1-, 3-, 6-, and 12-month timescales using ERA5 reanalysis data from 1974 to 2023. New hydrological insights Trend analysis reveals a shift from seasonal droughts before 2004 to prolonged events. Northern China and Mongolia emerge as major long-term drought hotspots. SPEI and EDDI consistently display greater sensitivity to temperature-driven droughts than SPI. GLM analysis shows that minimum temperature has the strongest association with drought intensification (η²p = 0.046–0.105), followed by dewpoint temperature (η²p = 0.037–0.077). EDDI demonstrates the highest sensitivity in minimum temperature (η²p = 0.105), whereas SPI exhibits the weakest response (η²p = 0.046). Rising temperature and solar radiation intensify droughts, while higher dewpoint temperature reduces severity. These findings indicate that drought intensification in NEA is primarily associated with interacting temperature and energy-related processes rather than precipitation alone. This multi-index, climate-stratified approach provides a mechanistic understanding of water–energy interactions driving drought variability, supporting monitoring and adaptive water management under climate change.

title: Beyond static DPSIR: A CDPSIR-path dependency synthesis explaining 60 Years of groundwater policy failure in Rafsanjan, Iran
description: Publication date: August 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology: Regional Studies, Volume 66 Author(s): Elham Golkar, Ali Bagheri
abstract: Study region The Rafsanjan Plain aquifer in arid south‑eastern Iran (rainfall: 137 mm/year) has been a “forbidden plain” since 1974. Despite five decades of policies, groundwater levels declined 23.5 m (1983–2019), with extraction (∼683 MCM/year) far exceeding recharge (∼432 MCM/year). Pistachio cultivation (∼80,000–100,000 ha) accounts for ∼503 MCM/year of extraction. Study focus Why have all policies since 1966 failed to halt decline? Moving beyond static assessments, we conduct a root‑cause analysis using a novel synthesis: Grounded Theory within an extended CDPSIR (Context‑Driving Forces‑Pressures‑State‑Impacts‑Responses) framework, combined with path dependency theory and causal loop diagrams. We trace 160 years (1861–present) across five periods to identify critical junctures, self‑reinforcing mechanisms, and lock‑in effects. New hydrological insights for the region The crisis is not a technical failure but path‑dependent lock‑in from export‑oriented pistachio monoculture. Five critical junctures (1861 cotton boom, 1921 pistachio transition, 1962 Land Reform, 1979 Revolution, 1982 Fair Water Distribution Law) activated self‑reinforcing mechanisms—increasing returns, learning, coordination, adaptive expectations, institutional complementarity, and technological lock‑in—that raised deviation costs. By the 1980s, only wells running dry provided any corrective force. Past policies (drip irrigation, forbidden plain, legalization amnesties) failed because they were overwhelmed by lock‑in structures. We derive transferable conditions and propose agrivoltaics on non‑productive orchards to break the lock‑in.

title: A physics-informed data-driven framework for 30m soil moisture estimation from multi-source datasets
description: Publication date: August 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology: Regional Studies, Volume 66 Author(s): Yixin Jiang, Jun Zhang, Ziyi Cai, Yulin Chen, Sa Wei, Miao Liu, Ze Jiang, Yy Yi Liu, Wenchao Ma
abstract: Study region Hebei Plain, Hebei Province, China. Study focus Accurate, high-resolution soil moisture (SM) estimation is crucial for field-scale hydrological modeling, agricultural management, and climate research, yet current approaches remain limited by sparse in situ observations and coarse spatial resolution of satellite-based products. To address these challenges, this study develops a robust physics-informed data-driven framework for estimating 0–10 cm SM at 30 m resolution by integrating multi-source datasets through spatiotemporal data fusion and machine learning models. New hydrological insights The proposed framework consists of three key methodological advances. First, to bridge the spatial resolution gap and ensure high-quality inputs, we systematically evaluated four spatiotemporal data fusion algorithms, identifying Enhanced Spatial and Temporal Adaptive Reflectance Fusion Model (ESTARFM) as superior for maintaining consistent spectral and spatial representation of surface reflectance and temperature at 30 m resolution, achieving the highest r and the lowest RMSE, EDGE and LBP values across most cities. Second, we constructed a hybrid feature set coupling physically interpretable indices, such as the Temperature Vegetation Dryness Index (TVDI), with multi-source reanalysis and topographic data, ensuring an efficient predictor set through multicollinearity diagnosis. Third, using Optuna-driven automated hyperparameter optimization, we benchmarked ten machine-learning algorithms, finding that Random Forest (RF) exhibited the most robust performance with r of 0.921, R² of 0.835, RMSE of 2.512% and near-zero bias (−0.041%) against in situ SM observations. The resulting 30 m soil moisture maps effectively resolve fine-scale landscape heterogeneity. Overall, this study provides a robust, scalable, and application-ready ML-based framework for generating SM products with high spatiotemporal resolution, offering valuable support for regional water resource management and drought monitoring in complex agricultural landscapes.

title: Graph transformer-based flood susceptibility mapping: Application to the French Riviera and railway infrastructure under climate change
description: Publication date: August 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology: Regional Studies, Volume 66 Author(s): Sreenath Vemula, Filippo Gatti, Pierre Jehel
abstract: Study region The French Riviera watershed in southeastern France (≈2650 km²) extends from steep alpine headwaters to a densely urbanised Mediterranean coast traversed by the SNCF rail network, and has suffered repeated destructive floods, including the 1994 and 2010 Var floods, the 2015 Côte d’Azur flood, and the 2020 Storm Alex. Study focus Traditional machine-learning (ML) approaches achieve high point-wise metrics (AUC-ROC, accuracy) but fail to produce the spatially coherent predictions needed for reliable infrastructure-exposure estimation. We propose a graph transformer (GT) architecture incorporating a feature-similarity graph regularised by Laplacian positional encodings and spatial attention, and benchmark it against six traditional ML models, and show that these point-wise metrics alone are insufficient and should be complemented by spatial autocorrelation metrics (Moran's I, Geary's C) when evaluating multi-class flood predictions. Using topographic, hydrologic, and environmental features, we further project flood susceptibility and railway-track exposure for 2050 under RCP 4.5 and RCP 8.5 scenarios. New hydrological insights for the region The GT achieved AUC-ROC ≈ 0.974 (slightly below XGBoost ≈ 0.990) but substantially improved spatial coherence (Moran’s I ≈ 0.612, Geary’s C ≈ 0.473 versus XGBoost 0.409 and 0.589, and RF 0.474 and 0.523). Its smooth boundary delineation produced markedly different distributions: the GT classified 6.2% of the area as very-high with 35.6% railway exposure, versus 55–57% very-high area and 46–52% railway exposure for ML models; the GT very-high extent closely matches the 172.6 km² historical inundation inventory. Accumulated Local Effects analysis confirmed elevation, stream power, and precipitation as dominant monotonic drivers consistent with flood hydrology. Scenario-conditional projections for 2050 under RCP 4.5 (Q95) and RCP 8.5 (Q95) indicate very-high areas could expand to ≈ 28% and ≈ 36.3%, with railway exposure reaching ≈ 64% and ≈ 67.4%. The GT framework provides a replicable blueprint for regions seeking spatially accurate flood susceptibility mapping.

title: Prediction of regional water and land resource carrying capacity using support vector machines supported by Monte Carlo coupled black-winged kite optimization algorithm
description: Publication date: August 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology: Regional Studies, Volume 66 Author(s): Kun Cheng, Xingyang Zhang, Nan Sun, Bao Zhu
abstract: Study region Heilongjiang Province in Northeast China. Study focus Studies on the carrying capacity of water and land resources (WLRCC) provide a critical basis for achieving the efficient use of these resources in the region. Traditional forecasting methods only calculate specific values at a single point in the future, failing to reflect the uncertainty of future water and land resource carrying capacity. Furthermore, the classification criteria for water and land resource carrying capacity are neither comprehensive nor accurate. To address these issues, this study employs a combined objective-subjective approach to establish classification criteria and proposes a forecasting method based on the coupling of Monte Carlo simulation with the Black Kite algorithm to optimize support vector machines, thereby resolving the issue of one-dimensional forecasting results for regional water and land resource carrying capacity. New hydrological insights for the region The carrying capacity of water and land resources in Heilongjiang Province will continue to show an overall upward trend from 2030 to 2040. Concurrently, the standard deviation—a measure of system variability—will increase significantly, with Jiamusi, Shuangyashan, and Qitaihe exhibiting the most pronounced increases, with standard deviation growth rates reaching 288%, 283%, and 198%, respectively. The findings of this study can provide guidance for the management and development of regional water and land resources.

title: Benchmark-guided insights into hybrid process-based-deep learning models for continental-scale streamflow prediction across the United States
description: Publication date: August 2026 Source: Journal of Hydrology: Regional Studies, Volume 66 Author(s): Daneti Arun Sourya, Velpuri Manikanta, Maheswaran Rathinasamy
abstract: Study region United States of America (USA) Study focus Recent studies have explored hybrid process-based (PB) - deep learning (DL) approaches, yet it remains unclear when hybridisation is necessary and whether it systematically improves performance across diverse catchments. To address this, we propose a benchmark-guided evaluation framework applied to 531 U.S. catchments. A suite of 17 simple benchmark (BM) models was used to establish a catchment-specific performance critical range based on modified Kling-Gupta Efficiency (KGE). Models exceeding the benchmark were classified as skilful, while those below were considered underperforming. This study identifies catchments where PB hydrological models outperform BM expectations, while DL, i.e., long short-term memory (LSTM) model, underperform relative to BM expectations. For these catchments, we investigate whether integrating PB model outputs of soil moisture (SM) and/or discharge (Q) into LSTM architectures improves streamflow simulation. The objective is to determine under which catchment conditions hybrid PB-LSTM configurations provide measurable performance gains and which PB-derived inputs are most effective. New hydrological insights for the region The hybrid configurations produced clear improvements over standalone LSTMs, with nearly 30% of catchments shifting from fair to good performance categories. Feature importance analysis indicates that PB-derived SM consistently enhances prediction skill by improving representation of hydrologic memory and subsurface dynamics. These results demonstrate that benchmark-guided hybridisation provides a systematic and interpretable strategy for improving data-driven streamflow modelling across diverse hydroclimatic conditions.

title: Revisiting the hydrogeological water balance of Banyoles Lake (northeast Catalonia, Spain): Implications for sustainable groundwater exploitation
abstract: Abstract Balancing groundwater exploitation with ecological preservation requires robust conceptual models, particularly in karst systems where aquifer–lake interactions are complex and highly sensitive to human and climatic pressures. Banyoles Lake (northeast Catalonia, Spain) is a groundwater-fed karstic-tectonic system of exceptional ecological value, yet its hydrogeological functioning remains insufficiently understood. This study revisits its water balance by integrating meteorological, limnological, hydrochemical, and isotopic data into an updated hydrogeological analysis. Results indicate that regional groundwater inflow from the Banyoles–Alta Garrotxa system contributes ~11.4 × 10 6 m 3 /year, equivalent to ~54% of total inputs to the lake, while local recharge through runoff and shallow aquifers represents only ~23%. Outflows are dominated by drains (~16.2 × 10 6 m 3 /year, 77% of total) and evaporation (~2.3 × 10 6 m 3 /year 11%). The refined conceptual model highlights the predominance of upward vertical flows from confined limestone aquifers through a karstified gypsum formation, which govern lake recharge and explain the observed sulphate enrichment of lake water. This framework challenges conventional interpretations that treat the lake surface as a constant-head boundary, instead recognizing it as a dynamic hydrogeological unit controlled by potentiometric head of the aquifer beneath, which has seldom been addressed in the hydrogeological literature. By clarifying the processes sustaining Banyoles Lake hydrogeology, this report provides a novel conceptual framework essential for sustainable groundwater governance under increasing climatic stress.
